{"artifact_digest":"sha256:0ede06f3692e3038c4ba7c22962c47f338f7d10e91475181413be989d65aeb79","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/0e/0ede06f3692e3038c4ba7c22962c47f338f7d10e91475181413be989d65aeb79.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:5dc013e697cd629fbd40ddf7b02f7b0d5cee7442f9a7dae5c7eeaca3b264d76f","bundle_entry_key":"t336-w727-c011","bundle_id":"population.w727-t336-psd-kernel-tail-006","claim_kind":"theorem","conditions":[],"domain":"Gaussian processes; kernel approximation; Bayesian prediction","draft":"w727/bundle_006.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:learning.transformers:draft-t336-w727-c011-psd-kernel-tail-gp-kl","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# C011 v1: a PSD kernel-tail interface for noisy GP prediction

Kind: bound. Target: none (reviewer-authorized kernel-truncation continuation).
Status: proof (unaudited). No novelty claim. This is a conditional interface;
it does not supply an RBF rank-versus-error theorem or a raw-input encoder.
The solver corollary depends on unaudited C010 v1. The kernel perturbation
lemma below is independent of that construction. C004's accepted feature
perturbation argument is background, not re-audited here.

## 1. Statement and hypotheses

Let k and k_p be real symmetric PSD kernels on X. Assume k(x,x)<=1 and
h=k-k_p is also a PSD kernel with sup_x h(x,x)<=eta, eta>=0. These conditions
imply 0<=k_p(x,x)<=1 and |h(x,z)|<=eta by PSD Cauchy-Schwarz.
Let the observation noise variance be s>0. Fix any context of length l<=n,
with arbitrary locations, a query x_*, and labels |y_i|<=B. Here n is a
nonnegative integer and B>=0. These are pointwise GP conditioning formulas;
a probabilistic interpretation assumes an exogenous design and the stated GP
prior and independent Gaussian observation noise, not arbitrary adaptive design.

Let (m,v) and (m_p,v_p) be the noisy-query posterior mean and variance for
k and k_p respectively, conditioning on the same context labels. Then

    |m-m_p| <= C_mu eta,
    0 <= v-v_p <= C_v eta,
    s <= v_p <= v <= s+1,
    C_mu = n B/s + n^2 B/s^2,
    C_v = 1 + 2n/s + n^2/s^2.

The lower bound on v-v_p requires h PSD, not merely entrywise error control.
The constants deliberately use n even when l<n.

## 2. Mean and absolute variance perturbation

For l>0 write K=(k(x_i,x_j)), u=(k(x_i,x_*)), a=k(x_*,x_*),
A=K+sI, and similarly K_p,u_p,a_p,A_p. PSD gives A,A_p>=sI.
Kernel Cauchy-Schwarz and the tail bound imply

    ||u||,||u_p|| <= sqrt(l), ||y||<=sqrt(l)B,
    ||u-u_p||<=sqrt(l)eta, ||K-K_p||_op<=l eta,
    ||A^{-1}||,||A_p^{-1}||<=1/s.

The matrix norm bound follows from the Frobenius norm (l^2 entries).
The resolvent identity, with its sign explicit, is

    A^{-1}-A_p^{-1}=A^{-1}(A_p-A)A_p^{-1},
    ||A^{-1}-A_p^{-1}||<=l eta/s^2.

Split m-m_p as

    (u-u_p)^T A^{-1}y + u_p^T(A^{-1}-A_p^{-1})y.

Cauchy-Schwarz gives (l B/s+l^2 B/s^2)eta <= C_mu eta.
For the quadratic posterior correction use the exact decomposition

    u^T A^{-1}u-u_p^T A_p^{-1}u_p
      =(u-u_p)^T A^{-1}u
       +u_p^T A^{-1}(u-u_p)
       +u_p^T(A^{-1}-A_p^{-1})u_p.

Its absolute value is at most (2l/s+l^2/s^2)eta.
Since |a-a_p|<=eta and v=s+a-u^T A^{-1}u, this proves the absolute
variance error bound. When l=0, m=m_p=0 and v-v_p=a-a_p; the assertions
follow directly without zero-dimensional inverse conventions.

## 3. Why the variance is ordered

For w in R^l define

    F_k(w)=a-2w^T u+w^T(K+sI)w.

Completing the square gives min_w F_k(w)=a-u^T A^{-1}u=v-s.
Also F_k(w) is the sum of the nonnegative joint-kernel quadratic form
(-w,1)^T K_joint (-w,1) and s||w||^2. Thus v>=s, and w=0 gives v<=s+a.
The same statements hold for k_p. For every w,

    F_k(w)-F_{k_p}(w)=(-w,1)^T h_joint (-w,1)>=0.

Taking minima preserves this inequality: v-s>=v_p-s. Combined with
Section 2 and a<=1 this proves every variance assertion in Section 1.
This argument also covers the empty context directly. It does not infer
posterior ordering solely from an ordering of the context covariance block.

For necessity of the tail-PSD premise for this ordering argument, on a
singleton domain choose constant kernels k=1/2 and k_p=1. Both are PSD and
their uniform difference is 1/2, but the empty-context noisy variances are
s+1/2 and s+1, in the reverse order. This example violates h PSD.

## 4. Joint forward-KL allocation

Let eps>0. Choose a PSD tail certificate satisfying

    eta <= min(1/2, sqrt(s eps)/(2(1+C_mu)),
                      s sqrt(2 eps)/(2 C_v)).

Suppose a finite-kernel predictor outputs (mhat,vhat) with

    s<=vhat<=v_p,
    |m_p-mhat|<=sqrt(s eps)/2,
    v_p-vhat<=s sqrt(2 eps)/2.

The preceding bounds imply

    |m-mhat|<=sqrt(s eps),
    0<=v-vhat<=s sqrt(2 eps).

Write z=(v-vhat)/vhat>=0. The exact forward Gaussian KL is

    KL(N(m,v)||N(mhat,vhat))
      = (z-log(1+z))/2 + (m-mhat)^2/(2 vhat).

For all z>=0, z-log(1+z)<=z^2/2: the difference of right minus left
vanishes at zero and has derivative z^2/(1+z)>=0. Consequently

    KL <= (v-vhat)^2/(4s^2)+(m-mhat)^2/(2s) <= eps.

No triangle inequality for KL is used.

## 5. Conditional transformer corollary and remaining obstruction

If k_p has a supplied p-dimensional feature map with norm at most one,
C010 v1 at accuracy eps_c=eps/4 supplies the two error inequalities in
Section 4 and s<=vhat<=v_p. Indeed its residual delta budget implies
|m_p-mhat|<=sqrt(s eps_c) and
v_p-vhat<=s sqrt(2 eps_c). Its exact-output boundary cases also satisfy them.
Its token and size claims remain those of C010: p fixed auxiliary tokens,
width 9p+4, at most four heads, depth 2T+3. This is a dependency on that
unaudited construction, not a new independent audit or an architecture change.

The hardest remaining step for an explicit RBF result is a primary-source
certificate giving a finite p with uniform PSD diagonal-tail <=eta on the
specified compact domain, followed by the intended input-encoding choice.
A Mercer L1 tail or an average-case kernel error alone does not meet this
uniform hypothesis. [Thm 206 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $\cA_N=\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)$ be a sequence of $L$-Lipschitz algorithms, as in Definition~\ref{d:Lip}. Let $\chi^N\equiv \chi_{\cA_N}$, and assume further that
    \[
    \frac{1}{L^2} \le (\chi^N)'(p) \le L^2
    \]
for all $0\le p\le 1$. Consider a Brownian bridge terminating at $(\bG,\bg^\aux)$, and let $\vX^N\equiv (\vX^{\RomI:\RomIII},X^\Ising)^N$ be the resulting $\R^4$-valued process defined by \eqref{e:X.decomp}--\eqref{e:vX}. Let $\vX^{\trunc,N}$ be the truncation given by Definitions~\ref{d:trunc}--\ref{d:buckets.Ising}, and let $\vY^N$ be the spatial rerandomization of $\vX^{\trunc,N}$ from Definitions~\ref{d:rerand} and \ref{d:rerand.Ising}. Let $\vD^N$ and $\vQ^N$ denote respectively its discrete-time drift and covariation with respect to the filtration given by the buckets --- see Definitions~\ref{d:D} and \ref{d:Q} below ($\vD^N$ is $\R^4$-valued, while $\vQ^N$ is $\R^{10}$-valued).

We make
$(\vY,\vD,\vQ)^N$ into continuous-time $\R^{18}$-valued processes by taking the linear interpolation on each time interval $[q_d,q_{d+1}]$. We also denote the piecewise constant variants $(\vY,\vD,\vQ)^{\bullet,N}$, so for example $\vY^{\bullet,N}(t)=\vY^N(q_d)$ for all $[q_d,q_{d+1})$. Let $\mu_{\bG^N}$ be the law of $(\vY,\vD,\vQ)^N$ conditional on the disorder $\bG^N$, and let $\Q_N$ be the law of $\mu_{\bG^N}$. Let $\mu_{\bullet,\bG^N}$ be the law of $(\vY,\vD,\vQ)^{\bullet,N}$ conditional on the disorder $\bG^N$, and let $\Q_{\bullet,N}$ be the law of $\mu_{\bullet,\bG^N}$. Note that 
$\mu_{\bG^N},\mu_{\bullet,\bG^N}$ are probability measures on the space of $\R^{18}$-valued paths equipped with the uniform topology, and we equip the space of such measures with the topology of weak convergence.

If $N\to\infty$ with parameters satisfying Assumption~\ref{a:params}, then the measures $\Q_N$ are tight, with respect to the weak convergence topology described above. If $\Q_N\to\Q$ along an integer subsequence $N\to\infty$, then we have $\Q_{\bullet,N}\Rightarrow\Q_N$ along the same subsequence. For any subsequential limit $\Q$, if $\mu\sim\Q$ and $(\vY,\vD,\vQ)\sim\mu$, then $\vY$ is a semimartingale with drift $\vD$ and covariation $\vQ$. Moreover, $Y^\RomI$ is a finite-variation process while $Y^{\RomII}$, $Y^{\RomIII}$, and $Y^{\Ising}$ are martingales: this means $D^\sigma\equiv0$ for $\sigma\in\{\RomII,\RomIII,\Ising\}$, and $Q^{\RomI,\sigma}\equiv0$ for all $\sigma$. We also have $Q^{\sigma,\Ising}\equiv0$ for $\sigma\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII\}$. 

All the analogous statements hold with $\vY^{\frozen,N}$, $\vY^\frozen$, $\vD^\frozen$, $\vQ^\frozen$ in place of $\vY^N$, $\vY$, $\vD$, $\vQ$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Thm 206 of arXiv:2608.29416

[Theorem 28 of arXiv:2504.02435, 'Poisson-Voronoi percolation in higher rank'] Let $G$ be a connected higher rank semisimple real Lie group and $(X,d_X)$ be its symmetric space.
    Then for every $\eps>0$, $D\ge 0$ and $N\in \mathbb{N}$ there is $\lambda_0>0$ and $R>0$ such that 
    $$\mathbb{P}\left(\forall 1\le i\le N \ \exists z_i\in \mathcal{B}_R(o) \text{ such that }  \mathcal{B}_D(z_i)\subseteq C^{(\lambda)}_i\right)>1-\eps$$
    for every $0<\lambda\le \lambda_0$.

[Lemma l:mostly-lc-var of arXiv:2605.03718, 'Potential Hessian Ascent III:\\ Sampling the Sherrington--Kirkpatrick Model at $\beta < 1/'] Let $L, \alpha>0$. 
    Consider a probability measure $\mu$ with density $p$ on $\mathbb R$ such that $-(\log p)''(u)$ such that 
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $-(\log p)''(u)\geqslant -L$ everywhere, and
        \item $-(\log p)''(u)\geqslant \alpha$ except on a set of Lebesgue measure $M$.
    \end{enumerate}
    Fix $A>0$. 
    Then $\mu$ has log-Sobolev constant at least $\fc{\alpha}{2} \exp\pa{-\fc{M^2(L+\alpha)^2}{\alpha}}$. 
    
    Thus, $\mathop{{}\boldsymbol{\mathrm{Var}}}(\mu)\leqslant \fc2\alpha \exp\pa{\fc{M^2(L+\alpha)^2}{\alpha}}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Variance bound for mostly log-concave distribution

body:
[Lemma 16 (EOT with partial observations) of arXiv:2607.19176, 'Exponential Convergence of the Sinkhorn Algorithm for the Schrödinger Bridge with Regime S'] Let $X, Y, X', Y'$ be Borel spaces, and let $F : X \to X'$ and $G : Y \to Y'$ be measurable maps. Define
\[
T := F \otimes G : X \times Y \to X' \times Y', \qquad T(x,y) = (F(x),G(y)).
\]
Let $R \in \mathcal P(X \times Y)$ and $R' := T_{\#}R \in \mathcal P(X' \times Y')$. Given $\mu \in \mathcal P(X')$ and $\nu \in \mathcal P(Y')$, consider
\[
\inf \bigl\{ H(\pi \mid R) : \pi \in \mathcal P(X \times Y),\ T_{\#}\pi \in \Pi(\mu,\nu) \bigr\}
\qquad \text{and} \qquad
\inf_{\gamma \in \Pi(\mu,\nu)} H(\gamma \mid R').
\]

Assume that the right-hand problem admits a minimizer $\gamma^{*} \in \Pi(\mu,\nu)$ and that there exist measurable functions
$f : X' \to \mathbb R \cup \{-\infty\}$ and $g : Y' \to \mathbb R \cup \{-\infty\}$ such that
\[
\frac{\mathrm d \gamma^{*}}{\mathrm d R'}(x',y') = \exp\bigl(f(x') + g(y')\bigr).
\]

Then the left-hand problem admits a minimizer $\pi^{*} \in \mathcal P(X \times Y)$ satisfying
$T_{\#}\pi^{*} = \gamma^{*}$ and
$
H(\pi^{*} \mid R) = H(\gamma^{*} \mid R').
$
Moreover, $\pi^{*}$ admits the representation
\[
\frac{\mathrm d \pi^{*}}{\mathrm d R}(x,y) = \exp\bigl(f(F(x)) + g(G(y))\bigr).
\]

Own work, proof (unaudited), W719-T295-C013 v1; conditional method record, no specialist novelty asserted. For arbitrary time-varying symmetric positive definite H_t, fixed real vector a, b_t>0, mu_t>=0, eta_t>0 with H_t>=mu_t I+b_t aa^T and eta_t H_t<=I, the recursion d_(t+1)=(I-eta_t H_t)d_t-eta_t a u_t, y_t=a^T d_t, obeys ||d_T||^2+sum_(t<T) eta_t mu_t||d_t||^2+sum_(t<T) eta_t b_t y_t^2 <=||d_0||^2+sum_(t<T) eta_t u_t^2/b_t. In particular, equal-start input u_t=beta r_t, constant b_t=beta>0 and constant step give temporal l2 gain at most one. No commutativity or positive scalar response products are required. Proof: eta_t H_t<=I gives H_t^(-1)>=eta_t I. Expanding the new squared norm and using this inequality cancels the mixed input/state terms, giving ||d_next||^2<=||d||^2-eta d^T H d+eta u^2 a^T H^(-1)a. The directional lower bound gives a^T H^(-1)a<=1/b and d^T H d>=mu||d||^2+b(a^T d)^2. Sum over time. This implication is pathwise, even when matrices depend on the trajectory. For phase retrieval the exact full-gradient secant Q_t=(1/m)sum_j[p_j^2+p_j q_j+q_j^2-g_j^2]a_j a_j^T and scalar input u_t=((q_i^2-g_i^2)q_i)/m fit the recursion, with p_j=a_j^T x_t, q_j=a_j^T z_t, g_j=a_j^T x_*. The required directional curvature/smoothness of Q_t at linear m and the weighted input budget are unproved. The temporal l2 estimate does not supply a temporal supremum bound or all-time relative incoherence; a bounded input alone gives only a sqrt(T) pointwise estimate from this inequality. No actual nonlinear GD convergence is established.

[Lemma 10 of arXiv:2608.12070, 'Central limit theorems for a heavy-tailed subcritical Galton-Watson process with state-dep'] Let $\{Z,Z_i:i\ge 1\}$ be a sequence of i.i.d. non-negative random variables and satisfies 
$$\P(Z>x)\sim \frac{l(x)}{x^\alpha\Gamma(1-\alpha)},\quad x\to\infty, $$  
where $0<\alpha<1$, $l(x)$ is a function slowly varying at infinity.  Then as $n\to \infty$,  
\begin{align*}
\frac{S_n}{a_n}:=\frac{\sum\limits_{i=1}\limits^n Z_i}{a_n}\stackrel{d}{\rightarrow}   T,
\end{align*}
where  $\{a_n\}$ is an integer-valued sequence satisfying $na_n^{-\alpha}l(a_n)\to1$, and $T$ is a positive random variable with Laplace transform $\mathrm{e}^{-s^\alpha}$ ($s>0$). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 26 (Continuous-time coalescence--meeting comparison) of arXiv:2607.13183, '2607.13183'] Let $(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ be a finite irreducible reversible continuous-time chain on
$N\ge2$ states with generator $\mathcal L=P-I$, where $P$ is an irreducible
reversible transition kernel with stationary law $\pi$. Let
$t_{\rm meet}^{\rm ct}$ be
the worst-case expected meeting time of two independent copies, and let
$t_{\rm mix}^{\rm ct}$ be its total-variation mixing time. For the standard
continuous-time coalescing process driven by this chain and started with one
particle at every state,
\begin{equation}
        \E\coal
        \le C_{\rm KMS}\,t_{\rm meet}^{\rm ct}
        \left(1+\sqrt{\frac{t_{\rm mix}^{\rm ct}}
        {t_{\rm meet}^{\rm ct}}}\log N\right),
\end{equation}

body:
[Introthm 1 (Convergence via asymptotic equivalence with the target) of arXiv:2608.03353, '\bfseries A Direct Route to Markov Chain Convergence\\[2mm] \Large via Asymptotic Equivale'] Let $(\XX,\XXA)$ be a measurable space and  $T$ be a Markov kernel with invariant probability measure $\pi$ on
$(\XX,\XXA)$: $T \circ \pi = \pi$.
For $x \in \XX$ and $n \in \N$ let
\[
  T^{n}_{x}
  = T^{n}_{x,\acp{\pi}} + T^{n}_{x,\sgp{\pi}}
\]
be the Lebesgue decomposition of $T^{n}_{x}$ with respect to $\pi$, and assume that
for each $n$ the absolutely continuous part admits a density
$t_{n}(y \mid x)$ with respect to $\pi$ that is jointly measurable in $(x,y)$ --- as
it does, for instance, whenever $\XXA$ is countably generated.
Assume further:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},nosep,topsep=3pt,leftmargin=2.4em,itemsep=3pt]
  \item \emph{(asymptotic absolute continuity)} for every $x \in \XX$ the mass of the
        part of $T^{n}_{x}$ that $\pi$ does not see vanishes:
        \[
          T^{n}_{x,\sgp{\pi}}(\XX) \;=\; \sing\bigl( T^{n}_{x} \bigm| \pi \bigr)
          \;\longrightarrow\; 0
          \qquad\text{as } n \to \infty ;
        \]
  \item \emph{(asymptotic domination of the target)} for $\pi$-almost every
        $x \in \XX$ the mass of the part of $\pi$ that $T^{n}_{x}$ does not see
        vanishes:
        \[
          \sing\bigl( \pi \bigm| T^{n}_{x} \bigr) \;\longrightarrow\; 0
          \qquad\text{as } n \to \infty ,
        \]
        where $\sing(\pi\mid\alpha)$ denotes the mass of the part of $\pi$ that is
        singular with respect to $\alpha$.
\end{enumerate}
Then $\pi$ is the unique invariant probability measure of $T$, and
\[
  \sup_{A \in \XXA}\bigl| (T^{n}\circ\mu)(A) - \pi(A) \bigr| \;\longrightarrow\; 0
  \qquad\text{as } n \to \infty,
\]
for every probability measure $\mu$ on $(\XX,\XXA)$.

Conversely, each of the two hypotheses is implied by that conclusion, so the two
together characterise it. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Convergence via asymptotic equivalence with the target

body:
[Thm monotone-match of arXiv:2605.13004, 'Orientation in Poisson Cluster Processes via Imaginary Bispectra'] Assume that $h$ has a nonincreasing representative on $(0,\infty)$. Define $\rho_h$ for a.e. $x\in\mathbb{R}$ by
\begin{equation}
\rho_h(x):=\frac{h(|x|)-m(h*\check h)(x)}{2-m}.
\end{equation}
Then $\rho_h$ admits an even probability-density representative on $\mathbb{R}$; in particular, $\widehat{\rho_h}$ is real-valued. Let
\begin{equation}
p_n:=\frac{(2n-2)!}{2^{2n-1}n!(n-1)!}\,\frac{[m(2-m)]^n}{m},\qquad n\ge1.
\end{equation}
Then $\sum_{n\ge1}p_n=1$. If $K$ has law $\mathbb{P}(K=n)=p_n$, if $Y_1,Y_2,\ldots$ are i.i.d. with any even density representative of $\rho_h$, if $K$ is independent of $Y_1,Y_2,\ldots$, and if
\[
Y=\sum_{k=1}^K Y_k,
\]
then $Y$ has an even density $\varphi_h$ and
\begin{equation}
\widehat{\varphi_h}(\omega)=\frac{1-\sqrt{1-m(2-m)\widehat{\rho_h}(\omega)}}{m},
\end{equation}
where the square root is the positive real square root. Indeed, since $\rho_h$ is even, $\widehat{\rho_h}$ is real-valued, and
\[
1-m(2-m)\widehat{\rho_h}(\omega)
=
|1-m\widehat h(\omega)|^2
\ge (1-m)^2>0,
\]
so the branch is unambiguous. Moreover,
\begin{equation}
|1-m\widehat{\varphi_h}(\omega)|^2=|1-m\widehat h(\omega)|^2.
\end{equation}
Consequently, because $\varphi_h$ is even, the stationary branching-cluster process with the same immigrant rate $\nu$ and offspring density $m\varphi_h$ is reversible, and hence serves as an undirected comparison null in our sense. It has the same total intensity and full Bartlett spectrum as the one-sided model with offspring density $mh$. In the subcritical branching setting the complete reduced covariance measures are finite, so uniqueness of Fourier--Stieltjes transforms implies that these complete reduced covariance measures also agree. In addition, Corollary~(cor:symmetric-branching-real of the paper) shows that the reversible match has real complete and factorial third-order Fourier--Stieltjes transforms. If the reduced third factorial cumulant has an $L^1(\mathbb{R}^2)$ density, then its factorial bispectral density is real; the complete third cumulant differs only by the usual real diagonal Fourier--Stieltjes terms from Lemma~(lem:ordinary-factorial-bispectrum of the paper). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Thm 5 (The resultant distribution method) of arXiv:2608.06576, 'The Resultant Distribution Method: Universality for $p$-adic Random Matrices and Polynomia'] Fix a finite set $S\subseteq\Z_{>0}$.

\begin{enumerate}
\item
\emph{(Determination by resultant distributions).}
The law of a random polynomial $P^S\in\mathscr{P}^S$ is determined by the
distributions
$$
\val\left(\Res(P^S,Z)\right),
\qquad
Z\in\mathscr{P}^S.
$$
In particular, two random polynomials in $\mathscr{P}^S$ having the same
resultant-valuation distribution for every fixed $Z\in\mathscr{P}^S$ have
the same law.

\item
\emph{(Weak convergence from resultant distributions).}
Let $P_1^S,P_2^S,\ldots$ be random polynomials in $\mathscr{P}^S$. Suppose
that, for every fixed $Z\in\mathscr{P}^S$,
$$
\val\left(\Res(P_n^S,Z)\right)
$$
converges in distribution, and suppose that the sequence of random degrees
$\deg P_n^S$ is tight, in the sense that
$$
\lim_{D\to\infty}\sup_{n\geq 1}
\mathbf{P}\left(\deg P_n^S>D\right)=0.
$$
Then there exists a random polynomial $P_\infty^S\in\mathscr{P}^S$ such
that
$$
P_n^S\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}P_\infty^S.
$$

\item
\emph{(Convergence of root statistics and their expectations).}
Assume the hypotheses of the previous item, and let $P_\infty^S$ be the
resulting limiting random polynomial. Let $K_1,\ldots,K_m$ be finite
extensions of $\Q_p$, and let
$$
U\subseteq
\mc{O}_{K_1}^{\new}
\times\cdots\times
\mc{O}_{K_m}^{\new}
$$
be clopen. If $P_\infty^S$ is almost surely squarefree, then
$$
Z_U(P_n^S)\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}Z_U(P_\infty^S).
$$
If, in addition, the degree-tightness assumption is strengthened to
$$
\lim_{D\to\infty}\sup_{n\geq 1}
\E\left[
(\deg P_n^S)^m
\mathbf{1}_{\{\deg P_n^S>D\}}
\right]
=
0,
$$
then
$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}
\E\left[Z_U(P_n^S)\right]
=
\E\left[Z_U(P_\infty^S)\right].
$$
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: The resultant distribution method

body:
[Proposition 60 (Weak law of large numbers) of arXiv:2608.03353, '\bfseries A Direct Route to Markov Chain Convergence\\[2mm] \Large via Asymptotic Equivale'] Assume \hyp{A}{A}, \hyp{P}{P} and \hyp{S}{S}.
Then for every bounded measurable map $f : \XX \to \R$ and every $\mu \in \Prob$,
\[
  \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} f(X_{k}) \;\longrightarrow\; \int_{\XX} f \dd\pi
  \qquad\text{in } L^{2}(\Prb_{\mu}), \text{ hence in } \Prb_{\mu}\text{-probability.}
\]
More precisely, if $\int_{\XX} f \dd\pi = 0$ and $\sup_{x \in \XX}|f(x)| \le 1$ ---
to which the general case reduces by an affine change of $f$ --- then, with the
numbers
\[
  u_{m} := \int_{\XX} \bigl| (T^{m}f)(x) \bigr|\,\pi(\dd x),
  \qquad
  v_{j} := \tv{T^{j}\circ\mu - \pi}
  \qquad (j,m \in \Nz),
\]
where $(T^{m}f)(x) := \int_{\XX} f \dd(T^{m}\circ\delta_{x})$, one has the explicit
variance bound
\begin{equation}
  \Ex_{\mu}\Bigl[ \Bigl( \frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} f(X_{k}) \Bigr)^{\!2} \Bigr]
  \;\le\; \frac{1}{n} + \frac{2}{n}\sum_{m=1}^{n-1} u_{m} + \frac{4}{n}\sum_{j=0}^{n-1} v_{j}
  \qquad (n \in \N),
  
\end{equation}
in which $u_{m} \to 0$ and $v_{j} \to 0$, so that the right-hand side tends to $0$.

[Theorem Wallis 3' of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] We have the following integration formula over the sphere $S^{N-1}_\mathbb R\subset\mathbb R^N$, with respect to the uniform measure, valid for any exponents $k_i\in\mathbb N$,
$$\int_{S^{N-1}_\mathbb R}|x_1^{k_1}\ldots x_N^{k_N}|\,dx=\left(\frac{2}{\pi}\right)^{\Sigma(k_1,\ldots,k_N)}\frac{(N-1)!!k_1!!\ldots k_N!!}{(N+\Sigma k_i-1)!!}$$
with $\Sigma=[odds/2]$ if $N$ is odd and $\Sigma=[(odds+1)/2]$ if $N$ is even, where ``odds'' denotes the number of odd numbers in the sequence $k_1,\ldots,k_N$.

body:
[Theorem thm-phase of arXiv:2605.03385, 'Quantum Loewner evolution in quantum natural time: phases and Markov properties'] QLE$(\gamma^2, \eta)$ exhibits three phases:
\begin{itemize}
    \item (Dilute phase) For $\gamma \in (\sqrt3 - 1,2)$ and $\eta = \frac3{\gamma^2} - \frac12$, we have $\mathcal{A}^\gamma_\phi(K_\mathcal{S}) = 0$ a.s. 
    \item (Swallowing phase) For $\gamma \in (2\sqrt3-2,2)$ and $\eta = \frac{3\gamma^2}{16} - \frac12$, a.s.\ the function $s \mapsto \mathcal{A}^\gamma_\phi(K_s)$ is strictly increasing, has derivative zero almost everywhere, and is continuous at $\mathcal{S}$. Moreover $K_\mathcal{S} = \overline \mathbb{D}$.
    \item (Space-filling phase) For $\gamma \in (0,4/3)$ and $\eta = \frac{3\gamma^2}{16} - \frac12$, a.s.\ we have $\mathcal{S} = \mathcal{A}^\gamma_\phi(\mathbb{D})$ and $\mathcal{A}^\gamma_\phi(K_s) = s$ for all $s \in [0,\mathcal{S}]$, and $K_\mathcal{S} = \overline \mathbb{D}$.
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem thm-phase of arXiv:2605.03385

[Proposition Strandabove3 of arXiv:2604.07227, 'Transition probabilities of step-reinforced random walks'] Let $S$ be a generalized SRRW on a Euclidean space with reinforcement parameter $\alpha \in [0,1)$ and step distribution $\mu$ being genuinely d-dimensional. Then for any $r>0$, there exists a positive constant $C=C(r,\mu,\alpha)$ such that for all $n\geq 1$,

body:
[Thm cor: i.i.d. of arXiv:2411.01104, 'Gaussian universality of $p$-adic random matrix products via corners'] Let $A_1,A_2,\ldots\in\GL_n(\mathbb{Q}_p)$ be i.i.d. random matrices whose distributions are invariant under both left- and right-multiplication by $\GL_n(\mathbb{Z}_p)$. Let $\lambda(k)=(\lambda_1(k),\ldots,\lambda_n(k))=\SN(A_1\ldots A_k)$. For every $1\le i\le n$, let $A_1^{(i)}\in\Mat_{(n-i+1)\times n}(\mathbb{Q}_p)$ denote the submatrix of $A_1$ consisting of the last $n-i+1$ rows and all $n$ columns. 
\begin{enumerate}[left=0pt]
\item (Strong law of large numbers) Suppose that for all $1\le i\le n$, the expectation $\mathbb{E}|\SN(A_1^{(i)})|<\infty$ exists. Then we have
\begin{align}(\frac{\lambda_1(k)}{k},\ldots,\frac{\lambda_n(k)}{k})\rightarrow &(\mathbb{E}|\SN(A_1^{(1)})|-\mathbb{E}|\SN(A_1^{(2)})|,\ldots,\nonumber\\
&\mathbb{E}|\SN(A_1^{(n-1)})|-\mathbb{E}|\SN(A_1^{(n)})|,\mathbb{E}|\SN(A_1^{(n)})|)\nonumber\end{align}
almost surely as $k$ goes to infinity. 

\item(Central limit theorem) In addition to the conditions above, assume that for all $1\le i\le n$, the expectation $\mathbb{E}|\SN(A_1^{(i)})^2|<\infty$ exists. Then we have weak convergence
$$\frac{(\lambda_1(k)-k\mathbb{E}|\SN(A_1^{(1)})|+k\mathbb{E}|\SN(A_1^{(2)})|,\ldots,\lambda_n(k)-k\mathbb{E}|\SN(A_1^{(n)})|)}{\sqrt{k}}\Rightarrow N(0,L\Sigma L^T)$$
as $k$ goes to infinity, where $L^T\in\Mat_{n\times n}(\mathbb{Z}_p)$ is the transpose of the matrix
$$L=\begin{pmatrix}1 & -1 & & &\\ & 1 & -1 & &\\ & & \ddots & \ddots &\\ & & & 1 & -1\\ & & & & 1\end{pmatrix}$$

and $\Sigma=\Cov_{1\le i,j\le n}(|\SN(A_1^{(i)})|,|\SN(A_1^{(j)})|)$ is the covariance matrix.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Thm cor: i.i.d. of arXiv:2411.01104

body:
[Definition 1 ($q$-Demazure product) of arXiv:2604.06532, 'Random permutations from $q$-Demazure products'] Fix $q \in [0,1]$.
The \emph{$q$-Demazure product} of a simple transposition $s_i$ and a permutation
$\sigma \in S_n$ is the random permutation
\[
  s_i \cdot_q \sigma \;:=\;
  \begin{cases}
    s_i\sigma, & \text{if } \ell(s_i\sigma) > \ell(\sigma),\\[6pt]
    \begin{cases}
      s_i\sigma & \text{with probability } q,\\
      \sigma    & \text{with probability } 1-q,
    \end{cases}
    & \text{if } \ell(s_i\sigma) < \ell(\sigma),
  \end{cases}
\]
where $\ell(\sigma) = \#\{(a,b) : a < b,\, \sigma(a) > \sigma(b)\}$ is the number of
inversions of $\sigma$.
The $q$-Demazure product of a word $s_{i_1}\cdot_q \cdots \cdot_q s_{i_k}$ is defined by applying the rule
left-to-right with independent randomness at each step.
At $q=0$ this reduces to the \emph{Demazure product}; at $q=1$ it is the ordinary
group multiplication in $S_n$.
title: $q$-Demazure product

[Corollary 26 (Descent-wise cancellation polynomials) of arXiv:2609.01882, '\textbf{Coxeter Descents and Parabolic Homotopy Colimits}\\[2mm] \large A Hochster-type de'] For every $0\le d\le r$ there is a polynomial $\Theta_{r,d}(z)\in\mathbb N[z]$ such that
\[
\Psi_{r,d}(z)=
\begin{cases}
1+(1+z)\Theta_{r,0}(z),&d=0,\\
(1+z)\Theta_{r,d}(z),&0<d<r,\\
z^{r-1}+(1+z)\Theta_{r,r}(z),&d=r.
\end{cases}

body:
[Corollary 6 (Algorithmic pointwise upper bound for estimator decoding) of arXiv:2606.07931, 'Pointwise Complexity for Gaussian Fields:\\Upper Envelopes, Algorithmic Lower Bounds, and '] Work in the Gaussian location setup of Theorem~\ref{thm:nn-comparison}.
Thus \(T\) is embedded as \(\{v_t:t\in T\}\) in a Hilbert space,
\[
d(s,t)=\|v_s-v_t\|,
\qquad
Y=v_\Theta+\tau Z,
\qquad
X_t:=\langle Z,v_t\rangle ,
\]
where \(Z\) is standard Gaussian. Let \(\widehat\Theta=\widehat\Theta(Y)\) be a
decoder satisfying the approximate remainder comparison
\begin{equation}
\|Y-v_{\widehat\Theta(Y)}\|^2
\le
\|Y-v_\Theta\|^2+\varepsilon_{\rm up}
\end{equation}
under the joint law of \((\Theta,Y)\), for some nonnegative random variable \(\varepsilon_{\rm up}\).  For instance, \eqref{eq:comparison-decoder-condition} implies this condition with \(\varepsilon_{\rm up}=\varepsilon_{\rm cmp}\).

Suppose that a deterministic envelope \(A:T\to[0,\infty)\) satisfies
\begin{equation}
\mathbb P_Z\bigl\{\forall t\in T:\ |X_t|\le A(t)\bigr\}\ge 1-\delta .
\end{equation}
Then, with probability at least \(1-\delta\) under the joint law of
\((\Theta,Y)\),
\begin{equation}
d(\Theta,\widehat\Theta(Y))^2
\le
2\tau\bigl(A(\Theta)+A(\widehat\Theta(Y))\bigr)+\varepsilon_{\rm up}.
\end{equation}
Consequently, if
\[
D_T:=\sup_{s,t\in T}d(s,t)<\infty,
\]
then
\begin{equation}
\mathbb E d(\Theta,\widehat\Theta(Y))
\le
\mathbb E\sqrt{2\tau\bigl(A(\Theta)+A(\widehat\Theta(Y))\bigr)+\varepsilon_{\rm up}}
+\delta D_T .
\end{equation}
In particular, after adjoining an anchor point \(t_0\) with \(v_{t_0}=0\) and
\(X_{t_0}=0\) if necessary, one may take
\[
A(t)=A_{\mu,r_0,s_0}(t;\delta)
\]
from \eqref{eq:absolute-pointwise-gaussian} in
Theorem~\ref{thm:pointwise-gaussian}, with the prior extended to
\(T\cup\{t_0\}\), for instance as \(\bar\mu=\frac12\delta_{t_0}+\frac12\mu\), which changes the pointwise functional on \(T\) only by universal constants. This yields a pointwise-complexity upper bound for the
estimation risk. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Algorithmic pointwise upper bound for estimator decoding

body:
[Conj conjPhaseTransitionBehavior of arXiv:2411.18563, 'Lower tails for triangles inside the critical window'] For each $\eta$ sufficiently small (including the interval $[0,\eta_\ell)$), the following hold:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item There is a unique non-analytic point $c^\ast= c^\ast(\eta)$ of the rate function $\varphi_{\eta}(c)$ on the positive real axis.
        \item The phase transition is a first-order phase transition: the first derivative of $\varphi_{\eta}(c)$ is discontinuous at $c^\ast$.
        \item The max-cut fraction is an order parameter for the phase transition and jumps at the critical point: $g_{\eta}(c) =1/2$ for $c<c^\ast$, while $g_\eta(c) > 1/2$ for each $c \ge c^\ast$.
        \item At the critical point, the `ordered' state dominates: there exists $\varepsilon>0$ so that with $p=c^\ast/\sqrt{n}$, whp the max-cut fraction of $G(n,p)$ conditioned on the lower-tail event is at least $1/2+\varepsilon$. 
    \end{itemize} (Stated as a conjecture by the paper; open unless the paper says otherwise.)
title: Conj conjPhaseTransitionBehavior of arXiv:2411.18563

body:
[Lemma Lem:ResultsContinuants of arXiv:2609.01501, 'Singularities of star cluster algebras'] \phantomsection 
	
	\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
		\item 
		For $ k \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0} $,
		we have
		$ P_{2k+1} (0, \ldots, 0 ) = 0 $,
		$ P_{2k+1} (0, \ldots, 0, z_n ) = (-1)^k z_n $,
		and $ P_{2k} (0, \ldots, 0) = P_{2k} (0, \ldots, 0, z_n) = (-1)^k $.
		
		\item
		\color{black} 
		For $ j \in \{ 1, \ldots, n \} $, we have
		\[
			\frac{\partial P_n(z_1, \ldots, z_n)}{\partial z_j} 
			= P_{j-1}(z_1, \ldots, z_{j-1})\cdot P_{n-j}(z_{j+1}, \ldots, z_n) 
			\ .
		\]
		
		\item 
		There is no point at which two consecutive continuant polynomials vanish, i.e.,
		\[  
			V ( P_n (z_1, \ldots, z_n), P_{n-1} (z_1, \ldots, z_{n-1}) ) = \emptyset 
			\ .
		\]
		
		
		\item 
		The variety $ \mathfrak X := V(P_n (z_1, \ldots, z_n ) + \lambda) \subseteq \ensuremath{\mathbb{A}}_\kappa^n $ with $ \lambda \in \kappa $ is singular if and only if
		$ n = 2 k $ is even and $ \lambda = (-1)^{k+1} $.
		In the singular case,  $ \Sing ( \mathfrak{X} ) = V (z_1, \ldots, z_n )  $ and $  \mathfrak{X} $ has an isolated singularity of type $ A_1 $ at the origin.   
	\end{enumerate}

[Theorem 9 (LDP via finite-dimensional LDP and exponential tightness) of arXiv:2607.12666, 'Sample-path Large deviations for \\Scheduled Arrival Processes with Unpunctuality'] Let $\{X^{(n)}\}$ be a sequence of random elements of $D([0,T])$. Suppose that, for every $0<t_1<\cdots<t_m\le T$, the finite-dimensional projections
\[
\bigl(X^{(n)}(t_1),\ldots,X^{(n)}(t_m)\bigr)
\]
satisfy an LDP in $\R^m$ with speed $n$ and good rate function $I_{t_1,\ldots,t_m}$, and that $\{X^{(n)}\}$ is exponentially tight in $D([0,T])$. Then $\{X^{(n)}\}$ satisfies an LDP in $D([0,T])$ with speed $n$ and good rate function
\[
I(\phi)
=
\sup_{m\ge1}\;
\sup_{0<t_1<\cdots<t_m\le T}
I_{t_1,\ldots,t_m}\bigl(\phi(t_1),\ldots,\phi(t_m)\bigr).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: Let G = (V, E) be a finite graph. An independent set is a subset S of V such that no two vertices of S are joined by an edge of E; the independence number alpha(G) is the maximum size of an independent set in G. A clique is a subset K of V such that every two distinct vertices of K are joined by an edge of E; the clique number omega(G) is the maximum size of a clique in G. Note that omega(G) = alpha(G-complement), where G-complement is the complement graph. [standard, e.g. Diestel, Graph Theory]
title: Independence Number and Clique Number of a Graph

[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] For a block-transposed Wishart matrix $\widetilde{W}=(id\otimes t)W$ we have, in the $n=\beta m\to\infty$ limit, with $\beta>0$ fixed, the formula
$$\frac{\widetilde{W}}{d}\sim\gamma_{\beta}^1$$
with $\gamma_\beta^1$ being the shifted version of the semicircle law $\gamma_\beta$, with support centered at $1$.

[Theorem 2 (Equivariant flow matching via symmetrization) of arXiv:2608.26961, 'Gromov--Monge Flow Matching for Equivariant Graph Generation'] Let \(\pi\in\mathrm{c}_{\R^D}(\mu,\nu)\). Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item For every \(G\)-equivariant field \(v\),
\(J_\pi(v)=J_{\pi^G}(v)\). The field
\(v^{\pi^G}\) can be chosen \(G\)-equivariant and minimizes
\(J_\pi\) over all \(G\)-equivariant fields.
\item If the ODE of a \(G\)-equivariant field has a unique flow
\(\gamma_t\), then it induces a well-defined quotient flow
\(
\bar\gamma_t([x])\coloneqq[\gamma_t(x)].
\)
For every \(\eta\in\mP_2(\R^D)\),
\(
\mathfrak q_\sharp\gamma_{t,\sharp}\eta
=\bar\gamma_{t,\sharp}\mathfrak q_\sharp\eta.
\)
Hence the projected curve depends only on the quotient law
\(\mathfrak q_\sharp\eta\), not on the representative lift chosen at time
\(0\).
\item If \(G\subset\mathfrak S_D\) permutes coordinates and
\(\nu\) is supported on
\(\mathcal A^D\), \(\mathcal A=\{a_1,\ldots,a_M\}\), let
\[
q_t^{\ast,\pi^G,d}(n\mid z)
\coloneqq
\mathbb P_{\pi^G}(X'_d=a_n\mid Z_t=z).
\]
For \(g\in G\), let \(g\cdot d\) be the coordinate determined by
\((gz)_{g\cdot d}=z_d\). These coordinate posteriors can be chosen
equivariantly for \(d\in[D]\) and \(n\in[M]\):
\[
q_t^{\ast,\pi^G,g\cdot d}(n\mid gz)
=q_t^{\ast,\pi^G,d}(n\mid z).
\]
They minimize \( J_\pi^{\rm coord}\) over equivariant coordinate
kernels and recover \(v^{\pi^G}\) through
\eqref{eq:euclidean-fm-coordinate-endpoint-mixture}.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Equivariant flow matching via symmetrization

[Lemma lem:tiling of arXiv:2608.12954, 'Rainbow percolation'] $\mathsf H$ and $\mathsf H^\star$ are connected and locally finite, with
maximal degrees $5$ and $8$ respectively, and:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $\mathsf H$ has exactly one end: for every finite $F\subseteq V$
  the graph $\mathsf H-F$ has exactly one infinite component;
\item[(ii)] $\mathsf H$ is planar, and the boundaries of its bounded faces
  are exactly the triangles $\{(k,2j),(k,2j+1),(k+1,j)\}$ and the
  quadrilaterals $\{(k,2j-1),(k,2j),(k+1,j),(k+1,j-1)\}$, $k\in\mathbb{N}_0$,
  $j\in\mathbb Z$; the edges of $\mathsf H^\star\setminus\mathsf H$ are exactly the
  diagonals of the quadrilateral faces.
\end{enumerate}

Own-work draft; T419-C022 v2, proof (unaudited); no novelty claimed. Let r>=2, p=r+1, m>=r+1. Let Delta be a real m-by-p matrix with exactly r nonzero singular values, each equal to 1. Let G be r-by-p with independent standard normal entries. Set B_0=0, A_0=sG and perform simultaneous factor GD on q=||BA-Delta||F^2/2:

 B_next=B-eta(BA-Delta)A^T,
 A_next=A-eta B^T(BA-Delta).

For any 0<rho<1 define the positive, deterministic constants

 d=rho/3, c0=10r/d, a=1/(c0 sqrt(r)), b=sqrt(rp/d), xi=d^3/(9p),
 K0=sqrt(r)(b^2+1+4sqrt(r)), gamma=1/(6K0+1),
 T=ceil[log(8sqrt(r)/xi)/(gamma a^2)],
 Q=sqrt(r)/a, Q1=Q+1, b1=b+1,
 L=b1^2+2Qb1+1, H=Q1(Q1b1+sqrt(r)), Z=b1+Q,
 E=gamma H T exp(gamma L T), S=max{1,(8ZE/xi)^(1/4)}.

For every s>=S choose the single fixed step eta=gamma/s^2. With probability at least 1-rho, simultaneously for all integer t>=T,

 ||B_t A_t-Delta||F <= exp[-gamma xi^2(t-T)/(32s^4 K0)].

In particular, for every 0<eps<1 the residual is at most eps once

 t >= T + ceil[(32s^4 K0/(gamma xi^2)) log(1/eps)].

The step and the success event do not depend on eps. The scale threshold is finite but extremely conservative; no efficient numerical magnitude or useful practical threshold is asserted. This is a whole family at every rank, with a proper rank bottleneck on both input and output sides, but only condition number 1 and input co-rank 1. General aspect ratios, general spectra, moderate scales, expected risk and Target 2 are not asserted.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:0e0f575a67ab79154e4b9f27c0969e1aaa9de2b2dc30ab02f9279406be0b9960","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/0e/0e0f575a67ab79154e4b9f27c0969e1aaa9de2b2dc30ab02f9279406be0b9960.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:27e46e009fb20504f772ea97691212bc0ba71127310ba78fe9e8bc95d4eed499","bundle_entry_key":"corank-large-scale","bundle_id":"population.t419-corank-one-all-ranks-large-scale-gd-20261020","claim_kind":"theorem","conditions":[],"domain":"LoRA population GD and large unbalanced initialization","draft":"w705/bundle_011.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:optimization.lowrank:lora-corank-one-input-all-ranks-large-gaussian-scale-gd-rate","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# T419-C022 v2: large-scale GD for the proper input co-rank-one family

Kind: narrowed. Target: 1. Status: proof (unaudited). No novelty claimed.

This uses the published sufficient-deficiency-margin idea of Min, Tarmoun, Vidal and Mallada (arXiv:2105.06351, Corollary 5, p.10), the known invariant output span (Zhang, Liu and Chen, arXiv:2502.01235, Theorem 3.1/C.10), and the discrete imbalance/descent method of Du, Hu and Lee (arXiv:1806.00900, Appendix B, Claim B.1). None of these citations alone supplies the theorem below. Kunin et al., arXiv:2406.06158, Appendix A.2.4 and Theorem 4.2, give related unbalanced flow results under different structural assumptions. Prior searches did not establish novelty. The hardest step here is the finite-time fast/slow comparison in section 4, with constants that close its induction before using the endpoint bounds. It is proved below, but has not received an independent audit.

## Statement

Let r>=2, p=r+1, m>=r+1. Let Delta be a real m-by-p matrix with exactly r nonzero singular values, each equal to 1. Let G be r-by-p with independent standard normal entries. Set B_0=0, A_0=sG and perform simultaneous factor GD on q=||BA-Delta||F^2/2:

 B_next=B-eta(BA-Delta)A^T,
 A_next=A-eta B^T(BA-Delta).

For any 0<rho<1 define the positive, deterministic constants

 d=rho/3, c0=10r/d, a=1/(c0 sqrt(r)), b=sqrt(rp/d), xi=d^3/(9p),
 K0=sqrt(r)(b^2+1+4sqrt(r)), gamma=1/(6K0+1),
 T=ceil[log(8sqrt(r)/xi)/(gamma a^2)],
 Q=sqrt(r)/a, Q1=Q+1, b1=b+1,
 L=b1^2+2Qb1+1, H=Q1(Q1b1+sqrt(r)), Z=b1+Q,
 E=gamma H T exp(gamma L T), S=max{1,(8ZE/xi)^(1/4)}.

For every s>=S choose the single fixed step eta=gamma/s^2. With probability at least 1-rho, simultaneously for all integer t>=T,

 ||B_t A_t-Delta||F <= exp[-gamma xi^2(t-T)/(32s^4 K0)].

In particular, for every 0<eps<1 the residual is at most eps once

 t >= T + ceil[(32s^4 K0/(gamma xi^2)) log(1/eps)].

The step and the success event do not depend on eps. The scale threshold is finite but extremely conservative; no efficient numerical magnitude or useful practical threshold is asserted. This is a whole family at every rank, with a proper rank bottleneck on both input and output sides, but only condition number 1 and input co-rank 1. General aspect ratios, general spectra, moderate scales, expected risk and Target 2 are not asserted.

## 1. One Gaussian event; no independence multiplication

Write v0 for a fixed unit vector spanning ker(Delta), so Delta^T Delta=I-v0 v0^T. The following three events hold jointly with probability at least 1-3d=1-rho:

 sigma_min(G)>=a, ||G||F<=b, and |z^T v0|^2>=xi,

where z is any unit representative of the one-dimensional ker(G). Its sign does not matter.

For completeness the smallest-singular-value bound needs only a square submatrix, without a random-matrix theorem. Let H0 be the first r columns of G. It is nonsingular almost surely. For its j-th column, let delta_j be its distance from the span of the other columns. Conditional on those other columns, delta_j has the distribution |N(0,1)|. The j-th row of H0^{-1} has norm delta_j^{-1}, by its unit pairing with column j and zero pairing with all other columns. If sigma_min(H0)<a then ||H0^{-1}||F>1/a, and some row has norm >1/(a sqrt(r)). Thus some delta_j<a sqrt(r). A union bound and the normal density bound give

 Pr[sigma_min(H0)<a] <= r sqrt(2/pi) a sqrt(r) < d,

since a=d/(10r^(3/2)). Also GG^T dominates H0 H0^T, so the same lower bound holds for sigma_min(G). Markov gives Pr[||G||F>b]<=rp/b^2=d.

Gaussian right orthogonal invariance implies that the kernel line of G is uniformly distributed over unoriented lines in R^p. Indeed G O has the same law as G for every orthogonal O, and its kernel is O^T ker(G); the rotation-invariant probability on lines is the line of a uniform sphere vector. Consequently |z^T v0| has the law of |g_1|/||g|| for a standard Gaussian vector g in R^p, after rotating v0 to the first coordinate. This distributional representation makes no claim about independence from the preceding two events. The normal density bound gives Pr[|g_1|<d/2]<=d/sqrt(2pi)<d/2; Markov gives Pr[||g||^2>2p/d]<=d/2. Outside their union,

 |g_1|/||g|| >= d^(3/2)/(2sqrt(2p)) > d^(3/2)/(3sqrt(p))=sqrt(xi).

Thus the third event fails with probability at most d. A union bound over all three events finishes this section. Henceforth fix any G in their intersection.

## 2. Global descent and a factor bound

Use the deterministic boundedness lemma C014, whose proof is appended to the queued card and saved in proofs/C014_empirical_boundedness.md. Here C=I, D=W=Delta, q0=r/2,

 J=||A0 A0^T||F+1 <=s^2 b^2+1,
 R=||Delta||F+sqrt(2q0)=2sqrt(r),
 K=sqrt(r)(J+2R)<=s^2 K0,

where the last inequality uses s>=1. Since K0>=4r and gamma=1/(6K0+1), eta=gamma/s^2 <=1/(1+r). Also

 eta(6K+1) <= gamma(6K0+1/s^2) <=1.

Both hypotheses of C014 hold. Therefore, at every iterate,

 q_next<=q-(eta/2)||grad q||F^2,
 ||B||F^2+||A||F^2<=K<=s^2 K0.

These bounds hold before and after the fast phase. C014 proves them without assuming bounded iterates: descent is first proved on the segment to the proposed step in a factor ball of twice the current radius, then the telescoping Gram drift returns the endpoint to the original radius. Merely assuming a local Lipschitz constant along the unknown trajectory would not suffice.

## 3. The exactly solvable frozen-feature phase

Keep the input factor fixed at G and let Ubar_0=0,

 Ubar_next=Ubar-gamma(Ubar G-Delta)G^T.

Let M=GG^T, P=G^T M^{-1}G=I-zz^T, and Ustar=Delta G^T M^{-1}. Then

 Ubar_t=Ustar[I-(I-gamma M)^t],
 ||Ubar_t||F<=||Ustar||F<=sqrt(r)/a=Q.

Indeed M is symmetric with eigenvalues in [a^2,b^2], and gamma b^2<1, so the bracket has operator norm at most 1. Its multiplication on the right of Ustar does not require Ustar and M to commute. An SVD of G also shows

 ||Ubar_t G-Delta P||F <=sqrt(r)(1-gamma a^2)^t
                              <=sqrt(r) exp(-gamma a^2 t).

The irreducible frozen residual satisfies

 ||Delta(I-P)||F^2=||Delta z||^2
                 =1-(v0^T z)^2 <=1-xi.

Consequently its norm is at most sqrt(1-xi)<=1-xi/2. At t=T the transient term is at most xi/8, and the triangle inequality yields

 ||Ubar_T G-Delta||F<=1-3xi/8.

This is the place where p=r+1 and the equal singular values are used. A generic random row space in higher input co-rank need not achieve a frozen residual strictly below the smallest nonzero singular value.

## 4. Actual GD stays close for the finite fast phase

Set U_t=s B_t, V_t=A_t/s and epsilon=s^{-4}. Direct substitution in simultaneous GD gives the exact recurrences

 U_next=U-gamma(UV-Delta)V^T,
 V_next=V-gamma epsilon U^T(UV-Delta).

The initial conditions are U0=Ubar0=0, V0=G. Define

 d_t=||U_t-Ubar_t||F+||V_t-G||F.

Whenever d_t<=1, the current factors obey ||U||F<=Q1 and ||V||F<=b1. Expanding the difference of the fast gradients gives the exact matrix identity

 (UV-Delta)V^T-(Ubar G-Delta)G^T
 = (U-Ubar)VV^T + Ubar(VV^T-GG^T) - Delta(V-G)^T.

Using ||VV^T-GG^T||F <= (||V||op+||G||op)||V-G||F, ||Delta||op=1, and ||Ubar||F<=Q, its norm is at most

 b1^2 ||U-Ubar||F + (2Qb1+1)||V-G||F <=L d_t.

The slow gradient satisfies

 ||U^T(UV-Delta)||F <=Q1(Q1 b1+sqrt(r))=H.

The two updates therefore give

 d_(t+1) <=(1+gamma L)d_t+gamma epsilon H

at every current point with d_t<=1. Starting at d0=0, induction yields for 0<=t<=T

 d_t <=epsilon gamma H t exp(gamma L t) <=epsilon E<=xi/(8Z)<1.

To avoid a circular bootstrap: the displayed estimate at time t only invokes d_(t-1)<=1; the geometric-sum solution of the recurrence bounds the proposed next distance by epsilon E, which is strictly less than 1. Thus each new endpoint is admissible before the next recurrence is used. The last inequality is exactly the definition of S and s>=S.

Moreover

 ||UV-Ubar G||F <=||U-Ubar||F ||V||op + ||Ubar||op ||V-G||F
                 <=Z d_t<=xi/8.

At time T the actual population residual e_T therefore satisfies

 e_T=||B_T A_T-Delta||F=||U_T V_T-Delta||F<=1-xi/4.

## 5. Persistent positive margin and one fixed-step rate

Write Delta=U_D S0 where U_D has r orthonormal columns and S0 S0^T=I_r. Because B0=0 and both Delta and B_t lie in col(U_D), the B update preserves that subspace. Thus B_t=U_D R_t for a square r-by-r matrix R_t at every time, and

 e_t=||R_t A_t-S0||F.

Global descent from section 2 implies e_t<=1-xi/4 for all t>=T. Weyl's singular-value inequality then gives sigma_min(R_t A_t)>=xi/4, where the minimum here is the smallest of the r singular values of the r-by-p product. For square R_t and any A_t,

 sigma_min(R_t A_t)<=sigma_min(R_t)||A_t||op.

For example apply the transpose to a unit vector minimizing ||R_t^T x||. Since ||A_t||op<=s sqrt(K0), it follows that

 sigma_min(R_t)>=xi/(4s sqrt(K0)).

The A-gradient is R_t^T(R_t A_t-S0), so

 ||grad q||F^2 >=||grad_A q||F^2
               >=xi^2 e_t^2/(16s^2 K0).

Using q=e_t^2/2 and section 2 gives

 e_(t+1)^2 <=[1-gamma xi^2/(16s^4 K0)]e_t^2.

The bracket is in (0,1), as follows directly from s>=1, xi<1 and gamma<1. Iterating and using sqrt(1-x)<=exp(-x/2), and e_T<=1, proves the statement. Every update throughout this proof uses the same eta; no change of step at T or dependence on requested accuracy is hidden.

## Scope and strongest failure tests

If ker(G) is orthogonal to ker(Delta), the frozen residual can equal 1 and this route gives no positive margin. That is a measure-zero alignment, but its near-neighborhood explains the confidence-dependent xi and large S. If input co-rank exceeds one, the frozen Frobenius residual can exceed 1 even with a generic Gaussian row space; the present argument then fails. If target singular values are unequal, the same test must compare the frozen residual to sigma_r(Delta), not to 1; no general-spectrum assertion follows from this proof. Replacing the actual second update by frozen features forever would prove a different algorithm and is not done here. Positive-noise finite-sample dynamics have no exact invariant target output span, so this proof does not answer Target 2.

Exact rational recurrence/projector checks are auxiliary algebra checks only. They do not certify the Gaussian event, estimates at arbitrary real parameters, independent correctness, or novelty. Independent reviewer audit is required on version 2.


Full deterministic C014 boundedness component:
# T419-C014 v1: empirical GD boundedness with an initialization-dependent step

Kind: bound. Target: 2. Status: proof (unaudited). No novelty claimed.
This is an explicit anisotropic version of the published Gram-imbalance/descent method, not a solution of Target 2. It proves a trajectory component without assuming the iterates are bounded. The prior source is Du-Hu-Lee, arXiv:1806.00900, Theorem 2.2 and Appendix B, Claim B.1; its full convergence theorems have different initialization/step hypotheses. C009 already identifies the exact covariance metric and C010 the positive-noise empirical landscape.

## Statement

Let C be any real positive definite p-by-p matrix, D any real m-by-p matrix, and r>=1. Put lambda=lambda_min(C)>0, c=||C||op, ell=||D||op, W=D C^(-1), and

 q(B,A)=(1/2)||(BA-W) C^(1/2)||F^2,

with B m-by-r and A r-by-p. This is the empirical regression objective up to a constant when C=XX^T/n and D=ZX^T/n. Initialize at any finite deterministic factors B0,A0, and define

 q0=q(B0,A0), J=||A0 A0^T-B0^T B0||F+1,
 R=||W||F+sqrt(2q0/lambda),
 K=sqrt(r)(J+2R), L=6Kc+ell.

For any fixed

 0<eta<=min{1/(1+2q0),1/L},

simultaneous ordinary factor GD satisfies, for every integer t>=0,

 q_t<=q0,
 ||B_t||F^2+||A_t||F^2<=K,
 ||(A_t A_t^T-B_t^T B_t)-(A0 A0^T-B0^T B0)||F<=2eta q0<1,
 sum_(t>=0) ||grad q(B_t,A_t)||F^2<=2q0/eta.

In particular the gradient tends to zero, every accumulation point is critical, and for every integer T>=1,

 min_(0<=t<T) ||grad q(B_t,A_t)||F^2<=2q0/(eta T).

All constants are finite and computable from C,D and the initialization. There is no Gaussian assumption and no low-rank assumption on W. No iterate-convergence, saddle-avoidance or statistical-risk assertion is included.

## Exact identities and product/factor bounds

Let G=BA C-D. The two factor gradients are G_B=G A^T and G_A=B^T G. With E_t=A_t A_t^T-B_t^T B_t the first-order cross terms cancel exactly, giving

 E_(t+1)-E_t=eta^2(G_A G_A^T-G_B^T G_B),
 ||E_(t+1)-E_t||F<=eta^2(||G_A||F^2+||G_B||F^2).

This cancellation only uses dependence on BA and does not require isotropic C. Also

 (||B||F^2+||A||F^2)^2
 <=r [||AA^T-B^TB||F^2+4||BA||F^2].

To verify it, write P=B^TB,Q=AA^T. Scalar trace Cauchy-Schwarz gives (tr(P+Q))^2<=r tr((P+Q)^2), and cyclicity of trace gives tr((P+Q)^2)=||P-Q||F^2+4 tr(PQ), tr(PQ)=||BA||F^2. No commutation is assumed.

When q<=q0, positivity of C gives ||BA-W||F<=sqrt(2q0/lambda), hence ||BA||F<=R. If additionally ||E-E0||F<=1, then ||E||F<=J, so the preceding trace bound implies

 ||B||F^2+||A||F^2<=sqrt(r) sqrt(J^2+4R^2)<=K.

The initialization meets these conditions and therefore has pair norm at most sqrt(K).

## Descent established before closing the boundedness induction

Suppose at the current iterate the pair norm is at most sqrt(K), and preceding steps have valid descent inequalities. Then

 ||grad q||F<=||BA C-D||op sqrt(||B||F^2+||A||F^2)
             <=(Kc/2+ell)sqrt(K).

Because eta<=1/(6Kc+ell), the proposed next point has pair norm at most 2sqrt(K). The connecting segment also lies in that ball. On that ball the Hessian quadratic form in a perturbation (dB,dA) is

 ||(dB A+B dA) C^(1/2)||F^2+2<BA C-D,dB dA>.

Its absolute value is at most

 [c(||A||op^2+||B||op^2)+||BA C-D||op]
 times (||dB||F^2+||dA||F^2)
 <=[4Kc+(2Kc+ell)] (||dB||F^2+||dA||F^2).

Here the first summand uses Cauchy-Schwarz on dB A+B dA; the cross term uses |<G,dB dA>|<=||G||op||dB||F||dA||F. Thus the Hessian operator norm on the segment is at most L. Taylor's theorem along that segment proves

 q_next<=q-eta||grad q||F^2+(L eta^2/2)||grad q||F^2
        <=q-(eta/2)||grad q||F^2.

In particular q_next<=q0. Telescoping the descent inequalities, including the proposed step, and using q>=0 yields

 sum_(j=0)^t eta^2||grad q_j||F^2<=2eta q0
 <=2q0/(1+2q0)<1.

Summing the imbalance increments now proves ||E_next-E0||F<=2eta q0<1. The product/factor bound therefore puts the endpoint back in the smaller ball of pair radius sqrt(K). This closes the induction without assuming a bound before proving descent on the required larger segment. The q0=0 case is included: both gradients vanish, the sequence is constant, and all inequalities still hold.

## Consequences and exact remaining gap

Telescoping for every finite horizon gives the infinite summability bound. A nonnegative summable sequence tends to zero, so the gradients vanish. Bounded finite-dimensional factor pairs have convergent subsequences; gradient continuity makes every subsequential limit critical. The running-minimum bound follows by averaging the finite sum. These statements do not require that the entire sequence converges to one point.

For B0=0 and a Gaussian A0, this provides an allowed positive step after observing the initialization, conditional on every full-row-rank design. It does not supply a single positive step independent of the unbounded Gaussian initializer. C013 shows that unconditional expected-limit risk with such an initialization-independent fixed step can diverge even at rank one.

Combining this bound with the already verified empirical strict-saddle landscape C010 is insufficient to conclude global optimization. One must additionally show that the specified zero/Gaussian initialization does not approach a nonglobal critical point, with all hypotheses of a saddle-avoidance theorem checked for its lower-dimensional initial support and step rule. Vanishing gradients do not establish that. Even convergence almost surely would not by itself justify passing to expected population risk; a failure-tail/integrability or finite-stopping argument is separately required. The usual full-ambient absolutely-continuous random-initialization theorem cannot simply be cited for the plane B0=0.

Independent reviewer audit and any novelty assessment remain pending. f is continuous on a closed cylinder around (t_0,y_0)

body:
[Lemma lem:oco-disk-lower of arXiv:2608.25182, 'Minimax Alternating Regret \\for the Experts Problem and Online Convex Optimization'] Let
$
  \mathcal D=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^2:\|x\|_2\le1\}.
$
There exists a universal constant $c_0>0$ such that, for every $T\ge 5$, there is an oblivious distribution $\mathsf P_T$ over sequences of convex losses $f_1,\ldots,f_T:\mathcal D\to[0,1]$ for which every learner satisfies
\begin{align}
  \mathbb{E}_{f_{1:T}\sim\mathsf P_T}\bigl[\operatorname{Reg}^{\mathrm{alt}}_T\bigr]
  \ge c_0\log(1+T).
  
\end{align}
If the learner is randomized, the expectation also includes its internal randomness.

body:
[Corollary 63 of arXiv:2609.02850, 'Canonical-row Chern flow on Bott--Samelson towers:\\ realizable-volume models for Schubert'] The support of every ordinary Lascoux atom $\overline L_\alpha$ is
$M^\natural$-convex, and
\begin{equation}
 \Supp(\overline L_\alpha)
 =\Newt(\overline L_\alpha)\cap\ZZ^n.
\end{equation}
The positive-parameter polynomial $\overline L_\alpha^+(x;\beta)$ has
saturated Newton polytope in $\ZZ^{n+1}$.  Thus Conjecture~5.7 of
Monical--Tokcan--Yong holds.

[Corollary 7 (Delay after an abrupt change) of arXiv:2608.29465, 'Deciding When to Decide:\\Testing Operational Suboptimality Under Distributional Shift'] Under $H_1$ in \eqref{eq:dr_cpd_test} with first post-change index $\gamma$, let $t_\gamma$ be the first monitoring time with $t_\gamma-w+1\ge\gamma$, and assume the horizon reaches it. Its window lies entirely after the change, so $\Delta_{t_\gamma}=\Delta(z_0;\theta^\star,\mathbb P_1)$. If the margin condition of Theorem~\ref{thm:cpd_power} holds at $t_\gamma$, then
\[
\Pr\big(\hat t_{\rm alarm}-\gamma\le w+s-2\big)\longrightarrow1 .
\]

body:
[Theorem 4 of arXiv:2608.26565, 'A Horizon-Free Extrinsic Penrose Inequality'] Let $S\subset\mathbb R^3$ satisfy \eqref{eq:topology}, and suppose that
$\mathcal E_+$ is asymptotically flat in the sense of
Definition~\ref{def:af-end}. Assume
 \begin{equation}
 H_S\geq0\quad\text{on }S,
 \qquad H_S\in L^1(S_+).
 
\end{equation}
Then the following statements hold.
If $A_S=0$, then $m_+(S)\geq0$, with equality if and only if $q=0$ and,
after a rigid motion,
\[
 M=\{x_3>0\},\qquad S=\{x_3=0\}.
\]
If $A_S>0$, then
\begin{equation}
 m_+(S)\geq\sqrt{\frac{A_S}{\pi}}.
 
\end{equation}
If equality holds in \eqref{eq:main-inequality}, then $A_S$ is attained by a
free-boundary minimal disk $D$ that is outermost toward $\mathcal E_+$. After
a rigid motion,
\[
 D=\{(y,0):|y|\leq m_+(S)\},
\]
and the component of $S\setminus\partial D$ containing $\mathcal E_+$ is
$\mathrm{Cat}_{m_+(S)}^+$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 4 of arXiv:2608.26565

[Proposition 16 of arXiv:2607.29534, 'Expected signatures via partial integration, coordinate change and symmetrization'] There exists a graded Hopf algebra structure
$
    \left(
        T_{\mathcal{A}^{\prime\prime}}((\mathbb{R}^d)),
        \widehat{\otimes},
        \Delta_{\widehat{\shuffle}}
    \right)
$
for which
\begin{equation*}
    \symmetrizer:
    \left(
        T((\mathbb{R}^d)),
        \otimes,
        \Delta_{\shuffle}
    \right)
    \longrightarrow
    \left(
        T_{\mathcal{A}^{\prime\prime}}((\mathbb{R}^d)),
        \widehat{\otimes},
        \Delta_{\widehat{\shuffle}}
    \right)
\end{equation*}
is a Hopf algebra morphism. In particular,
\begin{equation}
    \Delta_{\widehat{\shuffle}}\circ\symmetrizer
    =
    \left(
        \symmetrizer\boxtimes\symmetrizer
    \right)
    \circ\Delta_{\shuffle}.
\end{equation}
Denoting by
\begin{equation*}
    \widehat{\shuffle}:
    \mathbb{R}_{\mathcal{A}^{\prime\prime}}\langle\mathcal{A}\rangle
    \times
    \mathbb{R}_{\mathcal{A}^{\prime\prime}}\langle\mathcal{A}\rangle
    \longrightarrow
    \mathbb{R}_{\mathcal{A}^{\prime\prime}}\langle\mathcal{A}\rangle
\end{equation*}
the corresponding graded dual product, $\Sigsym{Y}$ is group-like and,
equivalently, for all $u,v\in\mathcal{W}_{\mathcal{A}}$,
\begin{equation}
    \big\langle [u],\Sigsym{Y}\big\rangle
    \big\langle [v],\Sigsym{Y}\big\rangle
    =
    \big\langle
        [u]\widehat{\shuffle}[v],
        \Sigsym{Y}
    \big\rangle.
\end{equation}
Moreover, $\Psi$ and $\Psi^{-1}$ induce inverse graded automorphisms
$\widehat{\Psi}$ and $\widehat{\Psi}^{-1}$ on
$T_{\mathcal{A}^{\prime\prime}}((\mathbb{R}^d))$, characterized by
\begin{equation}
    \symmetrizer\circ\Psi
    =
    \widehat{\Psi}\circ\symmetrizer,
    \qquad
    \symmetrizer\circ\Psi^{-1}
    =
    \widehat{\Psi}^{-1}\circ\symmetrizer.
\end{equation}
The quotient pairing from \eqref{eq:quotient_pairing} is the pairing induced
by $\widehat{\Psi}$; that is,
\begin{equation}
    \big\langle
        \alpha,
        \widehat{\mathbf{a}}
    \big\rangle_\Psi
    =
    \big\langle
        \widehat{\Psi}^\ast(\alpha),
        \widehat{\mathbf{a}}
    \big\rangle
\end{equation}
for all
$\alpha\in
\mathbb{R}_{\mathcal{A}^{\prime\prime}}\langle\mathcal{A}\rangle$
and
$\widehat{\mathbf{a}}\in
T_{\mathcal{A}^{\prime\prime}}((\mathbb{R}^d))$.

Arb represents a real enclosure as[m +/- r],with an arbitrary-precision floating-point midpoint and a nonnegative magnitude bound. A valid interval extension contains the point-function image of every point in its input set. Basic arithmetic bounds both propagated input uncertainty and rounding of the computed midpoint; radius arithmetic rounds upward. Magnitudes use30-bit mantissas with arbitrary-size exponents,so their lower precision does not authorize dropping their error contribution. Domain checks remain necessary for division and square root. These arithmetic semantics do not certify a calling program,its input model,or a mathematical reduction. Johansson1611.02831v1 Section3.2,p6 and Section5,p7 describe the magnitude bounds and inclusion requirement; Section3.2 states assumptions on compiler floating-point transformations and elementary operations.
Arb implementation satisfying its documented arithmetic and compiler assumptions
valid operation domains
all input and rounding uncertainty retained
title: Arb (Johansson): midpoint-radius interval enclosures and upward-rounded error bounds

body:
Own-work proof draft (unaudited), no novelty priority claimed. For every oracle O there is one uniform family P_L^O with polynomial-time Boolean unnormalized weights, an explicit normalizer, exact polynomial-time normalized point probabilities and an exact uniform polynomial-time sampler, for which polynomial-time cumulative-probability evaluation implies NP^O=P^O. At L=2d+1 take C,b,w of lengths d,1,d and give weight one iff b=V_d^O(C,w), where V is a polynomial-time universal time-bounded oracle verifier. The normalizer is 2^(2d). Two CDF values recover the number of accepting witnesses: 2^(2d)[F(C,1,1^d)-F(C,0,1^d)]. Additive error at most 2^(-(L+2)) per value still decides whether this integer is positive. Strict CDFs work as well by adding the known point mass. Other lengths are dummy point masses. Thus easy point probabilities, even with exact sampling, cannot alone establish a cumulative-computability hypothesis under NP^O not contained in P^O/poly. This is not an AR KL lower bound and does not refute the PSamp extension of average-case completeness.
Standard deterministic polynomial-time universal oracle-verifier simulation

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:9e1d1c677956682809a9d586521cd9b97bb5331701eda763c0ead070e4a5c026","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/9e/9e1d1c677956682809a9d586521cd9b97bb5331701eda763c0ead070e4a5c026.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:8e537630f971aef139bab09ad3606f53b38917f60cadc3291435dad5ba3d65f8","bundle_entry_key":"universal-verifier-graph-cdf-oracle-collapse","bundle_id":"population.t410-verifier-cdf-bridge-obstruction-v2","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"oracle computational complexity; computable ensembles; cumulative probabilities; autoregressive limitations","draft":"w739/bundle_005.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:complexity.cryptography:universal-verifier-graph-cdf-oracle-collapse","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Easy point probabilities and sampling do not supply the PComp hypothesis

C011 v2. Target 2. Kind: route-failure. Status: proof (unaudited).
This is an explicit obstruction to a distribution-class substitution in the
IR2 literature route, not a new oracle construction or a novelty claim.

Fix any oracle O. There is a single uniform length-indexed family P_L^O
with polynomial-time 0/1 weights, known normalizer, polynomial-time exact
normalized point probabilities, and a uniform exact polynomial-time sampler,
such that polynomial-time evaluation of its lexicographic CDF would imply
NP^O=P^O. Even additive CDF precision 2^(-(L+2)) suffices for this collapse.
Therefore in any oracle sought by Target 2, this family is not in PComp^O
under the cumulative-probability convention of Bogdanov-Trevisan Definition 2.
This is NOT an AR KL lower bound, or an obstruction to samplable-distribution
extensions of average-case completeness.

## Uniform verifier and exact law

Let V_d^O(C,w) be a fixed universal, polynomial-time, Boolean oracle verifier
on pairs of d-bit strings. Interpret C as a self-delimited deterministic oracle
verifier program M and input x followed by padding. On malformed encodings
return zero. Otherwise simulate M(x,w) for at most d simulated steps and
return its accept bit, with timeout returning zero. This universal simulation
takes polynomial time in d, including oracle-query lengths. The verifier can
ignore unused witness bits. Its accepted-C language

    {C : exists w in {0,1}^d with V_d^O(C,w)=1}

contains a polynomial-time encoding of every NP^O problem: for its fixed
verifier, on input x choose d polynomially large enough for its code, x,
witness length and running time, and pad C to that length. Wrap the original
verifier to use just its prescribed witness prefix; surplus witness bits
are ignored. This padding is computable in polynomial time and does not
require deciding the NP predicate. Thus deciding positivity for all C decides
every NP^O language. Only this universal-verifier property is needed below.

At L=2d+1, d>=1, use words C b w, with |C|=|w|=d and |b|=1. Set their
weight to one iff b=V_d^O(C,w), otherwise zero. There is exactly one supported
word for each pair (C,w), so the normalizer is exactly 2^(2d). Every supported
word has probability 2^(-2d). An exact sampler chooses C and w uniformly and
outputs C V_d^O(C,w) w. At even lengths and the finitely many unused lengths,
put all mass at the all-zero word. Both the weight evaluator and the sampler
are single uniform polynomial-time oracle algorithms, without any NP oracle.

## Two CDF evaluations decide the verifier's existential predicate

Let F_L(z)=Pr[X lexicographically <= z] on L-bit words. For a fixed C let

    z_0=C 0 1^d,       z_1=C 1 1^d,
    K(C)=number of w with V_d^O(C,w)=1.

All words with first block preceding C occur in both CDFs and cancel.
F_L(z_0) includes the whole C,0 block; F_L(z_1) additionally includes the
whole C,1 block, and no later first block. Consequently, exactly,

    K(C) = 2^(2d) [F_L(z_1)-F_L(z_0)].                 (1)

Polynomial-time exact CDF evaluation therefore decides whether K(C)>0,
which by the encoding above implies NP^O=P^O. More robustly, if each CDF
value is computed with absolute error at most 2^(-(2d+3)), scaling their
difference as in (1) gives error at most 1/4. Comparing the result to 1/2
correctly distinguishes the integer K=0 from K>=1. Here 2d+3=L+2, so a
precision evaluator with runtime polynomial in L and requested bit precision
also yields the same collapse. This precision requirement is exponential
in L; inverse-polynomial absolute CDF accuracy alone is not enough for this
argument. In particular it does not imply a KL lower bound.

## Exact implication for the literature bridge

Bogdanov and Trevisan, Average-Case Complexity (2006), arXiv cs/0606037,
PDF page 17, Definition 2, define PComp through polynomial-time computation
of cumulative probabilities, and explicitly note that point probabilities
are then computable. Their implication is in that direction. The example
above excludes reversing it under NP^O not contained in P^O/poly, even after
adding exact samplability and a known normalizer. It is stronger than merely
not knowing how to normalize the weights, since the example's normalizer is
already explicit.

Thus our efficiently weighted-law hypothesis cannot simply be substituted
for PComp in a cited average-case theorem. The same survey separately gives
an extension from PComp to samplable distributions (section 1.1.5, citing
Impagliazzo-Levin); our example IS samplable, so it does not refute that
extension. Whether ALL efficiently weighted laws can be sampled in the
reported IR2 oracle, or whether direct AR approximation avoids sampling,
remains unresolved. No [IR2] construction has been obtained. The hardest
open piece remains final-oracle weighted-law coverage together with NP
circuit hardness. Target 2 remains OPEN.

The finite checks validate the two-CDF endpoint identity and rounding
threshold on small relations. They do not establish the complexity reduction
by enumeration. No independent audit or formal proof certificate is claimed.

## CDF endpoint convention clarification (version 2)

If the source writes a strict cumulative sum G(z)=Pr[X<z], our F(z) is
G(z)+P_L(z). The point mass is already polynomial-time exactly computable
in this construction. Thus a strict CDF evaluator gives the non-strict CDF
used in (1) with the same precision and polynomial overhead. This implication
does not rely on how a lexicographic successor is represented, including the
last supported word. The CDF-hardness conclusion therefore covers either
endpoint convention. body:
[Theorem thm:jakubowski of arXiv:2607.13748, 'Load Balancing with Individually Heterogeneous Servers'] The sequence of probability measure-valued processes $(\eta^n:n\in\mathbb{N})$ with sample paths in $\mathbb{D}_{\mathcal{P}(E)}[0,T]$, where $E$ is a metric space, is tight provided that
\begin{itemize}
\item[(J1)] for every $\bar{\rho}>0$, there exists a compact set $\mathcal{K}_{\bar{\rho}}\subset\mathcal{P}(E)$ such that
$$\liminf_{n\to \infty}\mathbb{P}(\eta^n(t)\in\mathcal{K}_{\bar{\rho}}\ \text{for all }t\in[0,T])\ge 1-\bar{\rho}.$$
\item[(J2)] there exists a family $\mathcal{F}$ of real-valued maps on $\mathcal{P}(E)$ that separates points, is closed under addition, and such that $(H(\eta^n):n\in\mathbb{N})$ is tight in $\mathbb{D}_\mathbb{R}[0,T]$ for every $H\in\mathcal{F}$.
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Jakubowski's criteria, Theorem 4.6 in \cite{Jakubowski1986}

[Lemma funclimit1 of arXiv:2412.03325, 'Functional limit theorem for branching processes \\ in nearly degenerate varying environme'] Assume that condition (C1)--(C3) are satisfied for a BPVE $(X_n)_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ defined in (equation eq:X of the paper).
Then, for any $0 < u \leq t$,
\[
\lim_{n \to \infty}
\mathbf{E}\left[s^{X_{A(nt)}}  | X_{A(nu)} = 1 \right] =
1 - \frac{u}{t} \left(
\frac{1}{1-s} + \frac{\nu}{2} \left(1 - \frac{u}{t}\right)
\right)^{-1} = h_{u/t}(s),
\]
that is, $\mathcal{L}(X_{A(nt)} | X_{A(nu)} = 1 )$ converges 
in distribution to a linear fractional distribution with 
generating function $h_{u/t}(s)$.

[Proposition 1 (Stochastic approximation) of arXiv:2607.22438, 'A deterministic scalar reduction for the phase transition in two interacting urns'] Let \(\alpha>1\) and \(p\in[0,1]\). Let \(\Lambda_p^{(\alpha)}\) be the equilibrium set of
\[
 \dot z=F_p^{(\alpha)}(z)
\]
on \([0,1]^2\). The vector field is a gradient field: $F_p^{(\alpha)}=\nabla L_p^{(\alpha)}$,
where
\begin{equation}
 L_p^{(\alpha)}(x,y)
 =(1-p)\{G(x)+G(y)\}+2pG\!\left(\frac{x+y}{2}\right)
 -\frac{x^2+y^2}{2},
 \qquad
 G(t)=\int_0^t h(u)\dd u .
\end{equation}
Stability is understood relative to the invariant square \([0,1]^2\). An equilibrium
\(z_*\in\Lambda_p^{(\alpha)}\) is called stable if it is a strict local maximum of
\(L_p^{(\alpha)}\) relative to \([0,1]^2\). We call \(z_*\) unstable if the top
eigenvalue \(\lambda_+(z_*)\) of \(DF_p^{(\alpha)}(z_*)\) is positive.

Moreover:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}, leftmargin=*]
    \item for \(p>0\), the equilibrium set \(\Lambda_p^{(\alpha)}\) is finite;

    \item every equilibrium other than
    \[
      (0,0),\qquad \left(\frac12,\frac12\right),\qquad (1,1)
    \]
    lies in one of the two off-diagonal rectangles
    \[
      \left(0,\frac12\right)\times\left(\frac12,1\right),
      \qquad
      \left(\frac12,1\right)\times\left(0,\frac12\right);
    \]

    \item the urn process \((x_n,y_n)\) converges almost surely to an equilibrium of the ODE;

    \item if \(z_*\in\Lambda_p^{(\alpha)}\) is stable, then
    \[
      \PP_p^{(\alpha)}
      \left(\lim_{n\to\infty}(x_n,y_n)=z_*\right)>0;
    \]

    \item if \(z_*\in\Lambda_p^{(\alpha)}\) is unstable, then
    \[
      \PP_p^{(\alpha)}
      \left(\lim_{n\to\infty}(x_n,y_n)=z_*\right)=0 .
    \]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem thm:separation of arXiv:2609.01270, 'Farey Structure in Modulo Krinkle Tilings:\\ Mediant Splicing and Generation of Prototiles'] \leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\emph{(1)}] \emph{Core generation.} For every reduced $(m,k)$, the core edge
sequence (angles $2\pi s_j/n$, $j=0,\dots,k-1$) is reconstructed exactly from the leaves
of the decomposition tree---single unit edges of angle $0$---by iterated fan-twist
splicing (the core part of Theorem~(thm:splice of the paper)).
\item[\emph{(2)}] \emph{Decoration attachment.} Define a \emph{template} to be a
boundary word of the shape
\[
(\text{decorations})^*\;\;
(\text{contiguous core run }\mathsf{C}_0\cdots\mathsf{C}_{k-1}\text{ or }\mathsf{C}_1\cdots\mathsf{C}_{k-1})
\;\;(\text{decorations})^*,
\]
where a
\emph{decoration token} is an edge whose direction is a multiple of $k$---angle
$2\pi c/t$ with $c\in\{0,\dots,t-1\}$, invariant across parents and child---and call a
pair $(\ell,u)$ of templates \emph{closed} if, counting $\mathsf{C}_0$ as the letter $\mathsf{Z}$
(both have angle $0$), the decoration vector sums of $\ell$ and $u$ agree. For every
closed template pair, mediant splicing lifts: core edges rotate by the fan-twist
amounts of Theorem~(thm:splice of the paper), decoration edges are unchanged, and the spliced
part is the child part of the same template pair. Every row of
Table~(tab:templates of the paper) is a closed pair with decorations $\mathsf{Z},\mathsf{K}$; there $\ell$
and $u$ even use one multiset of directions.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently every prototile part of every variant is obtained as ``one unit edge
$\to$ (iterated splicing) $\to$ core $\to$ (finitely many decoration edges)'', and

[Lemma 21 of arXiv:2609.04153, '\vspace*{-3cm}Smooth autonomous fast dynamo action on the three-torus'] For any $s \in [0,\infty)$, the map $F_{u,s}: \TT^2 \to \TT^2$ defines a smooth diffeomorphism, so that $F_{u,m}$ preserves the area measure $u_3(a,0) \dd a$. Furthermore, the return time $\overline \tau^m_u(a)$ is given by 
$$
\overline\tau^m_u(a)=\int_0^m \frac{1}{u_3(F_{u,s}(a),s)} \dd s.
$$
Finally, there holds the explicit expression 
$$
\Phi_u^{\overline\tau^m_u(a)}(a,0)=(F^m_{u,1}(a),m).
$$

[Definition Permutation Symmetric Property of arXiv:2412.07936, 'Simple Norm Bounds for Polynomial Random Matrices via Decoupling'] Suppose ${\bf F}({\bf x})$ is a degree-d homogeneous multilinear polynomial random matrix, i.e.,\xspace
$$
{\bf F}({\bf x}) =  \sum_{{\bf i} \in {\mathcal T}^d_n} \left( {\bf A}_{{\bf i}} \cdot \prod_{j \in \{i_1,\dots, i_d \}} x_j\right),
$$
where $\{{\bf A}_{{\bf i}}\}_{{\bf i} \in {\mathcal T}^d_n}$ is a multi-indexed sequence of deterministic matrices of the same dimension. ${\bf F}({\bf x})$ is permutation symmetric if ${\bf A}_{i_1, \dots, i_d} = {\bf A}_{i_{\sigma(1)}, \dots, i_{\sigma(d)}}$ for any permutation $\sigma \in \mathfrak{S}_d$ and any $(i_1, \dots, i_d) \in {\mathcal T}^d_n$.
title: Permutation Symmetric Property

[Lemma lem:slopebound of arXiv:2411.08018, 'Last passage percolation in hierarchical environments'] Fix $a,b,c,d\in\mathbb{R}^2$ with $a\prec b\prec c\prec d$.
    Assume that
    \[
        \mathsf{Slope}(a,b)=\mathsf{Slope}(b,c)=\mathsf{Slope}(c,d)
    \]
    and that
    \begin{align}
        c_i-b_i \ge \max\{b_i-a_i,\ d_i-c_i\}\quad\text{for } i\in\{1,2\},
    \end{align}
    i.e. the rectangles are similar and the middle one has (weakly) larger sides than the other two. 
    Then for all $r\in(0,1)$, for all $v\in\mathsf{Cyl}_r(\mathsf{Rect}(a,b))$, and for all $w\in \mathsf{Cyl}_r(\mathsf{Rect}(c,d))$, we have that
    \begin{align}
        \frac{1}{1+2r} \le \frac{\mathsf{Slope}(v,w)}{\mathsf{Slope}(b,c)} \le 1+2r.
    \end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Corollary 121 (Covariance-energy response quotient) of arXiv:2608.04993, '2608.04993'] For $h,k\in H$ the following are equivalent:
\[
 [h]=[k]\text{ in }\mathscr E_a,
 \qquad
 \langle a(h-k),h-k\rangle=0,
 \qquad
 a^{1/2}h=a^{1/2}k.
\]
Consequently every continuous response built only from covariance pairings
$\langle a\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ descends uniquely to $\mathscr E_a$, and two
directions have the same response exactly when their difference lies in
$\ker a$.  Thus $\mathscr E_a$ is the response quotient for first-order
covariance-energy directions, defined before quasi-sure identification.

[Theoremalpha thm:iid of arXiv:2608.30829, 'Free energy and phase transition for\\ 2D directed polymers with critical spatial correlat'] In the case of an i.i.d.\ environment satisfying~(equation eq:integrability-omega of the paper), we have the following:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
  \item 
  In dimension \(d=1\), we have \(\beta_c=0\) and [Nak19] shows that
  \[
  \mathtt{F}(\beta) \sim - \frac16 \, \beta^4 \quad \text{ as } \beta\downarrow 0 \,. 
  \]

  \item 
  In dimension \(d=2\), we have \(\beta_c=0\) and [BCT25,BN26] show that there is a constant \(c>0\) such that we have (we assume here that \(\mathbb{E}[\omega(1,0)^3]=0\) to simplify the statement)
  \[
    -\, \frac{1}{c}\, \exp\Big( -\frac{\pi}{\beta^2} \Big) \leq \mathtt{F}(\beta) \leq   -\, c \,\exp\Big( -\frac{\pi}{\beta^2} \Big) \quad \text{ as } \beta\downarrow 0 \,.
  \]
  

  \item 
  In dimension \(d\geq 3\), we have \(\beta_c>0\) and [JL26] shows that 
  \[
    -\, \exp\Big(- u^{- \frac{2+d}{8 d} +o(1)} \Big) \leq \mathtt{F}(\beta_c +u) \leq -\, \exp\Big(- u^{-1+o(1)} \Big) \quad \text{ as } u\downarrow 0 \,,
  \]
  where the upper bound holds for Gaussian disorder.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition intro-ordinal of arXiv:2506.10448, 'Hitting probabilities and the Ekstr\"om--Persson conjecture'] Let $\mu \in \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^d)$, let $\underline{r}$ be a positive nonincreasing sequence, and  
let $C\subseteq \spt \mu$ be compact. Define compact sets $C_0^{\gamma}$ for
each ordinal number $\gamma$ as follows: 
\begin{enumerate}
  \item[i)] Set $C_0^0:=C$.
  \item[ii)] If $C_0^{\gamma}$ has been defined, set 
             $C_0^{\gamma+1}:=\Jmurz(C_0^{\gamma})$.
  \item[iii)] If $\lambda$ is a nonzero limit ordinal and $C_0^{\gamma}$ has been defined for 
              every $\gamma<\lambda$, set 
        \[
        C_0^{\lambda}:=\bigcap_{\gamma<\lambda}C_0^{\gamma}.
        \]
\end{enumerate}        
Then there exists a countable ordinal $\beta_0$ such that 
$C_0^{\beta_0+1}=C_0^{\beta_0}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 80 (Measurable contraction selection) of arXiv:2607.10813, '2607.10813'] Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F)$ be a measurable space, let $B$ be a separable Banach
space, let $G\in\mathcal F$, and let $R>0$.  Suppose
\[
 \Phi:\Omega\times\overline B_R\longrightarrow B
\]
is jointly Borel measurable and that there is a deterministic $0\le\lambda<1$
such that, for every $\omega\in G$, the map $z\mapsto\Phi(\omega,z)$ sends
$\overline B_R$ into itself and is $\lambda$-Lipschitz.  Then the unique fixed
point $z_*(\omega)$ on $G$, extended by $0$ on $G^c$, is strongly measurable
as a $B$-valued map.  On $G$ it is the pointwise and norm limit of the measurable Picard iterates
\[
 z_0=0,
 \qquad
 z_{m+1}(\omega)=
 \mathbf1_G(\omega)\Phi(\omega,z_m(\omega)).
\]

[Prop 12 of arXiv:2605.23659, '2605.23659'] Define
\[
\Gamma^{(0)}_t:=O^{\ast,(0)}(T(\eta_t))
\quad (t\ge0).
\]
Then
\begin{align}  
\Gamma^{(0)}_t=T(\eta_t)-\Gamma(t)
\quad (t\ge0). 
\end{align}
Moreover, if \(j_0:=f(0)\), the process \((\Gamma^{(0)}_t)_{t\ge0}\) has the same law on \(D([0,\infty),\bR)\) as \((Z^{(j_0)}(ct))_{t\ge0}\).
In particular, \((\Gamma^{(0)}_t)_{t\ge0}\) is a subordinator.

Furthermore, the process \((\Gamma^{(0)}_t)_{t\ge0}\) is independent of the family \((\Gamma^{(i)})_{i\in I}\). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Prop 12 of arXiv:2605.23659
