[Theorem 11 of arXiv:2508.04938, 'Perfect t-embeddings of doubly periodic Aztec diamonds'] Let~$\cT_N$ and  $\cO_N$ denote the perfect t-embedding and its associated origami map of the Aztec diamond of size~$\ell N$ with $(2\times\ell)$-periodic weights described above. Let~$(\xi,\eta)$ be a point in the liquid region~$\mathcal F_R$ of the Aztec diamond. Then
\begin{equation*}
(\cT_N(\xi,\eta),\cO_N(\xi,\eta))\to \left(\mathcal Z(\Omega(\xi,\eta)),\vartheta(\Omega(\xi,\eta))\right)
\end{equation*}
as~$N\to \infty$, 
where~$\Omega:\mathcal F_R\to \mathcal{R}_0$ 
a diffeomorphism (properly defined in Proposition~\ref{prop:diffeomorphism_2xell}) known as a critical point map~\cite{}, and the convergence is uniform on compact subsets of~$\mathcal F_R$. 

Moreover, the following limits exist: 
\[\lim_{(\xi,\eta)\to \mathcal F^{\operatorname{gas}}_i}(\cT_N(\xi,\eta),\cO_N(\xi,\eta))
\quad \text{ and }\quad
\lim_{(\xi,\eta)\to \mathcal F^{\operatorname{frozen}}_j}(\cT_N(\xi,\eta),\cO_N(\xi,\eta))\] 
for all $i=1,\ldots, \ell-1$ and $j=1, \ldots, 4$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem pre:gamblersRuin of arXiv:2605.19835, 'Reemergence of the Epidemic Threshold in SIRS Infections on Connected Stars'] {feller1957introduction}}]
    In the gambler's ruin game, a player starts with some amount of money $P_0 \in \mathOrText{\mathds{N}}_{\geq 1}$ and then repeatedly throws a coin that shows head with probability $p \in (0,1)$, independent of all other outcomes. If it shows heads, the player's money increases by~$1$, otherwise, it decreases by~$1$. The game ends at time~$T$ when the player either reaches the lower bound $\ell \in \mathOrText{\mathds{N}}_{< P_0}$ or the upper bound $u \in \mathOrText{\mathds{N}}_{> P_0}$ of money.
    Let $(P_t)_{t \in \mathOrText{\mathds{N}}}$ be the amount of money that a player has in a gambler's ruin game that has a probability of $p \in (0,1)\setminus\{1/2\}$ for them to win in each step. Let $q=1-p$.  Then
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $\Pr{P_T = \ell} = \frac{1-(p/q)^{u-P_0}}{1-(p/q)^{u-\ell}}$ and
        \item $\Pr{P_T = u} = \frac{1-(q/p)^{P_0-l}}{1-(q/p)^{u-\ell}}$.\qedhere
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 26 of arXiv:2609.02785, 'Characterization of Stanley-Reisner varieties by their automorphism group'] Every $\varphi\in\Aut(X_\Delta)$ permutes the irreducible components
$\{V_F: F\in\mathcal{F}(\Delta)\}$, with $|F|=|\varphi(F)|$ for the induced
permutation of facets. Consequently $\varphi$ preserves the cone locus
$$
Y_\Delta:=\bigcap_{F\in\mathcal{F}(\Delta)}V_F
=\{x\in X_\Delta: x_l=0\text{ for every }l\notin c(\Delta)\}
\cong\AF^{|c(\Delta)|},
$$
where $c(\Delta)\subseteq[n]$ denotes the set of cone vertices of $\Delta$.
In particular, if $\Delta$ has no cone vertex, then every automorphism fixes
the origin $0\in X_\Delta$, and hence preserves the maximal ideal
$\mathfrak{m}_0:=(\overline{x}_1,\dots,\overline{x}_n)\subseteq\KK[\Delta]$
and all of its powers.

[Proposition 16 of arXiv:2606.09121, 'Truncated Signature Information for Mixed Fractional Brownian Paths'] Let $D\Gamma_\mcH(\theta)$ be the Jacobian of \eqref{eq:Gamma-def}.  If $L\ge K$ and the scales are distinct, then

\]

[Theorem 1 ($L_p$ Brunn-Minkowski inequality) of arXiv:2609.00743, '$L_p$ Brunn-Minkowski inequality for the eigenvalue of generalized Monge-Ampère equation'] Suppose $k\ge 0$. Let $\Omega_0$ and $\Omega_1$ be bounded, smooth and strictly convex domains containing the origin as an interior point, and $\Omega_\alpha:=(1-\alpha)\Omega_0+_p \alpha\Omega_1$ be the $L_p$-Minkowski addition of $\Omega_0$ and $\Omega_1$, where $p:=k+1\ge 1$ and $\alpha\in[0,1]$. Then
\begin{equation}
    \lambda(\Omega_\alpha)^{-\frac{p}{2n}}\ge (1-\alpha)\lambda(\Omega_0)^{-\frac{p}{2n}}+\alpha\lambda(\Omega_1)^{-\frac{p}{2n}}.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: $L_p$ Brunn-Minkowski inequality

body:
[Definition Recursive Terminal Attachment of arXiv:2608.12415, 'Sharp Phase Transition for Ellipsoid Fitting'] Let \(s\) be a square vertex. A recursive terminal attachment at \(s\) is
generated by the following rules.

\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Base case: \(h_2\)-attachment.}
    The attachment may be a single \(h_2\)-edge from \(s\) to a circle vertex
    \(a\):
    \[
        s \xleftrightarrow{h_2} a .
    \]

    \item \textbf{Concatenated-path attachment.}
    For any \(t > 1\), let \(\tau_1,\ldots,\tau_t\) be backbone-dangling
    shapes with compatible circle boundaries, and let    \[
        \tau =\tau_t \circ \tau_{t-1}\circ \cdots \circ \tau_1
    \]
    denote their proper concatenation. $\tau$ is then attached by adding two $h_1$ edges connecting $s$ to $U_\tau$ and $V_\tau$ (assuming $U_\tau\neq V_\tau$).

\end{enumerate}
title: Recursive Terminal Attachment

[Lemma lem:Ttransform-2coord of arXiv:2601.04079, 'TV homogenization inequalities'] Fix $a,b\in[0,1]$ and $\lambda\in[0,1]$, and define
\[
a' := \lambda a + (1-\lambda)b,
\qquad
b' := \lambda b + (1-\lambda)a.
\]
Let
\[
\eta := 
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle \frac{\lambda(1-\lambda)(a-b)^2}{2(1-ab)}, & ab<1,\\
[1ex]
0, & ab=1,
\end{cases}
\]
and consider the row--stochastic $4\times4$ matrix (indexed by $00,01,10,11$)
\begin{equation}

M_{\lambda}(a,b):=
\left(\begin{array}{cccc}
1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
\eta & \lambda-\eta & (1-\lambda)-\eta & \eta \\
\eta & (1-\lambda)-\eta & \lambda-\eta & \eta \\
0 & 0 & 0 & 1 
\end{array}\right).
\end{equation}
Then all entries of $M_{\lambda}(a,b)$ are nonnegative, and for both $s\in\{+,-\}$,
\[
\Bigl(\Ber\!\left(\tfrac12+s\,\tfrac a2\right)\otimes \Ber\!\left(\tfrac12+s\,\tfrac b2\right)\Bigr)\,M_{\lambda}(a,b)
=
\Ber\!\left(\tfrac12+s\,\tfrac {a'}2\right)\otimes \Ber\!\left(\tfrac12+s\,\tfrac {b'}2\right).
\]

body:
[Lemma lem:tail-partition of arXiv:2608.28330, 'Realising atomless laws as distance distributions on metric measure spaces'] Fix $A>0$, and let $\eta$ be a finite atomless Borel measure on $(A,\infty)$ with
	unbounded support.  Given $\rho,\gamma>0$, there are pairwise disjoint
	intervals $B_i$, $i=1,2,\ldots$, which cover $(A,\infty)$ up to an
	$\eta$-null set and whose closures $J_i=\overline{B_i}$ in $\mathbb R$ satisfy
	\[
	0<\eta(B_i)\le\gamma,\qquad
	\operatorname{diam} J_i\le\rho,\qquad
	\sup J_i\le\inf J_j\quad\text{for }1\le i<j,
	\]
	and $\inf J_i\to\infty$ as $i\to\infty$.

[Corollary Dynamic formulation of $W_p$ of arXiv:2603.14163, '\LARGE \bf Tail Bounds for Queues with Abandonment: Constant, Moderate, Large Deviations, '] Let $\mathcal{L}(X), \mathcal{L}(Z') \in \mathcal{P}_p(\mathbb{R})$ and suppose there exists a weakly continuous curve $\mu_t:(0,\infty)\to\mathcal{P}_p(\mathbb{R})$ and a Borel vector field $v_t$ such that
    $\partial_t \mu_t + \partial_x(\mu_t v_t)=0$,
    $\sup_{t\in(0,\infty)} \|x\|_{L^p(\mu_t)}<\infty$. Moreover, suppose
    $\mu_t \Rightarrow \mathcal{L}(X)$ as $t\downarrow 0$, and
    $\mu_t \Rightarrow \mathcal{L}(Z')$ as $t\uparrow \infty$.
    Then
    \[
    W_p(\mathcal{L}(X),\mathcal{L}(Z'))
    \le
    \inf\left\{
    \int_{0}^{\infty}
    \left(\int_{\mathbb{R}} |v_t(x)|^p\,d\mu_t(x)\right)^{1/p}\!dt
    :\ \partial_t \mu_t + \partial_x(\mu_t v_t)=0,\ 
    \mu_t \overset{t\downarrow 0}{\Rightarrow} \mathcal{L}(X),\ 
    \mu_t \overset{t\uparrow \infty}{\Rightarrow} \mathcal{L}(Z')
    \right\},
    \]
    where $\Rightarrow$ denotes weak convergence. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Dynamic formulation of $W_p$

[Lemma 1 of arXiv:2609.03750, '\bf Pullback Measure Attractors, Zero-Noise Limits, and Moderate Deviations for 2D Stochas'] For every $v, \widetilde{v}, \widehat{v}\in V$, the trilinear form $b$ is continuous on $V\times V\times V$, and there exists a constant $C>0$ such that
 \begin{align}
&|b(v,\widetilde{v}, \widehat{v})|\leq C\left(|v|^{\frac{1}{2}}\|v\|^{\frac{1}{2}}\|\widetilde{v}\||\widehat{v}|^{\frac{1}{2}}\|\widehat{v}\|^{\frac{1}{2}}+|\partial_xv||\partial_z \widetilde{v}||\widehat{v}|^{\frac{1}{2}}\|\widehat{v}\|^{\frac{1}{2}}\right),\\
&\left| \langle B(\widetilde{v}, \widetilde{v}) - B(\widehat{v}, \widehat{v}), \widetilde{v} - \widehat{v} \rangle \right|
\leq C \|\widetilde{v}\| |\widetilde{v} - \widehat{v}| \|\widetilde{v} - \widehat{v}\|
+ C |\partial_z \widetilde{v}|  |\widetilde{v} - \widehat{v}|^{1/2} \|\widetilde{v} - \widehat{v}\|^{3/2}.
\end{align}
 Moreover, for all $v,\widetilde v,\widehat v\in V$,
 \[
 b(v,\widetilde v,\widetilde v)=0,
 \qquad b(v,\widetilde v,\widehat v)=-b(v,\widehat v,\widetilde v).
 \]
 If, in addition, $v\in D(A)$, then
\begin{align}
	\langle v\partial_xv+\mathcal W(v)\partial_zv,\partial_{zz}v\rangle=0.
\end{align}
The last identity is used at the Galerkin level before passage to the limit.
If \( v, \widetilde{v} \in V \) and \( \partial_z \widetilde{v} \in V \), then
\begin{equation}
	\|B(v, \widetilde{v})\|_{V'} \leq C\bigl( (|v| + |\partial_z v|)|\partial_{x} \widetilde{v}| + |v| \cdot \|\partial_z \widetilde{v}\| + |v| \cdot |\partial_z \widetilde{v}|^{1/2}\|\partial_z \widetilde{v}\|^{1/2} \bigr).
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 1 of arXiv:2609.03750

[Proposition prop:main-exact-eta-less-one of arXiv:2606.29557, 'Propagation of chaos for Belavkin equations beyond pure states'] Let Hypothesis ~(hyp:perfect-efficiency-tensorization-purity of the paper) (3) hold with
$\gamma_0\in\mathcal S(\mathcal H)$ and $\eta\in (0,1)$.    
Then, for every fixed $n\ge1$ and $T>0$, there exists 
$C_{\eta, T,n}>0$, independent of $N$, such that
\begin{equation}
  \sup_{0\le t\le T}
  \mathbb E\left[
    \left\|
      \rho_t^{N:n}-\Gamma_t^n
    \right\|_1
  \right]
  \le C_{\eta,T,n}N^{-1/16}.
  
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition prop:main-exact-eta-less-one of arXiv:2606.29557

[Lemma 13 of arXiv:2606.18866, 'Cram\'er-Type Moderate Deviations for Engel's Series via a Martingale Approach'] Under \eqref{eq:FS-A1}--\eqref{eq:FS-A2}, there is a constant $C>0$, depending only on $C_0$, such that, uniformly for
\[
 0\le x=o\!\left(\min\{\epsilon_n^{-1},\delta_n^{-1}\}\right),
\]
\begin{equation}
 \left|\log\frac{\Pp(S_n>x)}{1-\Phi(x)}\right|
 \le C\left[
 x^3(\epsilon_n+\delta_n)
 +(1+x)\{\delta_n|\log\delta_n|
 +\epsilon_n|\log\epsilon_n|\}
 \right].
\end{equation}
The same conclusion holds with $S_n$ replaced by $-S_n$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 13 of arXiv:2606.18866

[Prop prop2.11 of arXiv:2411.09988, 'A Study in Markov Chains, Loop-Erased Random Walk and Loop Soups'] The following are equivalent for an irreducible Markov chain.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item The chain is recurrent.
    \item For every $x, y \in A$, $\mathbb{E}^x[V_y] = \infty$.
    \item There exists $x, y \in A$ such that $\mathbb{E}^x[V_y] = \infty$.
    \item For every $x, y \in A$, $\mathbb{P}^x[V_y = \infty] = 1$.
    \item There exists $x, y \in A$ such that $\mathbb{P}^x[V_y = \infty] = 1$. 
\end{enumerate}

body:
[Theorem thm:vonLuxburg of arXiv:2606.14895, 'Effective Resistances and Commute Times in Sparse Random Geometric Graphs'] Let $G_n = (V_n, E_n)$ be an RGG with radius of connection $r_n$ from $n$ uniformly distributed points on $\mathbb{T}^2$ with vertex degrees $D_u$ and graph volume $\mathrm{Vol}(G_n) = \sum_{u\in V_n} D_u$. Suppose that the fixed pair of vertices $u$ and $v$ at positions $X_u$ and $X_v$ are separated by Euclidean distance $d(X_u,X_v) > 8r_n$. Assuming that $n r_n^2 / \ln n \to \infty$ as $n\to\infty$, there exists a constant $c$ such that the commute distance satisfies, with probability converging to $1$, 
\[
nr_n^2\left\vert\frac{1}{\mathrm{Vol}(G_n)}C_{uv} -
\left(\frac{1}{D_u}+\frac{1}{D_v}\right)\right| \leq c/nr_n^3\,.
\]
Therefore, further requiring that $r_n\to 0$ and $nr_n^3\to\infty$ yields
\[
C_{uv} \;\to\; \mathrm{Vol}(G_n)\left(\frac{1}{D_u} + \frac{1}{D_v}\right)\qquad almost\;surely\,.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 3 of von Luxburg et al.\ \cite{vonLuxburg2014} as applied to uniformly distributed points on $\mathbb{T}^2$

body: [Lemma Lem:etalelocaltarget of arXiv:2609.04023, 'Characterizing Contractions and Weighted Blowdowns'] Let $f: \mathcal{X}\rightarrow \mathcal{Z}$ be a morphism of quasi-compact algebraic stacks with finite diagonal and $\mathcal{L}$ be a line bundle on $\mathcal{X}$. Then $\mathcal{L}$ is $f$-ample if and only if for any surjective \'etale representable morphism $\mathcal{Z}'\rightarrow \mathcal{Z}$, the pullback $\mathcal{L}|_{\mathcal{X}'}$ is $f'$-ample for $f':\mathcal{X}':=\mathcal{X}\times_\mathcal{Z}\mathcal{Z}'\rightarrow\mathcal{Z}'$.

Let H: R^n → R be convex and superlinear, L = H*, g: R^n → R Lipschitz, and let u(x,t) = min_y ( tL((x-y)/t) + g(y) ) be the Hopf-Lax function. (i) If g is semiconcave with constant C, i.e. g(x+z) - 2g(x) + g(x-z) ≤ C|z|^2 for all x,z ∈ R^n, then u(x+z,t) - 2u(x,t) + u(x-z,t) ≤ C|z|^2 for all x,z ∈ R^n and all t > 0. (ii) If instead H ∈ C^2 with D^2H(p) ≥ θ I for all p and some θ > 0 (uniform convexity), and g is merely Lipschitz, then u(x+z,t) - 2u(x,t) + u(x-z,t) ≤ |z|^2 / (θ t) for all x,z and all t > 0. In dimension one, (ii) is equivalent to the one-sided (Oleinik) derivative bound u_x(x+h,t) - u_x(x,t) ≤ h/(θ t) for h > 0 in the distributional sense. This one-sided bound is what distinguishes the Hopf-Lax solution from other Lipschitz almost-everywhere solutions.
H convex and superlinear; L = H*
g Lipschitz (plus, in (i), semiconcave with constant C)
in (ii): H ∈ C^2 with D^2H ≥ θI, θ > 0
t > 0 (the bound in (ii) degenerates as t ↓ 0)

body: For differentiable problems, the KKT conditions at a point are: primal feasibility, dual feasibility (lambda >= 0), complementary slackness (lambda_i g_i(x) = 0 for each i), and stationarity (the gradient of the Lagrangian in x vanishes). Under a constraint qualification they are necessary for optimality; for convex problems they are also sufficient, and with Slater's condition they characterize the optima.

[Theorem 24 (See {\cite[Th.~1.11.6) of arXiv:2609.03098, 'Standing waves for Schr\"odinger equations with Kato class potentials and $L^\infty$-bound'] {rybakowski}}]
If $K_0\subset K\subset X$ are isolated invariant sets with respect to the semiflow $\Phi$ such that $K$ is irreducible, and
\[
\overline{0} \neq h(\Phi, K_0)\neq h(\Phi, K)\neq \overline{0},
\]
then there exists a full solution $u\colon \mathbb{R}\to K$ such that 
$u(\mathbb{R})\not\subset K_0$ and either $\alpha(u)\subset K_0$ or 
$\omega(u)\subset K_0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

   u\mapsto f(r+qu)-f(r),\qquad u\geq0,
\]
is almost periodic.

Let X be a nonnegative random variable (or f a nonnegative measurable function on a measure space, integrated against the measure) and a > 0. Then P(X >= a) <= E[X] / a. More generally, if phi: [0, infinity) -> [0, infinity) is nondecreasing and phi(a) > 0, then for any real random variable X, P(X >= a) <= E[phi(X^+)] / phi(a), and for any X and a > 0, P(|X| >= a) <= E|X|^p / a^p for every p > 0 (Markov applied to |X|^p). The bound is attained: for X taking the value a with probability m/a and 0 otherwise (0 < m <= a), E X = m and P(X >= a) = m/a.

body:
Let d,m>=1 and x in R^d be deterministic with ||x||_2=sqrt(d). Let w_i be iid N(0,I_d/d), a_i iid N(0,1/m), and suppose all hidden and output weights are independent. Put f(x)=sum_(i=1..m) a_i sigma(w_i^T x). Assume sigma:R->R is continuous and nonconstant, differentiable almost everywhere, has an almost-everywhere continuous derivative, and |sigma_prime(t)|<=C_sigma(1+|t|^(k-1)) almost everywhere for a fixed integer k>=1 and constant C_sigma>0. There is a C>0 depending only on sigma such that, for every delta in (0,1), with probability at least1-delta, ||grad f(x)||_2 <= C(1+log(1/delta)/sqrt(d))(1+1/sqrt(m delta)). Consequently for any deterministic s>0 and x_s=x-sign(f(x))*s*grad f(x), on the same event ||x_s-x||_2/||x||_2 <= (Cs/sqrt(d))(1+log(1/delta)/sqrt(d))(1+1/sqrt(m delta)). This is the size estimate; no sign-reversal success rate is asserted here.
Deterministic input of norm sqrt(d)
Independent hidden Gaussian vectors of variance1/d and Gaussian output weights of variance1/m

body: In calculus, Taylor's theorem gives an approximation of a -times differentiable function around a given point by a polynomial of degree , called the -th-order Taylor polynomial. For a smooth function, the Taylor polynomial is the truncation at the order of the Taylor series of the function. The first-order Taylor polynomial is the linear approximation of the function, and the second-order Taylor polynomial is often referred to as the quadratic approximation. There are several versions of Taylor's theorem, some giving explicit estimates of the approximation error of the function by its Taylor polynomial.

body:
[Proposition 19 of arXiv:2609.03191, 'On lifting representations and actions on curves of the metacyclic groups $C_{p^s}\rtimes '] We consider a cyclic $C_{p^s}$-extension of $k((t))$, its lower jumps $l_1<\cdots <l_s$, and its upper jumps $u_1<\cdots<u_s$. Then the following properties hold. 

\medskip
{\bf (1)} The lower and upper jumps determine uniquely each other by the recursive identities $l_1:=u_1$ and $l_i:=l_{i-1}+p^{i-1}(u_i-u_{i-1})$ for each $i\in\llbracket2,s\rrbracket$. 

\smallskip
{\bf (2)} For each $j\in\llbracket1,s\rrbracket $ we have $l_j=u_1+\sum_{i=1}^{j-1} p^i(u_{i+1}-u_i)$.

\smallskip
{\bf (3)} For each $j\in\llbracket1,s\rrbracket$ we have identities 
$$\sum_{i=1}^j \frac{l_i}{p^i}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^j p^{i-1}u_i}{p^j}$$
and
$$p^{j-1}u_j:=l_j+(p-1)\sum_{i=1}^{j-1}l_ip^{j-i-1}.$$

{\bf (4)} For $b\in\llbracket0,p^s-1\rrbracket$, write
\[
b=\delta_{1,b}+\delta_{2,b}p+\cdots+\delta_{s,b}p^{s-1}
\]
with $\delta_{i,b}\in\llbracket0,p-1\rrbracket$ for each $i\in\llbracket1,s\rrbracket$ and define
\[
N_{s,b}:=\sum_{i=1}^s p^{s-i}\bigl[p-1+(p-1-\delta_{i,b})l_i\bigr].
\] Then for each $b\in \llbracket1,p^s-1\rrbracket$, if $j\in\llbracket0,s-1\rrbracket$ is the largest such that $p^j\mid b$, then we have identities 
\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
N_{s,b-1}-N_{s,b}&=p^{s-j-1}\Big[l_{j+1}-(p-1)\sum_{i=1}^j p^{j+1-i}l_i\Big]\\
&=p^{s-j-1}[l_1+\sum_{i=1}^j p^i(u_{i+1}-pu_i)].
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
In particular, $N_{s,b-1}-N_{s,b}\ge p^{s-j-1}l_1\ge l_1>0$ and therefore we have $\frac{l_{j+1}}{p^{j+1}}-(p-1)\sum_{i=1}^j\frac{l_i}{p^i}\ge\frac{l_1}{p^{j+1}}>0$.

order, each member is reduced separately with respect to the order in

[Lemma 39 of arXiv:2511.10535, 'Eigenvalues of Brownian Motions on $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$'] There is a universal constant $c>0$ such that the following holds. 
    Let $G$ be an $N\times N$ matrix with standard real Gaussian entries, and assume the $N(N+1)/2$ pairs $\{(G_{ij},G_{ji}): 1\le i\le j\le N\}$ are jointly independent. 
    Then for any $N\times N$ complex matrix $A$, deterministic or random and independent of $G$, and any $k\ge c^{-1}\log N$,
    \[

body:
[Theorem thm:persistence pairing of arXiv:2608.29719, 'Persistence Pairing Graphs: Tracking Changes of Selected Homology Bases'] For the cellwise filtration
\[
K^0 \subseteq K^1 \subseteq \cdots \subseteq K^N,
\]
every persistence pair $(i,j)$ determines the interval
\[
[i,j),
\]
and every unpaired positive index $i$ determines the interval
\[
[i,\infty).
\]
For every positive index $i$, the interval cycle $\rho_i$ defined in~(equation eq:interval-cycle of the paper) represents the corresponding homology class throughout exactly this lifetime.

For the original filtration determined by $f$, a persistence pair $(i,j)$ determines the interval
\[
[f(\sigma_i),f(\sigma_j)),
\]
whereas an unpaired positive cell $\sigma_i$ determines
\[
[f(\sigma_i),\infty).
\]
If $f(\sigma_i)=f(\sigma_j)$, then the interval $[i,j)$ is created entirely by the auxiliary tie-breaking refinement and has zero length on the original filtration value scale. Such an interval is omitted from the usual
barcode.

body:
[Prop of arXiv:2411.09988, 'A Study in Markov Chains, Loop-Erased Random Walk and Loop Soups'] Suppose $D \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ is open, and $f : D \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^d$ is a function with continuous first and second derivatives. Then, for $x \in D$,
    \[\Delta f(x) = 2d \lim_{\epsilon \downarrow 0} \frac{MV(f; x, \epsilon)-f(x)}{\epsilon^2},\]
    where $MV(f; x, \epsilon)$ denotes the mean (average) value of $f$ on the sphere of radius $\epsilon$ centered at $x$, $\{y \in \mathbb{R}^d : |x-y| = \epsilon\}$.

body:
[Lem 12 of arXiv:2511.18861, 'Correlation Decay for Maximum Weight Matchings on Sparse Graphs'] Let $k \ge 1$. Let  $\xi_1, \xi_2, \ldots, \xi_k$ be independent Bernoulli random variables with means $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_k$ and let $W \ge 0$ be another independent random variable. 
Let  
\[ X= \xi_1 + \cdots + \xi_k \text { and  } \quad    Z_i  = X - \xi_i =   \sum_{j: j \ne i} \xi_j \text{ for each } i.\] 
Then we have
\begin{equation} 
  \sum_{i=1}^k p_i \E \Big [ \frac{1}{(1+ W+ Z_i)(2+ W + Z_i)} \Big ] \le \E \Big [ \frac{\mathbf{1}_{\{ X>0 \}}}{1+ W+ X} \Big].    
  \end{equation}
title: Lem 12 of arXiv:2511.18861

body:
[Lemma lem:sensitivity of arXiv:2604.13968, 'Divisible sandpiles via random walks in random scenery'] Let~$G=(V,E)$ be an infinite, locally finite, connected graph, and fix
		vertices $o, v\in V$. Let~$\xi^{(v)}$ denote the scenery obtained by replacing~$\xi(v)$ with an independent copy~$\xi'(v)$.
		Then for each~$n\geq 1$,
		\begin{equation}
			\bigl|u_n(o;\xi)-u_n(o;\xi^{(v)})\bigr|
			\leq g_n(o,v)\,|\xi(v)-\xi'(v)|\,.
		\end{equation}
		If the walk is transient, then
		\[
		u_\infty(o;\xi)\leq u_\infty(o;\xi^{(v)})+g(o,v)\,|\xi(v)-\xi'(v)|\,,
		\]
		and the same bound with $\xi$ and $\xi^{(v)}$ interchanged. In particular, if both values are finite, then

			\bigl|u_\infty(o;\xi)-u_\infty(o;\xi^{(v)})\bigr|

body: [Abstract of arXiv:2609.03856, 'Consensus time for asynchronous $\ell^p$ relaxation: graph dependence'] We study the asynchronous $\ell^p$ relaxation introduced by Amir, Nazarov, and Peres \cite{amir2025convergencerateellpenergyminimization}: at each step, a uniformly chosen vertex minimizes its incident $\ell^p$ energy. For the profile $f_t$ after $t$ updates, let \[ \mathsf T_p(G,1/2):= \sup_{\lVert f_0\rVert_\infty\le1} \E\bigl[\min\{t\ge0:\osc(f_t)\le1/2\}\bigr]. \] For $1<p<\infty$, we obtain graph-dependent estimates for boxes, trees, and conductance expanders. On the nearest-neighbor box $[L]^d$, for $d,L\ge2$ and $n=L^d$, the answer is, up to logarithmic factors, $nd^{1/(p-1)}L^{p/(p-1)}$ for $1<p<2$ and $ndL^2$ for $p\ge2$. On bounded-degree trees, an explicit rerooting-invariant parameter $T_G$ determines the answer up to logarithmic factors; for arbitrary trees it gives upper and lower bounds that differ additionally by the maximum degree. If the volume conductance $h(G)\ge h_0>0$, then $\mathsf T_p(G,1/2)=\Theta_{p,h_0}(n\log n)$ without a degree assumption. At $p=\infty$, every connected graph satisfies $\mathsf T_\infty(G,1/2)\ge c nD^2/\Delta$, where $D$ and $\Delta$ are its diameter and maximum degree.
title: Abstract of arXiv:2609.03856: Consensus time for asynchronous $\ell^p$ relaxation: graph dependence

body:
For the minimal spanning forest of a homogeneous Poisson process in R^d, connectivity (a single tree) is proved only for d = 2 (Alexander) and is open for every d >= 3. The Lyons-Peres-Schramm theory (Minimal spanning forests, Ann. Probab. 2006, on transitive graphs; the Poisson case is its continuum analogue) does not settle it: uniqueness of the infinite cluster makes the free and wired minimal spanning forests coincide, and the absence of percolation at criticality makes every tree of the wired forest one-ended, but neither gives a single tree. The same argument would make the minimal spanning forest of Z^d connected for d >= 11, where theta(p_c) = 0 is known from the lace expansion and uniqueness holds by Burton-Keane, and that question is open (Lyons-Peres, Probability on Trees and Networks, Question 11.35). The Newman-Stein heuristic predicts infinitely many trees when d > 8.

Assumes: homogeneous Poisson process in R^d, Euclidean edge lengths

body: [Lem 9 of arXiv:2604.25725, 'What is The Probability That A Random Graph With A Given Degree Sequence is Connected?'] For all sufficiently small $\epsilon>0$, the following holds. Let $\cD$ be such that $m$ is large enough, $d(n) \le \sqrt{m}(\log{m})^6$, and $D^*\ge\eps m$. Then with probability $1-o(m^{-8\log\log{m}})$, all the vertices  of degree at least $\sqrt{m}(\log{m})^{-2}$ are in the same component.

body:
[Main1 16 of arXiv:2609.00483, 'On Embedding Hamming Spheres with Applications to Positive Curvature'] Assume $\Z_p^r$ acts effectively and isometrically on a closed, positively
curved manifold $M^n$ with a fixed point $x\in M$, where $p \in \{3,5,7,11,13,17,19\}$ and $n \ge 13$. 
Suppose
\begin{multline*}
r>
\frac12\Bigl(1-H_p(J_p(\tfrac14))\Bigr)n
+\frac32\log_p n
+\log_p\!\left(\frac{p-1}{2}+\frac1n\right)
-\frac12\log_p 2 \\
\qquad
+\frac12\log_p\!\left(\frac{8(1-J_p(\tfrac14))}{J_p(\tfrac14)}\right)
+\log_p(p-1)
=: G(n,p).
\end{multline*}
where $H_p$ and $J_p$ are the $p$-ary entropy and Johnson functions defined in Section \ref{2}. Then $M$ is homotopy equivalent to $S^n$, $\RP^n$, $\CP^{n/2}$, or a lens space.
title: Main1 16 of arXiv:2609.00483

\[
\lvert c_J(\xi,d,\ell)\rvert
\le C2^{\ell-m_{\xi,d}}
\qquad
(0\le\ell<m_{\xi,d}),
\]
and
\[
\lvert c_J(\xi,d,\ell)\rvert\le C
\qquad
(\ell\ge m_{\xi,d}).
\]

[Proposition prop:tight1 of arXiv:2412.02160, 'A functional central limit theorem for weighted occupancy processes of the Karlin model'] Assume $|a_{i+j}-a_i| \le Cj^\beta$ with $\beta\in[0,\alpha/2)$. 
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item For all 
$p\in[1,\alpha/{2\beta})$,
 we have, for some constant $C$, 
\begin{equation}
{\mathbb E}\abs{\what W_n(t)-\what W_n(s)}^{2p} \le C \pp{\sigma_n^2|t-s|^{\alpha} + \sigma_n^{2p}|t-s|^{\alpha p}}, \mbox{ for all } 0\le s<t\le 1, n\in{\mathbb N}.
\end{equation}
\item For some constant $C>0$, almost surely, 
\begin{equation}
\abs{\what W_n(t)-\what W_n(s)}\le C (N(nt)-N(ns) + n(t-s)), \mbox{ for all } 0\le s\le t\le 1.
\end{equation} 
\end{enumerate}
As a consequence, if in addition 
\[
\beta\in\bigg[0,\frac{\alpha^2}2\bigg) \quad\mbox{ and }\quad p\in\pp{\frac1\alpha,\frac{\alpha}{2\beta}}, 
\]
the process $\sigma_n^{-1}\what W_n$ is tight in $D([0,1])$.

[Thm main of arXiv:2603.17858, 'Decay of correlations and zeros for the hard-core model'] Let $\Delta\in \mathbb{N}$ and let $\lambda^\star>0$.
    Let $\mathcal{G}$ be a family of graphs of maximum degree at most $\Delta$. If the hard-core model on $\mathcal{G}$ satisfies very strong spatial mixing at $\lambda^\star$, then there exists $\varepsilon>0$ such that for each $G=(V,E)\in \mathcal{G}$ and $\Vec\lambda\in B(\lambda^\star,\varepsilon)^V$ we have $Z_G(\Vec \lambda)\neq 0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Lemma lemm_BH of arXiv:2503.24372, 'A criterion on the free energy for log-Sobolev inequalities in mean-field particle systems'] Let $N \geq 1$ and $\mu$ be a probability measure on $\R^N$ satisfying a log-Sobolev inequality with constant $\gamma_{\rm LS}>0$. 
Take $F:\R^N\to\R$ to be smooth and compactly supported and a Lipschitz function $H:\R^N\to\R$.
Then:

\begin{equation} 

\cov_{\mu}(F^2,H)^2
\leq 
\frac{4}{\gamma_{\rm LS}^2}  \sup_{x\in\R^N}|\nabla H (x)|^2 \, 
\E_{\mu}[F^2] \; \E_{\mu}\big[|\nabla F|^2\big],
\end{equation}

with the notation $|\nabla H (x)| = \big( \sum_{i =1}^N (\partial_{x_i}  H (x))^2 \big)^{1/2}$.
The same bound holds for a vector valued function $H(x)\in\R^d$.

Let $H_i:\R\to\R$ be Lipschitz ($1\leq i\leq N$) and let $F:\R^N\to\R$ be smooth and compactly supported. Then:

\begin{equation}

\sum_{i=1}^N\cov_{\mu}(F^2,H_i(x_i))^2
  \leq 
  \frac{4}{\gamma_{\rm LS}^2} \max_{1\leq i\leq N}\|H'_i\|^2_\infty \;  \E_{\mu}[F^2] \;  \E_{\mu}\big[|\nabla F
  |^2\big] 
  .
\end{equation}

[Proposition 13 of arXiv:2608.09700, 'A general paracontrolled ansatz for singular SPDEs'] For any $\tau\in\mcB$ and $i\geq -1$ we have the relation
		\[
		[\tau]_i =  \widetilde{ \PPi}(\tau)_i - \sum_{q\geq 1} (-1)^{q-1} \sum_{\tau_q\prec\cdots\prec\tau_1\prec\tau} \widetilde{ g}\big(\tau/\tau_1\big)_{<i-1} \cdots \,  \widetilde{ g}\big(\tau_{q-1}/\tau_{q}\big)_{<i-1} \,  \widetilde{ \PPi} \big(\tau_q\big)_i.
		\]
		Likewise for $\tau/\sigma\in \mcB^+$ we have
		\begin{align*}
			[\tau/\sigma]_i &=  \widetilde{ g}(\tau/\sigma)_i 
			\\
			&\quad - \sum_{q\geq 1} (-1)^{q-1}  \hspace{-0.5cm}\sum_{\sigma\prec\sigma_q\prec\cdots\prec\sigma_1\prec\tau} \widetilde{ g}\big(\tau/\sigma_1\big)_{<i-1}\cdots \, \widetilde{ g}\big(\sigma_{q-1}/\sigma_{q}\big)_{<i-1} \,  \widetilde{ g}\big(\sigma_q/\sigma\big)_i.
		\end{align*}

The inclusion is strict whenever mu has sets of arbitrarily small positive measure (e.g. Lebesgue measure on [0,1]). (c) In general (e.g. Lebesgue measure on R^n) there is no inclusion in either direction between L^p and L^q for p different from q.

[Lemma 19 of arXiv:2607.23791, 'Precise cover times for branching random walks on Hamming graphs: (iterated) logarithmic c'] \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=*]
\item
Fix $C<\infty$.  For all $d$ large enough, uniformly for
$0\le D\le C\log\log d$ and
$r\in\{0,\ldots,d\}$ with $r\le C\log\log d$, if
$e^{-\chi D}R^r\le1$, then, for any start $x$ and target $y$ satisfying
$d_{\rm H}(x,y)=d-r$,
\begin{equation}
 \Pp_x\!\left(\tau_y\le x_\star d-D\right)
 \gg_C e^{-\chi D}R^r.
\end{equation}

\item
There is a constant $\delta>0$ such that, for every
$0\le\ell\le d$ and every $x,y$ satisfying
$d_{\rm H}(x,y)\le d-\ell/2$,
\begin{equation*}
 \Pp_x\!\left(\tau_y\le x_\star d-2\delta\ell\right)\gg1
\end{equation*}
for all $d$ large enough.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] A Hilbert space is a complex vector space $H$, with a scalar product on it $<x,y>$, taken linear at left and antilinear at right,
$$<\lambda x,y>=\lambda<x,y>\quad,\quad <x,\lambda y>=\bar{\lambda}<x,y>$$
which is complete with respect to corresponding norm
$$||x||=\sqrt{<x,x>}$$
in the sense that any sequence $\{x_n\}$ which is a Cauchy sequence, having the property $||x_n-x_m||\to0$ with $n,m\to\infty$, has a limit, $x_n\to x$.

[Defn of arXiv:2609.01791, 'Minimum $b_2$ of symplectic fillings of lens spaces'] A \textit{left-right sequence} is a (possibly empty) finite string of ``L''s and ``R''s. A left-right sequence associated with a sequence of deep blowups is the string of ``L''s and ``R''s recording whether the blowup happened at the left side or right side of the trough for each blowup.

We read a left-right sequence from left to right in chronological order. Thus $RRL$ means: first perform a deep blowup on the right of the trough, then another on the right, and finally one on the left.

Given a left-right sequence $S$, we define the tuple $apply(S)$ to be the adjusted value tuple obtained by applying the corresponding sequence deep blowups on the trough in the adjusted value tuple $(1,-1,1)$.
title: Unnumbered defn of arXiv:2609.01791, 'Minimum $b_2$ of symplectic fillings of lens spaces'

[Definition 13 (Planar duality; Figure~\ref{fig:dual_graph}, \textsc{Right}) of arXiv:2605.28473, 'The BKT transition and surface tension differentiability'] Let $G$ be a leafless connected finite planar graph embedded in the plane; we call it
    the \emph{primal graph}.
    Write $\partial G\subset V(G)$ for the set of vertices incident to the outer face.
    The corresponding \emph{dual graph} $G^*$ is defined as follows.
    \begin{itemize}
        \item Its vertex set $V(G^*)$ is the disjoint union of:
            \begin{itemize}
                \item The set of \emph{inner} faces of $G$,
                \item The set of edges of $G$ incident to the outer face.
            \end{itemize}
        \item The edge set $E(G^*)$ is in natural bijection with $E(G)$.
        \item The graph boundary $\partial G^*\subset V(G^*)$ is defined as the set of
            dual vertices corresponding to the edges incident to the outer face of $G$.
    \end{itemize}

    This gives an efficient set-theoretic definition of the dual graph.
    We typically use it through its natural planar embedding,
    see Figure~\ref{fig:dual_graph}.
title: Planar duality; Figure~\ref{fig:dual_graph}, \textsc{Right}

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For simple random walk on the incipient infinite cluster of critical percolation, or more generally on critical random media with anomalous volume growth, Kesten's argument establishes subdiffusive behavior, that the walk's typical displacement after n steps scales as n^{1/(2+theta)} for some theta>0 rather than the diffusive n^{1/2}, by combining a volume-growth estimate showing balls of radius r typically contain of order r^{d_f} points, with d_f the fractal (volume) dimension of the cluster, and an effective-resistance estimate showing R_eff(0, B(0,r)^c) grows faster than linearly, of order r^{1+theta}, reflecting the long dangling ends and low-conductance bottlenecks characteristic of the critical cluster. Combining volume growth and resistance growth via the Nash/heat-kernel machinery, or a direct expected-exit-time computation, gives the subdiffusive exponent. The argument does not give the exact value of the subdiffusivity exponent in most dimensions, only bounds, with the precise exponent known rigorously only in specific settings such as sufficiently high dimension or tree-like/hierarchical models, and it is specific to critical (not subcritical or supercritical) percolation geometry, where the fractal, tree-like structure with many bottlenecks is essential to the argument. Typical failure: Assuming the subdiffusivity exponent established for one setting, such as high-dimensional or tree-based incipient infinite clusters where exact computation is possible, transfers to two-dimensional critical percolation, where the exact random-walk dimension remains a major open problem; volume-growth and resistance-growth exponents are model- and dimension-specific quantities that must be independently estimated rather than imported across models with superficially similar critical geometry. Canonical reference: Kesten, 1986, Annales de l'Institut Henri Poincare, Probabilites et Statistiques; Barlow, Jarai, Kumagai and Slade, 2008, Communications in Mathematical Physics.
the walk is on the incipient infinite cluster or a similarly statistically self-similar critical random graph
a known or boundable volume-growth exponent d_f for balls in the cluster
a known or boundable effective-resistance-growth exponent reflecting the bottleneck/dangling-end structure
typically also requires the cluster's law to have appropriate scale-invariance, or at least comparable behavior across scales

[Theorem 12 (Sharp Stieltjes moment determinacy of the factor) of arXiv:2606.18458, 'Stable size-biasing and the positive scale-mixture order of generalized Gaussian laws'] Let $0<p\le q$, and let $V_{p,q}$ be the unique positive factor in Theorem~\ref{thm:main}. Then $V_{p,q}$ is Stieltjes moment-determinate if and only if
\[
\frac1p-\frac1q\le2 .
\]
Equivalently, it is Stieltjes moment-indeterminate if and only if $1/p-1/q>2$. In particular, $V_{p,p}=1$ and the boundary case $1/p-1/q=2$ are determinate.

body: [Theorem 5.3 of arXiv:2509.26030, 'Muon Outperforms Adam in Tail-End Associative Memory Learning'] If Assumptions 5.1 and 5.2 hold, with fixed $\alpha,\beta$ such that $\alpha\neq\beta$, and $K$ goes to infinity, we obtain the following results for one-step gd, Muon, and Adam. • For gd, for any $\widetilde{E}$ and $E$ satistifying Assumption 5.1, we have $\displaystyle\varrho_{\text{GD}}^{\epsilon}=O(\epsilon^{-r(\alpha,\beta)}K^{r(\alpha,\beta)-1}),\text{ where }r(\alpha,\beta)=\min\bigg\{\frac{\alpha(1-\beta)}{\beta(1-\alpha)},\frac{\beta(1-\alpha)}{\alpha(1-\beta)}\bigg\}<1.$ • For Muon, for any $\widetilde{E}$ and $E$ satistifying Assumption 5.1, we have $\displaystyle\varrho_{\text{Muon}}^{\epsilon}\geq 1-\epsilon\bigg(1+O\bigg(\frac{\log K}{K}\bigg)\bigg),\text{ and }G_{\text{Muon}}(W_{0})=-\widetilde{E}E^{\top}+O\bigg(\frac{1}{K}\widetilde{E}J_{K,K}E^{\top}\bigg),$ where $J_{K,K}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times K}$ is the matrix with all elements equal to $1$. The big- $O$ notation for matrices means that for $A=O(B)$, each entry satisfies $A_{ij}=O(B_{ij})$ for all $i,j$. • For Adam, there exist $\widetilde{E}$ and $E$ satisfying Assumption 5.1 such that $\varrho_{\text{SignGD}}^{\epsilon}\geq 1-\epsilon.$ There also exist $\widetilde{E}^{\prime}$ and $E^{\prime}$ satisfying Assumption 5.1 such that $\displaystyle\varrho_{\text{SignGD}}^{\epsilon}=O(\epsilon^{-0.7}K^{-0.3}),\text{ and }\frac{\sigma_{\min}\big(G_{\text{SignGD}}(W_{0})\big)}{\sigma_{\max}\big(G_{\text{SignGD}}(W_{0})\big)}\leq 25\%,$ where $\sigma_{\max}$ and $\sigma_{\min}$ are the largest and smallest singular values, respectively.

[De 1 of arXiv:2607.28078, '2607.28078'] (1) Fix a filtered probability space carrying an $\mathbb{R}^m$-valued Brownian motion $B$ and an $\mathcal{F}_0$-measurable random variable $X_0$. An adapted continuous $\mathbb{R}^d$-valued process $X$ is called a \emph{strong solution} of (\ref{2.1}) if
\[
\mathbb{E} \int_{0}^{t}\bigg\{\big\|b(s,X(s),\mathcal{L}_{X(s)})\big\|_{\mathbb{R}^d}+\big\|\sigma(s,X(s),\mathcal{L}_{X(s)})\big\|^2_{\mathbb{R}^{d\times m}}\bigg\}ds<\infty,\,\, t\geq0,
\]
and if, $\mathbb{P}$-almost surely,
\[
X(t)=X_0+\int_{0}^{t}b(s,X(s),\mathcal{L}_{X(s)})ds+\int_{0}^{t}\sigma(s,X(s),\mathcal{L}_{X(s)})dB(s),\,\, t\geq0,
\]
where $\mathcal L_{X(t)}\in\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)$ for every $t\geq0$. \emph{Pathwise uniqueness} holds if any two such strong solutions defined with respect to the same $B$ and the same $X_0$ coincide almost surely.
		
(2) A pair $(\tilde{X}(t),\tilde{B}(t))_{t\geq0}$ is called a \emph{weak solution} of $(\ref{2.1})$ if it solves the equation on some stochastic basis $(\tilde{\Omega},\tilde{\mathcal{F}},\{\tilde{\mathcal{F}}_t\}_{t\geq0},\tilde{\mathbb{P}})$ and $\tilde B$ is an $\mathbb R^m$-valued Brownian motion on that basis.

 \begin{itemize}
 \item[(P1)] The segments $[\hat a^\circ_k,\hat b^\circ_k]$ indexed by $k\in[K]$ are disjoint and at distance at least $\eps$ from each other.
 \item[(P2)] $\forall k \in [K] \qquad [\alpha_k-\eps,\beta_k+\eps]\subseteq [\hat a^\circ_k,\hat b^\circ_k]\subseteq [\hat a_{h^k},\hat b_{h^k}]$.

 \item[(P6)] The random $3K$-tuple $(\hat{\boldsymbol{a}}^\circ, \hat{\boldsymbol{b}}^\circ, \boldsymbol{N}^\circ)$ is a deterministic affine function of the random $K$-tuple $\boldsymbol{Q}^\circ$. \liminf_{\eta\downarrow0}\eta^{2}(\log(1/\eta))^{2}\,\mathbb{E}[N_{\mathrm{in}}(\eta)]\ge c_{-}.
\end{equation}
In particular, after decreasing $c_{-}$ if necessary, there exists $\eta_{0}>0$ such that, for every $0<\eta<\eta_{0}$,
\[
\mathbb{E}[N_{\mathrm{in}}(\eta)]\ge\frac{c_{-}}{\eta^{2}(\log(1/\eta))^{2}}.
\]

[Cor 2 of arXiv:2604.26316, 'Smallest distances between zeros of Gaussian analytic functions'] Let $\sigma_k$ be the $k$-th smallest distance between all pairs of zeros,  
		then its limiting density satisfies 
		$$\lim_{n\to\infty} \mathbb P\Big(\big(\frac 18\big)^{1/4}n^{3/4}\sigma_k\in [x,x+ dx]\Big)=\frac{ 4x^{4k-1}}{(k-1)!}e^{-  x^4}dx.$$
		Furthermore, let $\pi_k$ be the location of $\hat z_{ij}$ such that $d_g(z_i,z_j)$ equals $\sigma_k$, then $\pi_k$ is asymptotically independent of $\sigma_k$, and tends to the uniform measure with respect to the volume form, i.e.,  for any $U\subseteq M$,
		$$
		\lim_{n\to\infty}\P(\pi_k\in U)=\int_{U}\frac\omega\pi. 
		$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma lem:reduced-same-shell-increment of arXiv:2607.29330, 'Large deviations for the maximum of\\ the generalized TAP free energy'] Fix a regular \(f\in(f_{\mathrm{eq}},f_1)\), write
		\(\theta=\theta_f\) and \(\zeta=\zeta_f\), and let \(q\) be the first
		positive contact point of \(\zeta\). Let \(X\) be the
		Auffinger--Chen process associated with \(\zeta\). For
		\(\varepsilon>0\), fix \(\mathbf{m}\in(-1,1)^N\), and define \(b_i\) by
		\[
		m_i=\partial_x\Phi_\zeta(q,b_i).
		\]
		Write \(\mathbf{b}=(b_i)_{i\le N}\).
		Assume that
		\[
		|q_\mathbf{m}-q|\le\varepsilon,
		\qquad
		W_2\left(
		\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\delta_{b_i},
		\mathrm{Law}(X_q)
		\right)\le\varepsilon.
		\]
		For \(f'\in[f-\varepsilon,f+\varepsilon]\), condition on
		\[
		F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})=Nf',
		\qquad
		\nabla F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})=0.
		\]
		Assume also that
		\[
		\left|
		f'
		+\frac1N\left(
		F_{\mathrm{TAP}}(\mathbf{m})-F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})
		\right)
		-f
		\right|
		\le\varepsilon.
		\]
		Denote the corresponding conditional expectation by
		\(\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{m},f'}\).
		There is a centered Gaussian field \(G_\mathbf{m}\), independent of the
		conditioned value and gradient, such that, for every fixed
		\(r\in(-q,q)\),
		\begin{equation}
			\begin{aligned}
				F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m}')-F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})
				&=G_\mathbf{m}(\mathbf{m}')
				+\sum_{i=1}^N\left[
				\frac{\xi'(r)}{\xi'(q)}m'_i b_i
				+\Phi_\zeta^*(q,m'_i)-\Phi_\zeta(q,b_i)
				\right]\\
				&\quad+N\theta\bigl[\xi(r)-r\xi'(r)-\xi(q)+q\xi'(q)\bigr]
				+N o_\varepsilon(1)+N o_\delta(1)+o_N(N),
			\end{aligned}
		\end{equation}
		uniformly when \(\lvert q_{\mathbf{m}'}-q\rvert\le\delta\) and
		\(\lvert R(\mathbf{m},\mathbf{m}')-r\rvert\le\delta\). Here
		\(o_N(N)/N\to0\) for fixed \(\varepsilon,\delta\), while
		\(o_\varepsilon(1)\to0\) and \(o_\delta(1)\to0\) as their respective
		parameters tend to zero. All errors are uniform over the displayed
		\(\varepsilon\)-window conditions. For two points
		\(\mathbf{m}'^1,\mathbf{m}'^2\) in this slice,
		\[
		\frac1N\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{m},f'}\left[
		G_\mathbf{m}(\mathbf{m}'^1)G_\mathbf{m}(\mathbf{m}'^2)
		\right]
		=
		\xi(R_{12})-
		\frac{\xi'(r)^2}{\xi'(q)}R_{12}+C_r
		+o_\varepsilon(1)+o_\delta(1)+o_N(1),
		\]
		where \(R_{12}=N^{-1}\langle\mathbf{m}'^1,\mathbf{m}'^2\rangle\) and \(C_r\) depends
		only on \(q\) and \(r\).

body: Noether's theorem states that every continuous symmetry of the action of a physical system with conservative forces has a corresponding conservation law. This is the first of two theorems published by the mathematician Emmy Noether in 1918. The action of a physical system is the integral over time of a Lagrangian function, from which the system's behavior can be determined by the principle of least action. This theorem applies to continuous and smooth symmetries of physical space. Noether's formulation is quite general and has been applied across classical mechanics, high energy physics, and recently statistical mechanics.
title: Noether's theorem

[Lemma lem3 of arXiv:2608.30848, '\huge \bf Limit Laws of the Iterated Logarithm Under Sub-linear Expectations'] Let $\{X_n;n\ge 1\}$ be a sequence of independent random variables on a sub-linear expectation space $(\Omega,\mathscr{H},\widehat{\mathbb E})$ satisfying ((eqexpressbyP of the paper)). Denote
$$ \mathcal{F}_n=\sigma(X_1,\ldots,X_n) \; \text{ and }\; \mathcal{F}_0=\{\emptyset,\Omega). $$
Then for each $P\in\mathscr{P}$, we have
$$ E_P\big[\varphi(X_n)|\mathcal{F}_{n-1}\big]\le \widehat{\mathbb E}[\varphi(X_n)]\;\; a.s., \;\; \varphi\in C_{b,Lip}(\mathbb R). $$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: The heat equation is the parabolic partial differential equation u_t = k Laplacian(u) for a function u(x, t), with k > 0 the diffusivity. On R^n with initial data u(x, 0) = f(x), the solution is the convolution of f with the heat kernel (4 pi k t)^(-n/2) exp(-|x|^2 / (4 k t)); solutions smooth out instantly and obey the maximum principle.
title: Heat Equation

body:
[Definition 10 of arXiv:2506.13913, '2506.13913'] {Multi-dimensional Itô Integral}{}
 let $(W_t)_{t \geq 0}$ be a standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion. Furthermore, let $f(t, \omega): [0, T] \times \Omega \to \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$ be a matrix of $\mathcal{F}_t$-adapted processes such that each entry $f_{ij}(t, \omega)$ belongs to the space $L^2([0, T] \times \Omega)$, i.e.,
 \[
\mathbb{E}\left[ \int_0^T \| f(t) \|_F^2 \, \mathrm{d}t \right] < \infty,
\]
where $\| f(t) \|_F$ denotes the Frobenius norm of the matrix $f(t)$. Then the \textbf{multi-dimensional Itô integral} is defined as:
\[
\int_0^T f(t) \, \mathrm{d}W_t = 
\begin{pmatrix}
\sum\limits_{j=1}^d \int\limits_0^T f_{1j}(t) \, \mathrm{d}W_t^j, \dots, 
\sum\limits_{j=1}^d \int\limits_0^T f_{nj}(t) \, \mathrm{d}W_t^j
\end{pmatrix}^\top,
\]
where each term is a sum of scalar Itô integrals.
title: Definition 10 of arXiv:2506.13913

[Lemma 5 (Slope-jump representation) of arXiv:2608.31157, 'Sharp Approximation Rates for Neural Networks with Affine Latent Parameterizations'] Let $\varphi:\R\to\R$ be continuous and piecewise linear with breakpoints
$\kappa_1<\cdots<\kappa_J$.  Suppose its slope is $m_0$ to the left of
$\kappa_1$, is $m_j$ between $\kappa_j$ and $\kappa_{j+1}$ for
$j=1,\ldots,J-1$, and is $m_J$ to the right of $\kappa_J$.  Then
\begin{equation}
 \varphi(x)
 =\varphi(\kappa_1)+m_0(x-\kappa_1)
 +\sum_{j=1}^{J}(m_j-m_{j-1})\varrho(x-\kappa_j).
\end{equation}
Consequently, $\varphi$ is realized by an architecture in
$\Arch(5,2J+2)$.  If $\varphi(\kappa_1)$ and all its slopes are affine
functions of a latent vector, the realization can be chosen so that every
parameter slot is affine in that vector.

[Definition 19 of arXiv:2608.17509, '2608.17509'] For \(\sigma\in L^\infty(\mathbb R)\), define the truncated Wiener--Hopf operator \(W_L(\sigma)\) on \(L^2(0,L)\) by
\[
(W_L(\sigma)f)(x')
=
\frac{1}{2\pi}
\int_0^L
\int_{\mathbb R}\sigma(\xi)e^{i\xi(x'-x)}f(x)
\,\mathrm d\xi\,\mathrm dx,
\qquad 0<x'<L,
\]
in the Fourier-multiplier sense. Equivalently, if \(f\) is extended by zero to \(\mathbb R\), then \(W_L(\sigma)f\) is the restriction to \((0,L)\) of the inverse Fourier transform of \(\sigma\widehat f\).

[Ppn 255 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] We have $\chi'(1) \le L^2$.

\begin{proof}
Throughout this proof we abbreviate $\bg\equiv(\bG,\bg^\aux)$.  Consider small positive $\delta$, and define
    \[\begin{aligned}
    \bx&=\cA( (1-\delta)^{1/2}\bg+\delta^{1/2}\bg')\,,\\
    \by &= \E(\bx\,|\, \bg)\,,\\
    \bz &= \bx-\by\,.
    \end{aligned}\]
By iterated expectations, we have
    \[
    \frac{\E(\by,\by)}{N}
    =\frac{\E(\bx,\by)}{N}
    =\chi(1-\delta)\,, 
    \]
as well as $\E(\by,\bz)=0$. It follows that
    \beq
    \chi(1)
    =\frac{\E(\bx,\bx)}{N}
    =\frac{\E(\by,\by)}{N}+\frac{\E(\bz,\bz)}{N}
    =\chi(1-\delta) + \frac{\E(\bz,\bz)}{N}\,.\eeq
Let us treat $\bz$ as a function of $\bg'$ for fixed $\bg$. Note that $\E(\bz\,|\,\bg)=0$. Since $\cA$ is $L$-Lipschitz, we see that $\bz$ is $(L\delta^{1/2})$-Lipschitz as a function of $\bg'$. It follows (using e.g.\ Lemma~\ref{l:lip.subgaus}) that
    \[
    \frac{\E(\bz,\bz)}{N} \le O(L^2\delta)\,.
    \]
Recalling \eqref{eq:bz}, we see that $\chi(1-\delta) \ge \chi(1)-O(L^2\delta)$, which implies $\chi'(1) \le L^2$ as claimed. 
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition 27 (Qualitative observability alone does not choose a topology) of arXiv:2608.04993, '2608.04993'] The finite-rank central restart algebra and point-separation by all scalar linear
probes do not determine a Banach completion.  For every pair
$1\le r_A,r_Q\le\infty$, the same finite-dimensional algebraic skeleton supports
orthogonally natural coefficient geometries with Schatten exponents
$(r_A,r_Q)$.  Their dual state gauges have exponents $(r_A',r_Q')$, with compact
operator completion at an $\infty$ endpoint, and are generally inequivalent.
Nevertheless the complete dual probe families separate the same finite-rank
points and reconstruct the same central product.  Hence the principal
$\mathcal S_2/\mathcal S_1$ split is selected by the quantitative Brownian
response laws, not by qualitative separation alone.

body: In probability theory, Lindeberg's condition is a sufficient condition for the central limit theorem (CLT) to hold for a sequence of independent random variables. Unlike the classical CLT, which requires that the random variables in question have finite variance and be both independent and identically distributed, Lindeberg's CLT only requires that they have finite variance, satisfy Lindeberg's condition, and be independent. It is named after the Finnish mathematician Jarl Waldemar Lindeberg.
title: Lindeberg's condition

[Theorem 5 of arXiv:2609.01462, 'Parametrized LS category and group actions'] Let $d\colon G\to K$ be a derivation relative to an action of $G$ on $K$ and let 
$s_d\colon G\to K\rtimes G$ be given as $s_d(g):=(d(g),g)$. Pick any $K\rtimes G$-module

[Lemma lem333 of arXiv:2411.08303, 'The discrepancy in min-max statistics between two random matrices with finite third moment'] Let  $\xi \sim N\left(0, \Sigma^{\xi}\right)$  and  $\eta \sim N\left(0, \Sigma^{\eta}\right)$  be independent  n -dimensional Gaussian vectors, and define
		
		$$\zeta(t)=\sqrt{t}\xi +\sqrt{1-t} \eta, \quad t \in[0,1] .$$
		
		
		Then we have for every smooth function  $p$ 
		$$\frac{d}{d t} \mathbb{E}[p(\zeta(t))]=\frac{1}{2} \sum_{i, j=1}^{n}\left(\Sigma_{i j}^{\xi}-\Sigma_{i j}^{\eta}\right) \mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\partial^{2} p}{\partial x_{i} \partial x_{j}}(\zeta(t))\right] ,$$
		which means $$\begin{aligned} 
			\mathbb{E}[p(\xi)]-\mathbb{E}[p(\eta)]=&\mathbb{E}[p(\zeta(1))]-\mathbb{E}[p(\zeta(0))] \\
			=&\int_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}(\Sigma_{ij}^{\xi}-\Sigma_{ij}^{\eta})\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\partial^2 p}{\partial x_i \partial x_j}(\zeta (t)) \right]dt.\\  
		\end{aligned} $$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lem rationalmarkov of arXiv:2412.00593, 'A new approach to strong convergence II.\\The classical ensembles'] Let $p,q\in\mathbb{N}$ with $p\ge q$, let
$f\in \mathcal{P}_p$, and define the rational function 
$r:=\frac{f}{\tilde g_q}$. Then
$$
        \frac{1}{m!}\|r^{(m)}\|_{[0,\frac{1}{cp}]}
        \le 
        \bigg( e^{-p} (Cp)^m  +
        \frac{(Cp)^{3m}}{(m!)^2}\bigg) 
	\sup_{N\ge q}|r(\tfrac{1}{N})|
$$
for all $m\ge 1$, where $c,C$ are universal constants.
title: Rational Markov inequality

body:
[Dfn 13 of arXiv:2507.08909, 'Annealed almost periodic entropy'] If $S$ is any set (not necessarily finite), $Q$ is a positive semidefinite $S$-by-$S$ matrix, and $E,F$ are disjoint finite subsets of $S$, then we write
\[Q[F\mid E] := Q[F] - Q[F,E]Q[E]^\dag Q[E,F],\]
the generalized Schur complement of $Q[E]$ in $Q[E\cup F]$.  Now we define the \textbf{conditional log-determinant entropy of $F$ given $E$ in $Q$} by
\[\rmH_Q(F\mid E) := \log \det Q[F\mid E],\]
and the \textbf{log-determinant mutual information between $E$ and $F$ in $Q$} by
\[\rmI_Q(E\,;\,F) := -\log \det \big(I_{|F|} - (Q[F]^\dag)^{1/2}Q[F,E]Q[E]^\dag Q[E,F](Q[F]^\dag)^{1/2}\big).\]

[Lemma STassump of arXiv:2607.22991, 'Mixing times and spectra of non-equilibrium symmetric exclusion processes on general graph'] Consider the dynamics ${\mathcal Q}={\mathcal S}+{\mathcal H}$ with heat bath~${\mathcal H}$, as in~(equation Sin of the paper) and~(equation Hh of the paper),
and let ${\mathcal A}={\mathcal H}'-{\mathcal H}$ for some other heat bath~${\mathcal H}'$ as in~(equation A of the paper).  Let $T$ be a $\{0,1\} \times \{0,1\}$ matrix such that 
\begin{align} [S,T\otimes I + I \otimes T]&=0 ; \\
\forall v \; [H(v),T]&=0;  \\
\forall v \; [A(v),T]&=cA(v), 
\end{align}
and define
\begin{equation} {\mathcal T}=\sum_{v \in V} T(v) \otimes I(V\backslash \{v\}),  \end{equation}
where $T(v)$ is the operator applying $T$ at site $v$.

body:
[Theorem 13 of arXiv:2506.13913, '2506.13913'] {Itô's Integration by Parts}{}
Let \(\{X_t\}_{t \geq 0}\) and \(\{Y_t\}_{t \geq 0}\) be two Itô processes defined by
\[
\mathrm{d}X_t = \mu_X(t, X_t) \, \mathrm{d}t + \sigma_X(t, X_t) \, \mathrm{d}W_t, \quad
\mathrm{d}Y_t = \mu_Y(t, Y_t) \, \mathrm{d}t + \sigma_Y(t, Y_t) \, \mathrm{d}W_t,
\]
where \(W_t\) is a Brownian motion. Then, the product \(Z_t = X_t Y_t\) satisfies
\[
\mathrm{d}(X_t Y_t) = X_t \, \mathrm{d}Y_t + Y_t \, \mathrm{d}X_t + \mathrm{d}\langle X, Y \rangle_t,
\]
where \(\mathrm{d}\langle X, Y \rangle_t\) is the differential of the quadratic covariation process of \(X_t\) and \(Y_t\), given by
\[
\mathrm{d}\langle X, Y \rangle_t = \sigma_X(t, X_t) \sigma_Y(t, Y_t)^\top \, \mathrm{d}t.
\]
Therefore, expanding the terms explicitly gives
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{d}(X_t Y_t) 
&= \big( X_t \mu_Y(t, Y_t) + Y_t \mu_X(t, X_t) 
+ \sigma_X(t, X_t) \sigma_Y(t, Y_t)^\top \big) \, \mathrm{d}t \\
&\quad + X_t \sigma_Y(t, Y_t) \, \mathrm{d}W_t 
+ Y_t \sigma_X(t, X_t) \, \mathrm{d}W_t.
\end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 13 of arXiv:2506.13913

[Lemma lem-leading of arXiv:2605.15395, 'Equivalence and Separation for Multivariate Matrix-Exponential and Phase-Type Distribution'] Let $F$ and $G$ be non-zero polynomials over the real field in the variables $s_{1},\ldots,s_{n}$. Suppose that $F=GH$ for another polynomial $H$. Denote the leading homogeneous parts by $F_{\mathrm{top}}$, $G_{\mathrm{top}}$, and $H_{\mathrm{top}}$. Then
\[
  F_{\mathrm{top}}=G_{\mathrm{top}}H_{\mathrm{top}}.
\]
In particular, the leading homogeneous part of $G$ is a factor of the leading homogeneous part of $F$.

An unsigned three-edge forest is, after removing isolated vertices, exactly one of $3K_2$, $P_3+K_2$, $P_4$, $K_{1,3}$ (tag 10), and a signed forest can be switched so all three edges are ordinary differences. VERIFIED INDEPENDENTLY: cross products of ternary rows with all entries nonzero give exactly 16 canonical lines, matching this list. [Definition 33 of arXiv:2604.26026, 'Stochastic Ordering of Dependent Systems under Transformation Models and Archimedean Copul'] Let $\boldsymbol{\alpha}=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n),\,\boldsymbol{\beta}=(\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_n)\in\mathbb{R}^n$.
    \begin{enumerate}
    \item (\cite{marshall2011}, Definition~1.A.1)
     The vector $\boldsymbol{\alpha}$ is said to be majorized by another vector $\boldsymbol{\beta}$, denoted by $\boldsymbol{\alpha} \overset{m}{\preceq}\boldsymbol{\beta}$, if for each $\ell=1, \ldots, n-1$, we have $\sum_{i=1}^{\ell} \alpha_{i:n} \geq \sum_{i=1}^{\ell} \beta_{i:n}$ and $\sum_{i=1}^{n} \alpha_{i:n}=\sum_{i=1}^{n} \beta_{i:n}$, where $\alpha_{i:n}$ and $\beta_{i:n}$ represent the coordinates of $\boldsymbol{\alpha}$ and $\boldsymbol{\beta}$, respectively, ordered increasingly.
    \item (\cite{marshall2011}, Definition~3.A.1)
	A function $h:A\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is said to be Schur-convex (Schur-concave) on $A$ if
	$$
	\boldsymbol{\alpha} \overset{m}\succeq \boldsymbol{\beta} \Rightarrow h(\boldsymbol{\alpha}) \geq(\leq)\; h(\boldsymbol{\beta}),
    \quad \text { for all } \boldsymbol{\alpha},\, \boldsymbol{\beta} \in A.
	$$
\end{enumerate}
title: Definition 33 of arXiv:2604.26026

body:
[Prop 4 (Second-order origin of the empirical ranking) of arXiv:2608.30374, 'Compact and Infinite-Order Error Analysis\\ for Null-Space SVD Estimation'] Let
\(\lambda_{(0)}(\sigma)\leq\cdots\leq
  \lambda_{(m-1)}(\sigma)\)
be the increasingly ordered eigenvalues of \(A(\sigma)\), and let
\(P_{(i)}(\sigma)\) be rank-one eigenprojectors from an ordered
orthonormal eigenbasis.  When an eigenvalue is simple its projector is unique;
the associated unit eigenvector is unique up to sign.  For \(0\leq i<q_0\),
define
\begin{equation}
 R_{\mathrm{emp},i}^{\mathrm{ord}}(\sigma;\mathcal T)
   =\frac1\tau\operatorname{tr}\!\left(
      A(\sigma)P_{(i)}(\sigma)\right),
 \qquad
 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{emp},i}^{\mathrm{ord}}(\sigma)
   =\mathbb E_{\mathrm{tr}}
      [R_{\mathrm{emp},i}^{\mathrm{ord}}(\sigma;\mathcal T)].
 
\end{equation}
Then, exactly for every realization,
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{R_{\mathrm{emp},i}^{\mathrm{ord}}(\sigma;\mathcal T)
       =\frac{\lambda_{(i)}(\sigma)}{\tau}},
 \qquad
 R_{\mathrm{emp},0}^{\mathrm{ord}}\leq\cdots\leq
 R_{\mathrm{emp},q_0-1}^{\mathrm{ord}}.
 
\end{equation}
For every \(1\leq q\leq q_0\), these branch risks decompose the aggregate
risk, both before and after expectation:
\begin{equation}
 R_{\mathrm{emp},q}(\sigma;\mathcal T)
   =\sum_{i=0}^{q-1}R_{\mathrm{emp},i}^{\mathrm{ord}}(\sigma;\mathcal T),
 \qquad
 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{emp},q}(\sigma)
   =\sum_{i=0}^{q-1}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{emp},i}^{\mathrm{ord}}(\sigma).
 
\end{equation}
If \(\mu_0\leq\cdots\leq\mu_{q_0-1}\) are the ordered eigenvalues of
the effective matrix \(W\) in \eqref{eq:effective-splitting}, then
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{
 R_{\mathrm{emp},i}^{\mathrm{ord}}(\sigma;\mathcal T)
   =\frac{\sigma^2}{\tau}\mu_i+O_{\mathcal T}(\sigma^3),
   \qquad \sigma\downarrow0.}
 
\end{equation}
Thus \(W\), rather than an arbitrary clean null-space basis, governs the
first nonzero small-noise separations.  If \(W\) is simple, its locally
analytic labelled sheets coincide with \(\lambda_{(i)}\) for all sufficiently
small \(\sigma>0\).  At larger noise, an eigenvalue crossing may exchange
sheet labels; the parenthesized index always denotes instantaneous SVD order.

Under the Gaussian assumptions of \Cref{sec:equal-ranked-equal}, suppose
also that \(\tau\geq m\).  Then
\begin{equation}
 W\sim\operatorname{Wishart}_{q_0}(\tau-n,I_{q_0}),
 \qquad
 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{emp},i}^{\mathrm{ord}}(\sigma)
   =\frac{\sigma^2}{\tau}\,\overline\mu_i+o(\sigma^2),
 \quad \overline\mu_i=\mathbb E[\mu_i],
 
\end{equation}
and
\(\overline\mu_0<\cdots<\overline\mu_{q_0-1}\).
Let \(\overline{\V{\mu}}=(\overline\mu_0,\ldots,
\overline\mu_{q_0-1})^T\).  Consequently, if
\(\V{e}_{\mathrm{emp}}\) collects the expected ordered empirical risks, then
\begin{equation}
 \frac{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{emp},i}^{\mathrm{ord}}(\sigma)}
      {\|\V{e}_{\mathrm{emp}}(\sigma)\|_2}
 \longrightarrow
 \frac{\overline\mu_i}{\|\overline{\V{\mu}}\|_2}
 \quad(\sigma\downarrow0),
 
\end{equation}
which, when \(q_0>1\), is strictly ranked rather than uniform.  Moreover, for every
\(\sigma>0\) the Gaussian sample covariance has simple spectrum almost
surely, so the expected inequalities in \eqref{eq:exact-empirical-order}
are strict.
title: Second-order origin of the empirical ranking

[Definition definition-RWREdiscrete of arXiv:2507.19222, 'Convergence of the KMP model to the KPZ equation'] On a probability space $(\Omega^{(\epsilon)}, \mathcal{F}^{(\epsilon)}, \mathbb{P}^{(\epsilon)})$, we define the following random variables: for each bond $(x,x+1)$, let  $\left(\mathcal{I}_{x,x+1}^{(n)}\right)_{n\in \mathbb{Z}_{\geqslant 0}}$ be a Bernoulli process with parameter $\epsilon\in [0,1]$,  independent for each bond. 
	
	
	For each bond $(x,x+1)$ and each $n\in \mathbb{Z}_{\geqslant 0}$,  let  $B_{x,x+1}^{(n)}$ be an independent random variable distributed as  Beta$(\alpha,\alpha)$. 
	We denote a realization of the  environment by $(\text{Bin}, \omega)\in \Omega^{(\epsilon)}$, where  $\text{Bin}$ is a realization of the Bernoulli processes and $\omega$ is a realization of the Beta variables.
	
	
	Given $(\text{Bin}, \omega)\in \Omega^{(\epsilon)}$, we define a random walk $(X^{\epsilon}(n))_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geqslant 0}}$ as follows. If at discrete-time $n$, $X^{\epsilon}(n)=x$,  the update rule is as follows:
	\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=12pt]
		\item If $\mathcal{I}^{(n)}_{x-1,x} = \mathcal{I}^{(n)}_{x,x+1} = 1$ or if $\mathcal{I}^{(n)}_{x-1,x} = \mathcal{I}^{(n)}_{x,x+1} = 0$ the particle does not move. These events happen with probability $\epsilon^{2}$ and $1-2\epsilon(1-\epsilon)$ respectively. 
		\item If $\mathcal{I}^{(n)}_{x-1,x} = 1$ and $\mathcal{I}^{(n)}_{x,x+1} = 0$: the walker moves to $x+1$ with probability $1 - B^{(n)}_{x,x+1}$, or remains at $x$ with probability $B^{(n)}_{x,x+1}$. This event happens with probability $\epsilon(1-\epsilon)$.
		\item If $\mathcal{I}^{(n)}_{x-1,x} = 0$ and $\mathcal{I}^{n}_{x,x+1} = 1$: the walker moves to $x-1$ with probability $B^{(n)}_{x-1,x}$, or remains at  $x$ with probability $1 - B^{(n)}_{x-1,x}$. This event happens with probability $\epsilon(1-\epsilon)$.
	\end{itemize}
title: Definition definition-RWREdiscrete of arXiv:2507.19222

[Theorem thm:Mecke of arXiv:2607.17764, 'Non-vanishing uniqueness threshold for\\hyperbolic Poisson-Voronoi percolation\\in dimensi'] For $k \in \ensuremath{ \mathbb N},\lambda>0$ and $0\leq p\leq 1$, let $\ensuremath{{\mathcal Z}}_b,\ensuremath{{\mathcal Z}}_w$ be as above and let
$g : (\ensuremath{{\mathbb H}}^d)^k \times \Omega_{\text{PPP}} \times \Omega_{\text{PPP}} \to [0,\infty)$ be a nonnegative, measurable function.
Then

$$ \begin{array}{c} 
\displaystyle
\ensuremath{{\mathbb E}}\left[\sum_{\substack{z_1,...,z_k\in\ensuremath{{\mathcal Z}}_b\\ \text{distinct}}} g(z_1,...,z_k,\ensuremath{{\mathcal Z}}_b,\ensuremath{{\mathcal Z}}_w)\right] \\
= \\
\displaystyle 
\left(p\lambda\right)^k \int_{\ensuremath{{\mathbb H}}^d}\dots\int_{\ensuremath{{\mathbb H}}^d} \ensuremath{{\mathbb E}}_{p,\lambda}
\left[g(u_1,...,u_k,\ensuremath{{\mathcal Z}}_b \cup \{u_1,\dots,u_k\},\ensuremath{{\mathcal Z}}_w)\right] 
\mu({\dd}u_1)\dots\mu({\dd}u_k).
\end{array} $$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma L:location-bd of arXiv:2604.10020, 'The directed landscape in half-space'] Take $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $x \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$ with $x \le n/100$. Take parameters $\alpha, \beta$ satisfying that
$\alpha \ge 1/2 - n^{-1/6}$ and $\beta \in (2(1/2 - \alpha)\vee 0, 1/100)$. Define
$$
y^\pm(\beta) = \argmax_{y\in\llbracket-n, n + x \rrbracket} f^\pm(y, \beta), \quad \text{where }\quad f^\pm(y, \beta) = \frac{|y|}{1/2 \mp \operatorname{sgn}(y)\beta} + \mu[y-\operatorname{sgn}(y), 1; x, n]_\textsf{L}.
$$
Then we have $y^+(\beta)>0$, and
$|y^\pm(\beta) - (x \pm 8 \beta n)|\le 100 \beta^2 n + 1$.
Moreover, there are universal constants $C, c>0$ such that the following statements hold. Let
\[
y^\pm_* = \argmax_{y\in\llbracket-n,n+x \rrbracket} (Z^\pm(y) + X[y-\operatorname{sgn}(y),1; x,n]_\textsf{L}) .
\]
For any $\epsilon > C (1/2 - \alpha)\vee 0$ we have
\[
\mathbb{P}(|y^+_* - y^+(\beta)|\ge \epsilon n),\quad \mathbb{P}(|y^-_* - y^-(\beta)|\ge \epsilon n\;\text{and}\;y^-_*>0)\le 2\exp(- c \epsilon^3 n) + 2 \exp(-c\sqrt{n}).
\]
title: Lemma L:location-bd of arXiv:2604.10020

[Marklofdefinition 8 (Collision relation) of arXiv:2609.03112, '2609.03112'] Let $P_\alpha(m)=P_0(m)+\alpha\ell(m)+c$ on a lattice coset, where
$P_0$ is rational-valued, $\ell$ is a rational linear form, and
$\alpha\notin\Q$.  A pair $(m,n)$ is a \emph{bulk collision} if
\[
 \ell(m)=\ell(n),\qquad P_0(m)=P_0(n).
\]
The diagonal $m=n$ is always a bulk collision.  A \emph{collision graph} is
the graph of a map $\sigma$ for which $(m,\sigma(m))$ is a bulk collision for
all labels in its domain.
title: Collision relation

[Theorem thm:2nd_coef_kernel of arXiv:2607.04514, 'Boundary-layer asymptotics for Gaussian-smoothed singular measures'] Let \(A>0\) and assume (ass:standing of the paper) with \(r\geqslant 2\). Then there exists \(\sigma_0 >
  0\) such that, for every \((y,\sigma)\in\mathcal Y_{A,\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{S}},\sigma_0}\), \(x=\pi(y)\),
  \(a = a(y,\sigma)\), it holds that
  \begin{align*}
    p_\sigma(y) &= \sigma^{-k} (2\pi)^{-d/2} \left[ \mathsf C_0(a,x) + \sigma\mathsf C_1(a,x)
    + \sigma^2\mathscr E_1 (a,x,\sigma) \right], \\
    \log p_\sigma(y) &= -k\log\sigma - (d/2) \log(2\pi) + \mathsf L_0(a,x) + \sigma\mathsf L_1(a,x)
    + \sigma^2\mathscr E_{1,\log} (a,x,\sigma),
  \end{align*}
  where \(\mathsf L_0(a,x)=\log \mathsf C_0(a,x)\), \(\mathsf L_1(a,x)=\mathsf C_1(a,x)/\mathsf
  C_0(a,x)\), and \(\mathscr E_1(a,x,\sigma)\), \(\mathscr E_{1,\log}(a,x,\sigma)\) have all mixed
  derivatives up to order \(r-2\), in the variables \(a\), \(x\), and \(\sigma\), uniformly bounded
  for \(x\in\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{S}}\), \(\|a\|\leqslant A\), and \(0<\sigma\leqslant\sigma_0\). Derivatives
  in \(x\) are computed in the stratum coordinate \(\theta\), after writing \(x=\Phi(\theta,0)\). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 185 of arXiv:2605.03236, 'Stochastic It\^o Equations and Parabolic Second-Order Equations with singular Drift'] Let a   random field $u(t,x)$ be defined on $\bZ^{1}_{\infty}(4)\times \bZ^{d}_{\infty}(2)$.
Assume that there exist constants $ \gamma\geq2\kappa $, $K<\infty$
such that  for $t,s\in
\bZ^{1}_{\infty}(4),x\in\bZ^{d}_{\infty}(2)$
$$
E|u(t,x)-u(s,x)|^{\gamma}\leq 
K^{\gamma} |t-s |^{\gamma/2}, 
$$
$$
E\sup_{x,y\in \bZ^{d}_{\infty}(2)}\frac{|u(t,x)-u(t,y)|^{2\kappa}}
{|x-y|^{2\kappa-d}}\leq K^{2\kappa}.
$$
 Then, for every $0<\alpha<1-(d+2)/(2\kappa)$  
with probability one there exists
a continuous extension of $u$ on
$[0,1]^{d+1}$, called again $u$, and
an integer-valued $n=n(\omega,\alpha,\gamma,\kappa,d)$
such that for any $(t,x),(s,y)\in
[0,1]^{d+1}$ satisfying $|t-s|\leq 2^{-n}$ and $ |x-y | \leq 2^{-n}$  we have
\begin{equation}
                   
|u(t,x)-u(s,y)|\leq N(\alpha, d)K
(|t-s|^{\alpha/2}+|x-y|^{\alpha}).
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Own-work EXPOSITION OF A CLASSICAL METHOD; proof (unaudited); T421-W706-035 version1. Let U be open in R^d,d>=2. Let Gamma be a relatively closed embedded one-dimensional real-analytic submanifold of U without boundary,and W a connected embedded one-dimensional real-analytic submanifold of U without boundary. Then either W is contained in Gamma,or W intersect Gamma is discrete and countable. Thus a witness in W outside Gamma excludes a common open arc and forces countable intersections. This classical supporting lemma uses analytic local defining maps,the one-variable identity theorem,closedness,and second countability. In015 its application still requires the separately proved analytic stable fiber,proper embedded finite-time initialization curve away from zero,and continued nonphysical-history witness. The lemma does not independently verify those prerequisites or the p>1 nontracking theorem,and no novelty or new frontier move is claimed.
U open in R^d,d>=2
Gamma relatively closed,embedded,one-dimensional,real analytic,without boundary
W connected,embedded,one-dimensional,real analytic,without boundary

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:f24b2bb0f844f6b32d8e809754ae9ffb9b584bdc5854d535af5ccfb0f70118b3","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/f2/f24b2bb0f844f6b32d8e809754ae9ffb9b584bdc5854d535af5ccfb0f70118b3.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:cc6a978b1c69cef9d35e5e6a4580f5af6fbf600121dfbf5c25b033b876c5a478","bundle_entry_key":"analytic-curve-continuation","bundle_id":"population.analytic-curve-continuation-020","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"real analytic geometry and dynamical systems","draft":"w706/bundle_020.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:analysis.realanalytic:closed-real-analytic-curve-continuation-isolated-countable-intersections","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"T421-W706-035 v1; kind special; target1; proof (unaudited).
Classical supporting method, not a new frontier theorem or novelty claim.

LEMMA
Let U be open in R^d, d>=2. Let Gamma be a relatively closed embedded
one-dimensional real-analytic submanifold of U without boundary.
Let W be a connected embedded one-dimensional real-analytic submanifold
of U without boundary. Then either W is contained in Gamma or
W intersect Gamma is a discrete, hence countable, subset of W.
In particular, one witness w in W outside Gamma excludes every common
open arc, and implies countability of the intersection.

PROOF
If p is a nonisolated intersection point in W, choose an analytic
parameterization gamma:(-h,h)->W around p=gamma(0). By embeddedness
and analyticity of Gamma there is an ambient neighborhood O of p and
a real-analytic defining map F:O->R^(d-1), with Gamma intersect O equal
to F^(-1)(0). Shrink the parameter interval so gamma lands in O.
Distinct intersection points tending to p give zeros tending to zero
of every component of F composed with gamma. The one-variable analytic
identity theorem makes all components identically zero near zero.
Thus W has an open arc around p contained in Gamma.

Let C consist of points of W with a W-neighborhood contained in Gamma.
It is open. It is also closed in W: if p_j in C tend to p in W,
relative closedness of Gamma first implies p in Gamma. If the sequence
is eventually p, there is nothing to prove. Otherwise pass to distinct
p_j and apply the preceding local identity argument to obtain p in C.
Since W is connected, nonempty C equals W. Thus a nonisolated
intersection forces W subset Gamma. In the other case all intersection
points are isolated. W is second countable; assigning to each isolated
intersection the first basis element meeting the intersection only at
that point gives an injection into a countable basis. This proves
countability, without asserting a uniform separation between points.

APPLICATION TO015, WITH ITS PREREQUISITES EXPLICIT
At a fixed sufficiently late n, let W be one connected local physical
stable fiber with its clocks held fixed, and let Gamma_n be the finite
image of the standard-initialization line in the same physical R^3.
Restrict U to an open neighborhood containing the whole selected fiber
and excluding the physical origin. The fiber has X near +/-a!=0.
The origin is exactly the state from zero initial position, so no
parameter corresponding to a point of this fiber is the nonsmooth
zero-initialization parameter.

Section4 of015 supplies relative closedness from properness, embeddedness
from injectivity and the nonzero finite-time derivative, and analyticity
away from zero. Section2 supplies the connected analytic stable fiber.
Section3 supplies a point of that fiber without a sufficiently long
nonnegative-variance history, so it cannot belong to Gamma_n. Under
THOSE prerequisites the lemma gives discrete countable intersections.
Countability over sufficiently late integer n and both phases then
gives the asserted countable standard basin. No uniform bound on the
number of intersections is needed or obtained.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT PROVE
The lemma does not independently verify015's analytic stable graph,
its projection onto (X,alpha,sigma), or the continuation of its witness
to positive clocks. Certificate058 checks only the finite backward-cone
algebra. Claim021's p>1 result still needs independent audit of all
these prerequisites and its compact relation argument.

HYPOTHESES CANNOT SIMPLY BE DROPPED
Without relative closedness, Gamma=(0,1) times{0} and W=(0,2) times{0}
in U=R^2 share an arc but W is not contained in Gamma.
Without analyticity, the closed smooth graph of f(t)=0 for t<=0 and
f(t)=exp(-1/t^2) for t>0 shares a half-line with the x-axis but does
not coincide with it. These examples illustrate scope only; they are
not counterexamples to015, whose required hypotheses are stronger.

PROVENANCE
The proof is an elementary application of the classical one-variable
real-analytic identity theorem and the analytic submanifold chart
definition. This own-work exposition isolates a method already
used implicitly in015, not a claim of new mathematics. Its mathematical
proof and application remain unaudited by an independent reviewer.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:adbab65690b7bd52ea8d9c945708420fa1b03c907c42e73106529d4909ffe16a","revision_digest":"sha256:b63e66a6970a3cc4a8287c1669984fccf305b7b73b6f834e5c06e76b6f77ff8b","source_id":"own-work:T421-W706-035","source_revision":"version 1; classical supporting-method exposition; proof (unaudited); no novelty claim","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Corollary 59 (Intrinsic degree-two endpoint) of arXiv:2608.08756, 'Infinite-Dimensional L\'evy Area and Spectral Ancestry'] Consider symmetric-ideal completions of the finite-rank split state with
the following four properties:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2.8em]
\item finite-rank states are dense and every bounded pushforward
      \(L_\#\) is continuous;
\item the universal positive collision functional
      \(Q\mapsto\operatorname{Tr}Q\) is continuous;
\item the full exterior response is a faithful continuous area reader,
      and the scalar profile \(\mathfrak P_A\) is a continuous spectral
      reader for the singular-value topology;
\item the completion contains every continuous Hilbert-martingale state
      with uniformly bounded terminal trace energy.
\end{enumerate}
Then the collision coordinate must have trace-class strength.  Within the
weak and Lorentz scales, the universal area coordinate reaches exactly
the weak-trace frontier.  It cannot be replaced by any
\(\mathcal S_{p,\infty}\) with \(p<1\), by any finite
\(\mathcal S_{1,\rho}\), or by a little weak space with a prescribed
dimension-free decay modulus.  Requiring a separable finite-rank
completion therefore selects
\[
 H\times\mathcal S^0_{1,\infty}(H)_{\mathrm{skew}}
   \times\mathcal S_1(H)_{\mathrm{sa}}
\]
as the intrinsic degree-two split endpoint in this scale.

body:
[Theorem 9 of arXiv:2609.03403, 'Hyperpositive functions, sector bounded functions and a trace formula'] Let $(H_+ , H_-)$ be a pair of of selfadjoint operators defined on a separable Hilbert space $\mathcal H$, and with the following two properties:\\
   $(a)$ There is $m\in\mathbb N$ such that
   \[
     {\rm dim}\, \ran \left((H_+ -\w I)^{-1} - (H_- - \w I)^{-1}\right) = m,\quad \forall\w\in\mathbb C\setminus\mathbb R.
     \]
$(b)$ It holds that
\[
\ker \left((H_+ - \w I)^{-1} - (H_- -\w I)^{-1}\right)  = \left\{0\right\},\quad \forall\w\in\mathbb C\setminus\mathbb R.
\]
Then there exists a $\mathbb C^{m\times m}$ -valued positive function $F$ such that $\det F(z)\not\equiv0$ and
unitary transformations
\[
  U_+\,:\,\mathcal H\longrightarrow\mathcal  L(F )\quad{ and}\quad U_- \,:\,\mathcal H\longrightarrow \mathcal L(F^{-1})
    \]
with the following properties: for $\w\in\mathbb C\setminus\mathbb R$,
    \begin{eqnarray}
      U_+ (H_+ -\w I )^{-1} f &=& R_\w U_+ f,\\
      U_- (H_- -\w I )^{-1} f &=& R_\w U_- f,\\
M_{F^{-1}}U_+f&=&U_-f
\end{eqnarray}
where $M_{F^{-1}}$ denotes the operator of left multiplication by $F^{-1}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma le:ghf_approx_equicont of arXiv:2507.15589, 'Tightness of approximations to metrics on non-simple conformal loop ensemble gaskets'] Suppose we have a sequence $(X_n,d_n,f_n)$ of non-empty compact metric spaces each equipped with a bounded function $f_n\colon K_n \to Y$. Suppose that there is a sequence $r_n \searrow 0$ such that
 \begin{enumerate}[(i)]
  \item $(X_n,d_n) \to (X,d)$ in the GH topology.
  \item There exist $0_Y \in Y$ and $M \in (0,\infty)$ such that $\sup_{x \in K_n} d_Y(f_n(x),0_Y) \leq M$ for every $n$.
  \item For every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $\delta > 0$ so that $d_n(x,y) < \delta$ implies $d_Y(f_n(x),f_n(y)) < \varepsilon \vee r_n$ for every $n$.
 \end{enumerate}
 Then there is a subsequence $(X_{n_k},d_{n_k},f_{n_k})$ that converges in the GHf topology. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

 \frac{|\mathcal P|^2}
 {\displaystyle\prod_{j=1}^m

\end{equation}

body:
[Proposition prop:wheel-geodesics of arXiv:2609.02544, 'A finiteness theorem for geodesic Leech wheels'] Every geodesic of $W_{m+1}$ belongs to exactly one of the following four classes.
\begin{align*}
&uv_i, &&\text{weight }a_i;\\
&v_iv_{i+1}, &&\text{weight }b_i;\\
&v_iv_{i+1}v_{i+2}, &&\text{weight }b_i+b_{i+1};\\
&v_i u v_j\quad(0\le i<j<m,\ \{i,j\}\notin E(C_m)),
&&\text{weight }a_i+a_j.
\end{align*}
Consequently
\[
  t_{gp}(W_{m+1})=\frac{m(m+3)}2.
\]
Equivalently, for $n\ge5$,
\[
  t_{gp}(W_n)=\frac{(n-1)(n+2)}2.
\]

body:
[Theorem 6 of arXiv:2608.27630, 'Oriented planar maps and \\ annular mating of trees'] Fix $\kappa>0$, a vector $\underline{\rho}$ of weights and a vector $\underline{x}$ of force points. Let $(K_t)_{t\ge 0}$ be the hull at time $t$ of the SLE$_\kappa(\underline{\rho})$ process $\eta$ described by the Loewner flow \eqref{eqn-def-sle} with $(W_t)_{t\geq0}$ solving \eqref{eq:def-sle-rho}. Let $\mathfrak{h}_t^0$ be the harmonic function on $\mathbb{H}$ with boundary values 
	 	$$
	 	-\lambda(1+\sum_{i=0}^j \rho^{i,L})\ \ \text{on} \ [V_t^{j+1, L}-W_t, V_t^{j,L}-W_t)\ \  \text{and}\ \ \lambda(1+\sum_{i=0}^j \rho^{i,R})\ \text{on}\ \ [V_t^{j, R}-W_t, V_t^{j+1,R}-W_t)
	 	$$
	 	where $\rho^{0,R} = \rho^{0,L}=0$, $x^{0,L} = 0^-, x^{0,R} = 0^+, x^{k+1, L} = -\infty, x^{\ell+1, R} = +\infty$, $V_t^{0,L} = g_t(0^-)$ and $V_t^{0,R} = g_t(0^+)$. Set $\mathfrak{h}_t(z) = \mathfrak{h}_t^0( {g_t}(z))-\chi\arg  {g_t'}(z)$. Let $\mathcal{F}_t$ be the filtration generated by $(W, V^{i,q})$. Then there exists a coupling $(K,h)$ where $h = \tilde{h}+ \mathfrak{h}_0$ with $\tilde{h}$ being a zero boundary GFF on $\mathbb{H}$ such that the following is true. For any $\mathcal{F}_t$-stopping time $\tau$ before the continuation threshold, $K_\tau$ is a local set for $h$ and the conditional law of $h|_{\mathbb{H}\backslash K_\tau}$ given $\mathcal{F}_\tau$ is the same as the law of $\mathfrak{h}_\tau+\tilde{h}\circ  {g_\tau}$. Moreover, the curve $\eta$ is measurable with respect to $h$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Lemma stableTapMin of arXiv:2604.20660, 'The Legendre structure of the TAP complexity\\ for the Ising spin glass'] Fix $q\in (0,1)$ and let $\mu\in \mathcal{P}([-1,1])$ with $\int m^2\,\mu(\mathrm{d} m)=q$. Let $\zeta_\star\in\mathcal{P}([q,1])$ be the unique minimizer of $\mathrm{TAP}(\mu,\cdot)$
		and for every $N$, let $\zeta_N$ be the unique minimizer of $\mathrm{TAP}(\mu_N,\cdot)$,
		where $q_N:=\int m^2\,\mathrm{d}\mu_N(m)$.
		If $q_N\to q$ and $\mu_N\Rightarrow \mu$ weakly, then
		\begin{equation*}
			\mathrm{dist}(\zeta_N,\zeta_\star)\xrightarrow[N\to\infty]{} 0.
		\end{equation*}
		In particular, if $\int m^2\,\mu(\mathrm{d} m)=q$,
		$m_1,\ldots,m_N$ are i.i.d.\ with law~$\mu$,
		$q_N=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N m_i^2$,
		$\mu_N=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\delta_{m_i}$, and $\zeta_\mathbf{m}$ denotes the minimizer in
		Definition~(def:zetam of the paper), then for every $\varepsilon>0$,
		\begin{equation*}
			\mu^{\otimes N}\!\left(\mathrm{dist}(\zeta_\mathbf{m},\zeta_\star)>\varepsilon\right)\xrightarrow[N\to\infty]{} 0.
		\end{equation*}
title: Stability of the TAP minimizer
