[Theorem 128 of arXiv:2601.16377, '2601.16377'] Consider data specifying a master problem. Assume Conditions 1.,2.,3. of Assumption~\ref{Assumptions_Theta} for these data, and additionally assume the existence of a constant $C > 0$ for which the distance between any pair of points in $\bigcup_{h = 1}^{H} \big\{\hat{a}_h^{\mathfrak{m}},\alpha_h,\beta_h,\hat{b}^{\mathfrak{m}}_h\big\}$ is larger than $\frac{1}{C}$ and the absolute value of all these points is smaller than $C$. Then, the master problem \eqref{eq_Master_equationpre} has a unique solution
 \begin{equation}
 
 \forall h \in [H]\quad \forall z \in \amsmathbb{C} \setminus \amsmathbb{A}_h^{\mathfrak{m}}  \qquad F_h(z) = \Op_h\big[\boldsymbol{E}\,;\,\boldsymbol{\kappa}\big](z).
 \end{equation}
 For any $h \in [H]$, the solution operator $\Op_h$ is linear in $\boldsymbol{E}$ and $\boldsymbol{\kappa}$, depends smoothly on the parameters $\boldsymbol{\Theta}$ and $\boldsymbol{\alpha},\boldsymbol{\beta}$, and depends on the segments $(\amsmathbb{A}_g^{\mathfrak{m}})_{g = 1}^{H}$ and the domains $(\amsmathbb{M}_g)_{g = 1}^{H}$ only through the domain of definition (the precise meaning is explained in Chapter~\ref{Chapter_SolvingN}).

 Besides, it is continuous in the following sense. For any $2H$-tuple of compact subsets $(\amsmathbb{K}_g,\amsmathbb{K}_g^-)_{g = 1}^{H}$ such that
 \[
 \forall g \in [H]\qquad \amsmathbb{K}_g^- \subset \mathring{\amsmathbb{K}}_g \subset \amsmathbb{K}_{g} \subset \amsmathbb{C} \setminus \amsmathbb{A}_g^{\mathfrak{m}},
 \]
 there exists a constant $C' > 0$ depending only on these compacts and the constants in the assumptions such that, for any $\boldsymbol{E},\boldsymbol{\kappa}$ as in (iv)-(v), we have
 \begin{equation}
\max_{h \in [H]} \sup_{z \in \amsmathbb{K}_h} \big|\Op_h\big[\boldsymbol{E}\,;\,\boldsymbol{\kappa}\big](z)\big| \leq C' \cdot \Big( \max_{h \in [H]} \sup_{z \in \amsmathbb{K}_h^-} |E_h(z)| + |\!|\boldsymbol{\kappa}|\!|_{\infty}\Big).
\end{equation}
Besides, if $E_h(z)$ is holomorphic in $\amsmathbb{M}_h$ for each $h \in [H]$, then
\[
\forall h \in [H]\qquad \Upsilon_h[\boldsymbol{E}\,;\,\boldsymbol{0}] = 0.
\]

[Lem lem_slope_stop of arXiv:2606.23648, '\textsc{Optimal Stopping for a Diffusion with Unobserved Bernoulli Drift}'] Fix \(x\ge0\) and \(s = x + y>0\). If
    \begin{equation}
        k'(s)G(-x)+c\ge0,
    \end{equation}
    then immediate stopping is optimal at the point \((x,s-x)\):
    \(
        U(x,s-x)=k(s).
    \)
    At \(s=0\), immediate stopping is optimal as well.

[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2506.21516, 'On the visibility window for Brownian interlacements, Poisson cylinders and Boolean models'] Let $\alpha>0$ and $\rho>0$, let $\mathsf Q$ be a probability measure on $\R_+$. 
Let $\mathcal C$ be either the Brownian interlacements at level $\alpha$ with radius $\rho$ ($d\geq 3$) or the Poisson cylinders at level $\alpha$ with radius $\rho$ ($d\geq 2$) or the Poisson-Boolean model with intensity $\alpha$ and radius distribution $\mathsf Q$ ($d\geq 2$) satisfying \eqref{eq:BM-expected-volume}. 
There exists $\lambda>0$, which depends on the model and on the parameters of the model such that, conditioned on $x$ being visible from $0$, 
\[
\text{$\frac{Q_x}{\delta_{\|x\|}}$ converges weakly to the exponential distribution with intensity $\lambda$,}
\]
 as $x\to\infty$, where $\delta_r$ is the respective visibility window of the model. The parameter $\lambda$ is explicit for each of the models, see \eqref{eq:BI-lambda}, \eqref{eq:BM-lambda} and \eqref{eq:PC-lambda}. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 14 (Entire parameter dependence) of arXiv:2607.26377, '\textbf{Entire Logarithmic Signatures\\ of Bounded-Variation Paths in Finite Dimensions}'] Let $q,r\geq1$ and $T_0>0$, write $I=I_q$, let $\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_r:[0,T_0]\to\C$ be continuous bounded-variation paths, and let $K_1,\ldots,K_r:[0,T_0]\to M_q(\C)$ be continuous. Write
\[
\norm{K_j}_{\infty}=\sup_{0\leq s\leq T_0}\norm{K_j(s)}.
\]
For $u=(u_1,\ldots,u_r)\in\C^r$, let $V^u$ solve
\[
\dd V_s^u
 =V_s^u\sum_{j=1}^r u_j K_j(s)\dd\xi_j(s),
\qquad
V_0^u=I.
\]
Then $u\mapsto V_{T_0}^u$ is entire on $\C^r$.
Its Picard series converges absolutely and locally uniformly, and
\begin{equation}
\norm{V_{T_0}^u}
 \leq
 \exp\!\left(
   \sum_{j=1}^r
   \abs{u_j}\,\norm{K_j}_{\infty}\,
   \Var(\xi_j;[0,T_0])
 \right).
\end{equation}
All mixed derivatives may be computed term by term from the Picard series.

\[

\[

\qquad (m({\mathbf A}),{\mathbf B})\ \text{and }{\mathbf X}\ \text{are independent}.

A sequential coupling explores occupied intervals from changed exterior activities; its failure requires a chain in an independent dominating interval field reaching the center. One-dimensional uncovered points bound that event. Actual Gibbs interval occupations are not assumed independent. The sentence 'the naive guess rho^D proportional to r_D(x)^2 fails unless Z^D(D) is a.s. constant' is too strong: if Z^D = xi mu with xi a random scalar and mu deterministic, then Z^D(dx)/Z^D(D) = mu(dx)/mu(D) is deterministic and E[Z^D(dx)/Z^D(D)] = E Z^D(dx)/E Z^D(D) although Z^D(D) is random. The correct statement: rho^D differs from the normalised intensity E Z^D(dx)/E Z^D(D) exactly when the total mass Z^D(D) is not independent of the normalised measure Z^D(dx)/Z^D(D); for the DGFF extremal measure this independence fails (the mass and the shape are coupled through the Gibbs-Markov structure), so rho^D is not r_D(x)^2 dx normalised, but the argument in A001 does not prove that and the question stands. Key identity: rho^D = E[Z(dx)/Z(D)] equals E Z(dx)/E Z(D) iff the total mass is independent of the normalised measure (sufficient direction), not iff the mass is constant. [Definition def:antiHN of arXiv:2609.00978, 'Towards Categorical K\"ahler Geometry'] An \textbf{ascending-phase filtration} of an object $E\in\cA$ is a filtration 
    \[
    0=E_0\subset E_1\subset E_2\subset\cdots\subset E_n=E
    \]
    such that $0\neq A_i\coloneqq E_i/E_{i-1}$ are semistable for $i=1,\ldots,n$ with strictly ascending phases $\phi(A_1)<\phi(A_2)<\cdots<\phi(A_n)$. We write $E_{\leq\phi}\coloneqq E_k$, where $k=\max\left(\{0\}\cup\{i\mid\phi(A_i)\leq\phi\}\right)$ and regard the collection $(E_{\leq\phi})_\phi$ as an ascending $[0,1]$-filtration of $E$.

    If $E,F\in\cA$ are equipped with ascending-phase filtrations $(E_{\leq\phi})_\phi$, $(F_{\leq\phi})_\phi$, then a morphism $f\colon E\to F$ is said to be \textit{compatible} if it is filtration preserving, i.e.\ $f(E_{\leq\phi})\subseteq F_{\leq\phi}$.
title: Definition def:antiHN of arXiv:2609.00978

[Corollary 12 of arXiv:2609.03191, 'On lifting representations and actions on curves of the metacyclic groups $C_{p^s}\rtimes '] Suppose that $R$ contains $R_s$. Let $b\in\llbracket1,p^s\rrbracket$. Then the following properties hold.

\medskip
{\bf (1)} For each subset $\Lambda\in\mathcal P_b(\Xi_s)$, there exists a unique $R[H]$-module $\mathcal U(b;\Lambda)$ up to isomorphisms which is a lift of $U(b)$ and we have 
$$\kappa_{\mathcal U(b;\lambda)\otimes_R B}(\zeta)=\begin{cases}1\quad {\rm if}\quad \zeta\in\Lambda\\
0\quad {\rm if}\quad \zeta\notin\Lambda.\end{cases}$$ 
We have $\mathcal U(b;\Lambda)\cong R[x]/\bigl(\prod_{\zeta\in\Lambda} (x-\zeta)\bigr)$.

\smallskip
{\bf (2)} The isomorphism classes of lifts of $U(b)$ to $R$ are the $\mathcal U(b;\Lambda)$s with $\Lambda\in\mathcal P_b(\Xi_s)$.

\smallskip
{\bf (3)} The $R[H]$-module $\mathcal U(p^s-1;\Xi_s^{\ast})$ is the unique lift of $U(p^s-1)$ to $R$ with $r_{\mathcal U(p^s-1;\Xi_s^{\ast})}=0$ up to isomorphisms. Moreover, $\mathcal U(p^s-1;\Xi_s^{\ast})$ is uniquely defined over $R_0$, i.e., there exists a unique lift $\mathcal U_0(p^s-1;\Xi_s^{\ast})$ of $U(p^s-1)$ to $R_0$ up to isomorphisms with $\mathcal U_0(p^s-1;\Xi_s^{\ast})\otimes_{R_0} R\cong \mathcal U(p^s-1;\Xi_s^{\ast})$.

    Let $A$ and $D$ be subsets of $S$.
    The pair $(A,D)$ is called an \emph{asymptotically disjoint pair} (denoted by $A\pitchfork_\mathcal{E} D$) if any (equivalently, all) of the following equivalent conditions hold:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item the set $A\cap E[D]$ is bounded in $S$ for any $E\in \mathcal{E}$.
        \item the set $E[A]\cap D$ is bounded in $S$ for any $E\in \mathcal{E}$.
        \item the set $E[A]\cap E[D]$ is bounded in $S$ for any $E\in \mathcal{E}$.
        \item the set $E[A]\cap F[D]$ is bounded in $S$ for any $E,F\in \mathcal{E}$.
    \end{enumerate}

Status: proof draft (unaudited). The conclusion is local alignment. Applying Li-Luo-Lyu G.2 afterwards still requires its local-minimum hypothesis, or a separately proved extension; this file does NOT remove that theorem hypothesis by assertion.

## Statement
Let Sigma be symmetric positive definite, M invertible, both 2x2. Suppose the balanced rank-one first path zbar(t)=(bbar;abar) converges exponentially to a nonzero critical factor zstar=(bstar;astar), with ||zbar(t)-zstar||<=C exp(-lambda t), lambda>0, after choosing a local time origin. The critical endpoint need not minimize the loss over rank-one products. Put Gstar=(bstar astar^T-M)Sigma, Lstar=[[0,-Gstar],[-Gstar^T,0]], and s=sigma_1(Gstar)>0. Let v be its unit positive eigenvector. Let an actual width-w>=2 family at this local time zero satisfy
  ||z_epsilon(0)-zbar(0)||<=C0 epsilon,
  c0 epsilon<=||v^T X_epsilon(0)||F<=c1 epsilon,
  ||(I-vv^T)X_epsilon(0)||F<=h||v^T X_epsilon(0)||F,
where h is a sufficiently narrow fixed cone and the reference time origin is chosen sufficiently late so its remaining endpoint distance is small.

Then for some beta in (0,1) there are positive times t_epsilon with p(t_epsilon)=epsilon^beta, Z_epsilon(t_epsilon)->Z1=zstar zstar^T, and
  liminf v^T Z_epsilon(t_epsilon)v / ||Z_epsilon(t_epsilon)-Z1||F>0.
No balance-defect smallness hypothesis is needed beyond the stated active matching: the actual active column may lie on a nearby conserved-balance leaf.

## 1. The active Hessian grows strictly slower than the frozen inactive mode
The residual Gstar has rank one because Gstar astar=0 and Gstar^T bstar=0 with both factors nonzero; Gstar cannot vanish since M has rank two. Thus Lstar has eigenvalues s,0,0,-s, with simple top s and v perpendicular to zstar.

Let F(z)=(-G a;-G^T b) be the rank-one factor field and Jact=DF(zstar). If T maps an increment xi=(delta_b;delta_a) to delta_b astar^T+bstar delta_a^T, direct differentiation gives the symmetric-matrix identity
  Jact=Lstar-T^* S T,
where S maps a product increment P to P Sigma in the Frobenius inner product. S is positive definite and therefore T^* S T is positive semidefinite. It follows that r=largest eigenvalue(Jact)<=s. The inequality is STRICT: if equality held, a maximizing unit vector would have to belong to both the simple s-eigenspace of Lstar and the kernel of T. But for v=(p;q)/sqrt(2), its residual singular vectors satisfy p perpendicular to bstar and q perpendicular to astar, and
  T v=(p astar^T+bstar q^T)/sqrt(2)
has Frobenius norm squared (||astar||^2+||bstar||^2)/2>0. Positive-definite Sigma forbids its S-norm from vanishing. Hence r<s. The factor-scaling kernel gives r>=0.

Choose rplus with r<rplus<s. By symmetry and continuity, DF(z) has largest eigenvalue at most rplus throughout a small convex neighborhood of zstar. For actual/reference active factors in that neighborhood, the difference e=z_epsilon-zbar obeys the one-sided comparison
  D^+ E<=rplus E+C||X||F^2, E=||e||.
Here the feedback term is exactly -H(VW^T)z_epsilon and is bounded quadratically. This comparison uses the full ACTIVE derivative; it does not replace it by frozen inactive transport.

## 2. Cone growth and active forcing
Choose h>0 and eta>0 sufficiently small that
  eta(1+h)^2<h s,
  a=s-eta(1+h)>rplus,
  b=s+eta(1+h).
As long as the reference is sufficiently near zstar and E,||X|| are small, the exact dormant generator differs from Lstar by at most eta. The same symmetric cone calculation as in C005 gives q<=h p, a p<=p'<=b p, and ||X||F^2<=(1+h^2)p^2.

Since 2a>rplus, variation of constants with p(u)<=p(t)exp(-a(t-u)) gives
  E(t)<=C0 epsilon exp(rplus t)+C1 p(t)^2,
  C1=C(1+h^2)/(2a-rplus).
The distance of the actual active factor from zstar is therefore bounded by
  C exp(-lambda t)+C0 epsilon exp(rplus t)+C1 p(t)^2.       (A)

## 3. Choose an arrival scale that dominates BOTH active errors
Choose
  0<beta<min{lambda/(lambda+2b),(a-rplus)/(2a-rplus)}.
Both thresholds are positive. Stop when p reaches epsilon^beta. The growth bounds imply
  [(1-beta)log(1/epsilon)-log c1]/b <= t_epsilon
       <=[(1-beta)log(1/epsilon)-log c0]/a.
These estimates yield
  exp(-lambda t_epsilon)/epsilon^(2beta)
     =O(epsilon^[lambda(1-beta)/b-2beta])->0,
  epsilon exp(rplus t_epsilon)/epsilon^(2beta)
     =O(epsilon^[1-rplus(1-beta)/a-2beta])->0.
Until that threshold the active discrepancy is at most a constant times
  epsilon^[1-rplus(1-beta)/a]+epsilon^(2beta),
which tends to zero; the reference is already in a small endpoint neighborhood. Also ||X||<=sqrt(1+h^2)epsilon^beta. Thus, by continuation, the trajectory cannot leave the neighborhood before p hits the threshold, and the lower growth bound ensures that this happens. This verifies the assumptions used for the cone and active comparison on the entire stopping interval.

At the stopping time (A) gives ||z_epsilon-zstar||=O(epsilon^(2beta)), while ||X||F^2=O(epsilon^(2beta)). Therefore ||Z_epsilon-Z1||F<=C2 epsilon^(2beta), and positivity gives
  v^T Z_epsilon v=(v^T z_epsilon)^2+||v^T X||F^2>=epsilon^(2beta).
The asserted strong relative Gram alignment follows. QED, subject to independent review.

## Relation to the Gaussian family and remaining theorem gap
C008 supplies the required O(epsilon) active matching on every fixed first-escape shifted compact interval. C006 supplies normalized dormant matching, and C003 supplies its late unstable cone for any nonzero critical endpoint. If the canonical rank-one path is known to converge exponentially, these lemmas therefore produce strong Gram alignment even at a non-best rank-one endpoint.

This is NOT yet a general-data second-step theorem. G.2, as published, assumes a rank-constrained local minimum, which this extension deliberately does not assume. One must prove that the Gram Jacobian has the same simple dominant rate 2s and justify the local escape theorem under that checked hypothesis; one must also identify the selected rank-two orbit's forward endpoint without relying on energy below the globally best rank-one loss. Those are two further obligations, not consequences of an alignment inequality alone.

## 4. Convergence alone suffices for existence of an aligned arrival
The exponential reference assumption is needed only for the explicit power threshold in Section 3. For existence of suitable arrival times it can be removed altogether. Assume merely zbar(t)->zstar. Start late enough so the reference remains in the chosen local neighborhood for all future times. Sections 1-2 are unchanged and still give
  E(t)<=C0 epsilon exp(rplus t)+C1 p(t)^2, a>rplus.
For a fixed sufficiently small threshold delta>0, stop at p=delta. Before that stop, the upper stopping-time bound gives
  epsilon exp(rplus t)<=C delta^(rplus/a) epsilon^(1-rplus/a)->0.

At the stop the reference endpoint error tends to zero, and the homogeneous actual-reference error tends to zero as well, whereas the feedback is bounded by C1 delta^2.

Choose delta_n decreasing to zero. For each n choose epsilon_n decreasing strictly to zero, with epsilon_n<delta_n^n, so that for every epsilon<=epsilon_n the stop at p=delta_n is valid and both the reference tail and the homogeneous active error are at most delta_n^2. Set n(epsilon)=max{n:epsilon<=epsilon_n} for epsilon sufficiently small, and use the stop at delta_n(epsilon). All comparison constants are uniform for thresholds in the one fixed local neighborhood. Then n(epsilon)->infinity,
  ||Z_epsilon-Z1||F<=C delta_n(epsilon)^2,
  v^T Z_epsilon v>=delta_n(epsilon)^2.
These give convergence to Z1 and the same uniform positive relative-alignment lower bound. The condition epsilon_n<delta_n^n ensures the stopping times tend to infinity and initial p0 is below the threshold for large n. This is a diagonal choice of actual arrival times, not an interchange of infinite-time and small-initialization limits.

Accordingly the LOCAL EXISTENCE conclusion is valid with convergence alone; exponential convergence additionally gives the explicit epsilon^beta construction stated earlier. body:
[Lem 172 (eighth moment bounds for $X^{\RomII}$, $X^{\trunc,\RomII}$, and $X^{\frozen,\RomII}$) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $(a(q_d):0\le d\le \dmax)$
and $(a^\frozen(q_d):0\le d\le \dmax)$
be sampled as in Definition~\ref{d:rerand}.
For $N$ large enough, we have
	\[
	\E\bigg[\bigg(
	\sum_{\ell=a}^{b-1} 
	\Delta X^{\RomII}(q_d,a(q_{d+1}))
	\bigg)^8\bigg]
	\le L^{O(1)} (q_b-q_a)^4
	\]
for all $0\le a\le b\le \dmax$. The same bound holds 
with $\Delta X^{\trunc,\RomII}(q_d,a(q_{d+1}))$
or $\Delta X^{\frozen,\RomII}(q_d,a^\frozen(q_{d+1}))$
in place of $\Delta X^{\RomII}(q_d,a(q_{d+1}))$.

\begin{proof}
Let $\Delta_d$ be as in Remark~\ref{r:fourth.mmt}. We first define the (high probability) events
	\beq
	E_d\equiv \bigg\{
	\frac{\|\bar{\bg}(q_d)\|^2}{N} \le 2
	\bigg\} \in \cFt(q_d)\,,\quad
	E_\star=\bigcap_{d=a}^{b-1} E_d\,.
	\eeq
It follows using Lemma~\ref{l:y.subgaus} (with $\cFt(q_d)$ in place of $\cG(q_d)$, as discussed above) that, for any $\vartheta\in\R$,
	\[
	\ind\{E_d\}
	\E\Big[ \exp(\vartheta \Delta_d) \,\Big|\,\cFt(q_d)\Big]
	\le \ind\{E_d\}
	\exp \bigg\{ L^{O(1)} \delta
	\vartheta^2 \frac{\|\bar{\bg}(q_d)\|^2}{N} 
	\bigg\}
	\le \exp\Big(L^{O(1)} \delta\vartheta^2\Big)\,.
	\]
Recall that $\Delta_{a,b} \equiv \Delta_a + \ldots + \Delta_{b-1}$. Then
	\begin{align*}
	&\E\Big[ \exp( \vartheta \Delta_{a,b})
		\ind\{E_\star\} \,\Big|\,
		\cFt(q_{b-1})\Big]
	=\E\bigg[ \exp\bigg( \vartheta\sum_{d=a}^{b-1} \Delta_d\bigg)
		\ind\{E_\star\}
		\,\bigg|\,
		\cFt(q_{b-1})\bigg] \\
	&\qquad=
	\bigg\{ \exp\bigg( \vartheta\sum_{d=a}^{b-2} \Delta_d\bigg)
	\prod_{d=a}^{b-2} \ind\{E_d\}\bigg\}
	\cdot
	\ind\{E_{b-1}\}
	\E\Big[ \exp(\vartheta \Delta_{b-1})
		\,\Big|\,
		\cFt(q_{b-1})\Big]\\
	&\qquad\le
	\bigg\{ \exp\bigg( \vartheta\sum_{d=a}^{b-2} \Delta_d\bigg)
	\prod_{d=a}^{b-2} \ind\{E_d\}\bigg\}
	\cdot \exp\Big(L^{O(1)} \delta\vartheta^2\Big)\,.
	\end{align*}
Applying the same argument recursively gives
	\[
	\E\Big[ \exp( \vartheta \Delta_{a,b})
	\ind\{E_\star\}\Big]
	\le \exp\Big(L^{O(1)} (b-a) \delta \vartheta^2\Big)
	\le \exp\Big(L^{O(1)} (q_b-q_a) \vartheta^2\Big)
	\]
It follows by a Chernoff bound (using only $\P(E_\star)\ge1/2$)
	\[
	\P( |\Delta_{a,b}| \ge y \,|\,E_\star)
	\le 2 \exp\bigg( -\frac{y^2}{4 L^{O(1)} (q_b-q_a)}\bigg)\,,
	\]
and integrating this bound gives (cf.\ \eqref{e:subgaus.mmt})
	\[
	\E\Big[ (\Delta_{a,b})^8 \,\Big|\, E_\star\Big]
	\le \int_0^\infty 8y^{7}
	\P( |\Delta_{a,b}| \ge y \,|\,E_\star)\,dy
	\le L^{O(1)} (q_b-q_a)^4\,.
	\]
On the event $(E_\star)^c$ we can use the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality to bound
	\[
	\E\Big[ (\Delta_{a,b})^8 ; (E_\star)^c\Big]
	\le \Big( \E[(\Delta_{a,b})^{16}] \P(( E_\star)^c) \Big)^{1/2}
	\le \frac{L^{O(1)} (q_b-q_a)^4}{\delta^{O(1)}\exp(\Omega(N))}\,,
	\]
where the bound on $\E[(\Delta_{a,b})^{16}]$ follows very similarly to \eqref{e:weak.fourth.mmt.bound}. This is negligible since we assume  $\delta\gg 1/N$ (see Assumption~\ref{a:params}), and the claim follows.  It is straightforward to verify that the same argument applies with $X^{\trunc,\RomII}$ or $X^{\frozen,\RomII}$ in place of $X^{\RomII}$.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Test the weakest form, pairwise negative edge correlation, on small graphs exactly, and examine the q -> 0 limits. Result: At q -> 0 with p -> 0 appropriately the model becomes the uniform spanning tree, which is negatively associated (Feder-Mihail / Lyons determinantal), and at q = 1 the model is a product measure; the conjecture is that negative association holds for all 0 < q < 1, and even the pairwise statement Cov(omega_e, omega_f) <= 0 is open. On a single cycle of length n one can compute exactly: the random-cluster measure on the cycle with edge weight w = p/(1-p) gives the configurations 'all n edges' weight w^n q, 'n-1 edges' weight w^{n-1} q (n choices), and generally k edges missing (k >= 1) weight w^{n-k} q^k; two edges e, f are both open iff neither is among the missing ones; the covariance can be written in closed form and is <= 0 for q <= 1 by a direct check of the sign of a polynomial in w and q (the missing edges form a 'positive' k-dependent weight with q^k which is log-concave in k for q <= 1... ). I did not carry out the closed-form check in this batch; the cycle is the first non-trivial test case because on trees the model is a product measure. Recorded as the concrete next computation: verify Cov(omega_e, omega_f) <= 0 on cycles and on the theta graph for q in (0,1) symbolically. Obstruction: Even pairwise negative correlation lacks a general argument; the Feder-Mihail route needs a matroid-like structure absent for q in (0,1).
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-c0091-negative-association-for-the-random-cluster-model-with-q-1
No independent review; result status attempted_unsolved

[Definition 26 of arXiv:2605.02430, '\textbf{Scaling limit of the range of tree-valued branching random walks in random environ'] (\textbf{Real trees}) 
Let $(T, d)$ be a metric space; it is a {\it real tree} {if and only if} the following holds true.

\smallskip

\noi
\textbf{(a)} For any $\sigma_1, \sigma_2 \! \in\!  T$, there is a unique isometry 
$f:[0,d(\sigma_1,\sigma_2)] \! \rightarrow \! T$ such
that $f(0)\!=\! \sigma_1$ and $f(d(\sigma_1,\sigma_2))\! =\! \sigma_2$. Then, we set 
$\lgeo \sigma_1,\sigma_2\rgeo \! :=\! f([0,d (\sigma_1,\sigma_2)])$. 

\smallskip

\noi
\textbf{(b)} For any continuous injective function 
$g: [0, 1] \! \rightarrow \! T$, such that $g(0)=\sigma_1$ and $g(1)=\sigma_2$,  $g([0,1]) \! = \! \lgeo \sigma_1,\sigma_2\rgeo$. \cq

body: For any graph G (loops dropped, parallel edges allowed) with V vertices, E edges and b bipartite connected components: F(G) := SUM_{x in {-1,+1}^V} 2^{cut(x)} <= 2^{E-V+2b} 3^{V-b}, equivalently Z(G) = F/(2^V (3/2)^E) <= (4/3)^{E-V+b}. Equality holds exactly on forests. Interpretation: Z is the factor by which dependence among edge-cut indicators inflates E[2^cut] over independence, and the bound is (4/3)^{cycle rank - [non-bipartite]} per component.

\int\frac{\mathrm{Li}_{q;k_{1},\dots,k_{d}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{d-1},x_{d}z)}{z-a^{-1}}d_{q}z & =-\mathrm{Li}_{q;k_{1},\dots,k_{d},1}(x_{1},\dots,x_{d-1},x_{d}a^{-1},az),\\
\int\frac{1}{z-a^{-1}}d_{q}z & =-\mathrm{Li}_{q;1}(az),
\end{align*}
where $a\in\mathbb{C}^{\times}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

\[
P_k^{(m)}(u)\,u!

\]

P_k^{(m)}(u)=0

\]

[Theorem 19 of arXiv:2608.19832, 'Sharp Convex Concentration for Symmetric Random Tensors with Subgaussian Coordinates'] Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent and assume
\[
 \E X_i=0,\qquad \E X_i^2=1,\qquad \abs{X_i}\le K.
\]
Let $L>0$, let $f:H_d\to\R$ be convex and $L$-Lipschitz, and put
$Z=f(X^{\otimes d})$. Then, for every $d\ge1$ and
$0\le t\le c_KLn^{d/2}$,
\begin{equation}
 \Pp\{\abs{Z-\E Z}>t\}
 \le C\exp\left(-\frac{c_Kt^2}{L^2d^2n^{d-1}}\right).
\end{equation}
The variance scale $d^2n^{d-1}$ is sharp for nontrivial moderate deviations.
This already holds for one fixed bounded marginal law with an absolute support
bound.

$\langle C_\alpha:\alpha<\addN\rangle$ of Borel subsets of $I$ and a
Borel probability measure $\mu$ on $I$ such that:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
  \item $\mu(C_\alpha)=0$ for every $\alpha<\addN$, and
  \item $\mu^*\left(\bigcup_{\alpha<\addN}C_\alpha\right)=1$.

body: The PROBABILISTS' Hermite polynomials He_n are defined by He_n(x) = (-1)^n e^{x^2/2} d^n/dx^n e^{-x^2/2}, equivalently by the generating function exp(t x - t^2/2) = sum_{n >= 0} t^n He_n(x)/n!. The first few are He_0 = 1, He_1 = x, He_2 = x^2 - 1, He_3 = x^3 - 3x. They satisfy He_n' = n He_{n-1}, the three-term recursion He_{n+1}(x) = x He_n(x) - n He_{n-1}(x), and the orthogonality relation E[ He_m(Z) He_n(Z) ] = n! times the Kronecker delta, for Z standard Gaussian. Hence { He_n / sqrt(n!) } is an ORTHONORMAL BASIS of L^2 of the standard Gaussian measure on R, and the normalised basis satisfies the derivative relation d/dx ( He_n/sqrt(n!) ) = sqrt(n) ( He_{n-1}/sqrt((n-1)!) ). The PHYSICISTS' Hermite polynomials H_n(x) = (-1)^n e^{x^2} d^n/dx^n e^{-x^2} are orthogonal with respect to the weight e^{-x^2} instead, and the two families are related by H_n(x) = 2^{n/2} He_n( sqrt(2) x ), equivalently He_n(x) = 2^{-n/2} H_n( x / sqrt(2) ). Constants such as the sharp constant in the Gaussian Poincare inequality or the coefficients in a chaos expansion depend on which family is meant, so the convention must be stated. In several variables one takes products He_alpha(x) = prod_i He_{alpha_i}(x_i) over a multi-index alpha, with orthogonality E[He_alpha He_beta] = alpha! delta_{alpha beta} where alpha! = prod_i alpha_i!. [standard; e.g. Nualart, The Malliavin Calculus and Related Topics, 2nd ed., Section 1.1]

[Prop 45 of arXiv:2608.28200, '\textbf On the Formality of Configuration Spaces of $\aka$'] For $n'+n\ge2$, 
The cohomology group of $\A(\paka)$ is 
$$
H^\bullet(\paka)=
\begin{cases}
\OO^{hol}(\C^n)  & \bullet=0 \\
\overline{\C[\PPi ]\omega} & \bullet=n'+n-1 \\
0 & \text{else}
\end{cases}
$$
where $\OO^{hol}(\C^n)$ is the space of holomorphic functions on $\C^n$. The cohomology group of $\Adef(\paka)$ is 
$$

\Hdef(\paka)  = 
\begin{cases}
\C[\ZZi ]  & \bullet=0 \\
\C[\PPi ]\omega & \bullet=n'+n-1 \\
0 & \text{else}
\end{cases}
$$

For $n'=0,n=1$, we have 
$$
H^\bullet(\C\punctured) =
\begin{cases}
\OO^{hol}(\C\punctured)  & \bullet=0 \\
0 & \text{else}
\end{cases}
$$
$$
\Hdef(\C\punctured) =
\begin{cases}
\C [z,z^{-1}]  & \bullet=0 \\
0 & \text{else}
\end{cases}
$$

In both cases, there is a natural inclusion
$$
\Hdef(\paka) \hlra H^\bullet(\paka)
$$
which naturally identifies $\Hdef(\paka)$ with a dense subspace of $H^\bullet(\paka)$.
\iffalse
Moreover, the inclusion
$$

\Adef(\paka) \hlra \A(\paka)
$$
induces an injective map on cohomology groups, which identifies 
$$

\Hdef(\paka)  \slra 
\begin{cases}
\C[\ZZi ]  & \bullet=0 \\
\C[\PPi ]\omega & \bullet=n'+n-1 \\
0 & \text{else}
\end{cases}
$$
as a dense subspace of $H^\bullet(\paka)$.
\fi

body: In mathematical analysis, the inverse function theorem gives sufficient conditions for a function to have an inverse function. The essential idea is that if the best linear approximation to the function at a point is invertible, then with sufficient regularity assumptions, the function should also be invertible near that point. In its simplest form, the theorem states that if a real function f is differentiable in an open interval, with a continuous derivative, then in a neighborhood of any point where the derivative is not zero, f has an inverse function. The inverse function is also continuously differentiable, and the inverse function rule expresses its derivative as the multiplicative inverse of the derivative of f.
title: Inverse function theorem

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Explicit model calculation, comparison identities and remaining hypothesis obstruction Result: An explicit density shows the missing state information. Let patience D and E be independent mean-one exponentials and service X=D+E, with joint density f(x,y)=exp(-x) on x>y>0. A customer entering service after waiting w has X conditional on D>w distributed as w+Gamma(2,1). At service age a, its hazard is0 if a<w and (a-w)/(1+a-w) if a>w. Thus two customers of the same current service age can have different completion hazards because their entry waiting times differ. Check: Memorylessness gives D conditional on D>w equal to w plus a fresh exponential independent of E. The Gamma(2,1) survival function is (1+t)*exp(-t), yielding the stated hazard. The joint density integrates to1 and has precisely this conditional law. Obstruction: The unmarked service-age measure alone cannot close the dynamics. An augmented measure retaining entry-wait or residual-service marks can supply a martingale representation, but its tightness, boundary flux and uniqueness of the limit remain to be proved. A2025 unified fluid model lead concerns a directly constructed model and has not been verified as the requested stochastic limit theorem.

For \(m=1\), the trace discrepancy vanishes identically, and

[Theorem 21 (Exact aggregate-density formula) of arXiv:2609.01116, 'Vector-Carleson, Calder\'on, and Poisson--Atomic Criteria for\\ Generalized Hilbert Operat'] For every $K\ge1$,
\[
 \boxed{\Ccal_K(X)^2=\sup_{\lambda\in\Lambda}
 A_\lambda\gamma_K(\lambda),\qquad
 \Ccal_\infty(X)^2=\sup_{\lambda\in\Lambda}A_\lambda.}
 \tag{7.3}
\]
There is $c_p>0$ such that
\[
 c_p\delta_K(\lambda)^2\le1-\gamma_K(\lambda)
 \le\delta_K(\lambda)^\alpha.
 \tag{7.4}
\]
Consequently $\Ccal_K(X)\uparrow\Ccal_\infty(X)$, including an infinite
limit. All statements remain valid for coordinate tails.

[Lemma L:alpha0-tail of arXiv:2604.10020, 'The directed landscape in half-space'] Take $n/2 \le m \le n$. For any $\epsilon \in (0, 1)$ we have the bound
$$
\mathbb{P}(W(1, 1; n, m) < \mu(n, m) - \epsilon n) \le 2\exp\left(- c \epsilon^3 n^2 \right),
$$
where $c>0$ is a universal constant.
Moreover, for any $\alpha_0 \in (0, 1/2)$, $\alpha \in [\alpha_0, 1/2 - n^{-1/3}]$, and $\epsilon \in (0, 1)$ with $\mu_\alpha(n, m) - \epsilon n \ge \mu(n, m)$, we have 
$$
\mathbb{P}(W(1, 1; n, m) < \mu_\alpha(n, m) - \epsilon n) \le 2\exp\left(-  \frac{c\epsilon^2 n}{1/2 - \alpha} \right).
$$
where $c > 0$ is a constant depending on only on $\alpha_0$.

The \textbf{tree generated by $v_1,\dots,v_n$ in $T$} is the tree $T\langle v_1,\dots,v_n\rangle$ with vertex set
  \[
    \{v_1,\dots,v_n\} \cup \{v_i \wedge v_j, i \neq j\},
  \]
  and where two vertices are connected by an edge if the geodesic between the two in $T$ does not contain any other vertex of $T\langle v_1,\dots,v_n\rangle$.

[Theorem 14 of arXiv:2604.26026, 'Stochastic Ordering of Dependent Systems under Transformation Models and Archimedean Copul'] Assume the conditions of Corollary \ref{heterogeneous-sign}.
    \begin{enumerate}
	\item 
    If $T$ is increasing in its first argument, that is, $\alpha\le \beta$ implies that $T(\alpha,F)(x)\le T(\beta,F)(x)$, for every $x\in\mathbb{R}$, then, for each fixed $x\in\mathbb{R}$, the map $\balpha=(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n)\longmapsto F_{n-k:n}^{(\balpha)}(x)$	is increasing in each coordinate.
    
    \item 
    If $T$ is decreasing in its first argument, that is, $\alpha\le \beta$ implies that $T(\alpha,F)(x)\ge T(\beta,F)(x)$, for every $x\in\mathbb{R}$, then, for each fixed $x\in\mathbb{R}$, the same map is decreasing in each coordinate.
	\end{enumerate}
Consequently, if $\balpha=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n)$ and $\bbeta=(\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_n)$ are such that $\alpha_i\le \beta_i$, for every $i=1,\dots,n$, then
    \begin{enumerate}
    \item
    If $T$ is increasing in its first argument, then $X_{n-k:n}(\balpha)\geqst X_{n-k:n}(\bbeta)$,
    \item
    If $T$ is decreasing in its first argument, then $X_{n-k:n}(\balpha)\leqst X_{n-k:n}(\bbeta)$.
	\end{enumerate}

body:
[Lemma 14 of arXiv:2608.26662, 'Boundary–Moment Universality and Curvature Corrections in Random Geometric Graphs on Riema'] Assume $d\ge2$.  Use the displacement coordinates
$z=z_1$ and
$w=z_1-z_2$.
We set
$a=\ind_{\{|z|\le1\}}$,
$b=\ind_{\{|z-w|\le1\}}$,
$c=\ind_{\{|w|\le1\}}$,
and
$\widehat H_{\mathfrak h}(z,w)
:=
\overline{\mathfrak h}(a,b,c)$.
Then
\[
\widehat H_{\mathfrak h}\in BV_c(\R^{2d})
\]
holds. 
Moreover, for every
$\varphi\in C_c^1(\R^{2d};\R^d)$, we have
\begin{align}
\int_{\R^{2d}}
\varphi\cdot dD_w\widehat H_{\mathfrak h}
={}&
\int_{\R^d}\int_{\{|z-w|=1\}}
\Delta_b\mathfrak h(a,c)\,
\varphi(z,w)\cdot(z-w)
\,d\mathcal H^{d-1}(w)\,dz
\\
&-
\int_{\R^d}\int_{S^{d-1}}
\Delta_c\mathfrak h(a,b)\,
\varphi(z,w)\cdot w
\,d\sigma(w)\,dz,
\notag
\end{align}
where
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Delta_b\mathfrak h(a,c)
&:=
\mathfrak h(a,1,c)-\mathfrak h(a,0,c)\\
&=
\lambda_P(a+c)+(\lambda_K-3\lambda_P)ac,
\end{aligned}
\]
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Delta_c\mathfrak h(a,b)
&:=
\mathfrak h(a,b,1)-\mathfrak h(a,b,0)\\
&=
\lambda_P(a+b)+(\lambda_K-3\lambda_P)ab.
\end{aligned}
\]
The two measures on the right-hand side of \eqref{eq:BV-jump-measure}
are mutually singular; consequently, each of them is supported in
$\operatorname{supp}\widehat H_{\mathfrak h}$.

[Definition 23 of arXiv:2609.02105, 'Contact fundamental forms and \\ adjoint varieties'] Let $S \subset U(\fh)^*$ be a contact symbol system on the graded Heisenberg algebra $\fh$.
Regarding $U(\fh)^*$ as the space of  polynomial functions on the Heisenberg group $\sH$, the subspace $S \subset U(\fh)^*$ is a linear system of  regular functions on the affine variety $\sH$. [Lemma lem:resolvent-bounds of arXiv:2605.03718, 'Potential Hessian Ascent III:\\ Sampling the Sherrington--Kirkpatrick Model at $\beta < 1/'] Let $W, T$ be real symmetric matrices and $M$ be a Hermitian matrix of the same dimensions.
    Let
\[
    D \;:=\; W^{-1},
    \qquad
    X \;:=\; M + D,
    \qquad
    R \;:=\; X^{-1}.
\]
    Suppose that there is a $\gamma > 0$ so that $\min \Spec(|X|) \geqslant \gamma$ and $\|M\| \leqslant C_1$.
    Then when $k \geqslant 1$ and $j \geqslant 2$,
\begin{align*}
    &\ensuremath{\left\lVert R^k \right\rVert_\mathsf{op}} \;\leqslant\; \gamma^{-k},
    \qquad\qquad
    &&\ensuremath{\left\lVert DR^k \right\rVert_\mathsf{op}} \;\leqslant\; (\gamma + C_1)\gamma^{-k},
\\
    &\ensuremath{\left\lVert DR^jD \right\rVert_\mathsf{op}} \;\leqslant\; (\gamma + C_1)^2\gamma^{-j},
    \qquad\quad
    &&\schnorm{R^kDTDR^{j-k}} \leqslant\;\; (\gamma + C_1)^2\gamma^{-j}\schnorm{T}.
\end{align*}
If $\Im[M] = bI \ne 0$, we also have the imaginary-part bounds
\begin{align*}
    &\opnorm{\frac{1}{b}\Im[R]} \;\leqslant\; \gamma^{-2},
    \qquad\qquad
    \schnorm{\frac{1}{b}\Im[RDTDR]} \leqslant\;\; 2(\gamma + C_1)^2\gamma^{-3}\schnorm{T},
\\
    &\schnorm{\frac{1}{b}\Im[R^2DTDR]} \leqslant\;\; 3(\gamma + C_1)^2\gamma^{-4}\schnorm{T} + O(b^2).
\end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Bounds on resolvent products

body:
[Proposition prop:A5 of arXiv:2605.03703, 'Scaling Limits of Bivariate Nearly-Unstable Hawkes Processes and Applications to Rough Vol'] Suppose Assumptions~(A1)--(A4) hold but (A5) is dropped.
Define
\begin{equation}
\rho_{12} := \frac{\lambda_1^{1/\alpha_1}}{\lambda_2^{1/\alpha_2}} \in (0,\infty),
\end{equation}
so that $\varepsilon_T^1/\varepsilon_T^2 \to \rho_{12}$ as $T\to\infty$.
Then:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item \textbf{Modified cross-kernel.}
The renormalized cross-kernel $\tilde h_T$ (introduced in Section~(sec:cross-kernel of the paper), eq.~(equation eq:hT-def of the paper)) converges in
$L^2(\mathbb R_+)$ to
\begin{equation}
L_{12}^{(\rho)}
:= b_\infty^{12}\|\psi^{12}\|_1 \cdot (K_1 * K_2^{(\rho_{12})}),
\end{equation}
where $K_2^{(\rho_{12})}(t) := \rho_{12}^{-1}\,K_2(t/\rho_{12})$ is the
Mittag-Leffler kernel of the second component time-rescaled by $\rho_{12}$.
Under (A5), $\rho_{12}=1$ and $L_{12}^{(\rho)}=L_{12}$.

\item \textbf{C-tightness.}
The bivariate C-tightness of Proposition~(prop:tightness of the paper) remains valid
without (A5), with $L_{12}$ replaced by $L_{12}^{(\rho)}$.
The Hölder exponent of the cross-term is still $2(\alpha_1+\alpha_2)-1>2\alpha_2-1$,
since time-rescaling by $\rho_{12}$ does not change the singularity exponent.

\item \textbf{Modified limit system.}
The limit $(V^1,V^2)$ satisfies the limiting system~(equation eq:main-limit1 of the paper)--(equation eq:main-limit2 of the paper)
with $L_{12}$ replaced by $L_{12}^{(\rho)}$.
All subsequent results (Theorem~(thm:ALP-extension of the paper), uniqueness,
and Corollary~(cor:rho of the paper)) hold with this replacement, with the
decorrelation constant $C_\varrho$ modified by the factor $\rho_{12}^{\alpha_2-1}$
in the prefactor of $K_2^{(\rho_{12})}$.

\item \textbf{Reduction to (A5).}
Condition~(A5) is imposed for notational simplicity.
Without it, the same argument yields a time-rescaled cross-kernel
as described in part~(i); the parametric reparametrisation
$\lambda_2 \leftarrow \lambda_2\,\rho_{12}^{\alpha_2}$
(corresponding to a deterministic time-change of the second component's
near-criticality rate) recovers the form stated under (A5).
The restriction is therefore one of parametric normalisation, not structural content.
\end{enumerate}
title: Effect of dropping (A5)

[Definition def:FKG-ratio of arXiv:2505.02685, 'On the Spectral Expansion of Monotone Subsets of the Hypercube'] Fix a monotone set $A\subseteq\{0,1\}^{n}$ with at least 2 elements. We define the \emph{approximate FKG ratio} of the poset $A$ to be
$$\delta(A):=\min\left\{0,\inf_{f,g\in \mathsf{mono} _{A}\setminus \mathsf{const}_{A}}\frac{\Covs{A}{f}{g}}{\sqrt{\Vars{A}{f}\cdot\Vars{A}{g}}}\right\},$$
where $f$ and $g$ range over all non-constant monotone increasing functions from $A$ to $\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}$. Here, $\Covs{A}{f}{g}$ stands for the covariance of the random variable pair $(f(x),g(x))$ where $x$ is a uniformly random element of $A$.
title: Approximate FKG ratio

[Definition of arXiv:2609.03731, 'Weightings and Lie groupoids'] Let $A_\bullet$ be a filtration of $A$. For $k\le 0$ set $\ensuremath{\mathcal{I}}_k=C^\infty_G$. Inductively define $\ensuremath{\mathcal{I}}_1=\ensuremath{\mathcal{I}}_M\subset C^\infty_G$, and for $k>1$,
\[ \ensuremath{\mathcal{I}}_k=\{f\in \ensuremath{\mathcal{I}}_M\mid \forall i>0,\forall X\in \ensuremath{\mathcal{A}}_i, X^L f \in \ensuremath{\mathcal{I}}_{k-i}\}\subset C^\infty_G.\]
It is not difficult to verify by induction that $\ensuremath{\mathcal{I}}_\bullet$ is a nested sequence of ideals that we will refer to as the \emph{sequence of ideals $\ensuremath{\mathcal{I}}_\bullet\subset C^\infty_G$ associated to the filtration $A_\bullet$}.

body:
[Openquestion 36 (Degree/height and algorithmic complexity of crossover equations) of arXiv:2601.16580, 'Coin flipping and waiting times paradoxes \\ Why fair coins are exceptional'] For fixed patterns $(T_1,T_2)$ with a common coin bias $p$, the crossover equation $\Pr(T_1\!>\!T_2)=\tfrac12$
reduces to a polynomial identity after clearing denominators (equivalently, to $N_{T_1,T_2}(p)=0$ for an explicit integer polynomial).
Give general bounds (in terms of $|T_1|,|T_2|$) on:
\begin{enumerate}\itemsep3pt
\item[(i)] the degree of a reduced numerator polynomial $N_{T_1,T_2}$ (and how it relates to border data such as $S_{T_1}+S_{T_2}$),
\item[(ii)] the size of coefficients of $N_{T_1,T_2}$ (e.g.\ bit-length or $\ell_1$-norm bounds),
\item[(iii)] the bit‑complexity of isolating all real roots in $(0,1)$ (uniformly over all pairs of given lengths).
\end{enumerate}
Extend these questions to an $s$‑die with a multi‑parameter bias vector $(p_1,\dots,p_s)$: what can be said about the algebraic and computational complexity of the crossover hypersurface $\Pr(T_1\!>\!T_2)=\tfrac12$ inside the simplex? (Stated as a question by the paper; open unless the paper says otherwise.)
title: Degree/height and algorithmic complexity of crossover equations

[Proposition prop:self-dual of arXiv:2602.19192, 'Bakry--\'Emery Curvature of the Fractional Laplacian\\ via Fractional Brownian Covariance'] At $\gamma = 1$ ($H = 1/2$):
$\Psi_1(\xi,\eta)
= \min(|\xi|, |\eta|)\,\mathbf{1}_{\xi\eta > 0}$.
This is the covariance of standard Brownian motion.
The Cauchy process ($\gamma = 1$) is thus the unique stable process
whose carr\'e du champ has the covariance structure of standard
Brownian motion.
For opposite-sign frequencies, $\Psi_1(\xi,-\eta) = 0$:
positive and negative frequencies decouple completely.

[Corollary 66 of arXiv:2608.12947, 'Branch-stationary max-stable fields on rooted trees'] For \(v\in K\), define
\begin{equation}
  \Psi_{K,v}(x)
  =
  \E*{
    Z_v^\alpha\omega_{K,v}(x,Z)
  },
  \qquad x\in(0,\infty)^K.
  
\end{equation}
Then
\[
  0
  \leq
  \Psi_{K,v}(x)
  =
  \E*{
    \omega_{K,v}(x,\Theta^{[v]})
  }
  \leq1,
  \qquad
  \Psi_{K,v}(cx)=\Psi_{K,v}(x),
  \quad c>0,
\]
and
\begin{equation}
  \ell_K(x)
  =
  \sum_{v\in K}x_v\Psi_{K,v}(x).
  
\end{equation}
The field \(\eta\) is branch-stationary if and only if
\begin{equation}
  \Psi_{aK,av}(x^a)
  =
  \Psi_{K,v}(x),
  \qquad
  a\in\mathcal T,\quad
  v\in K,\quad
  x\in(0,\infty)^K,
  
\end{equation}
for every non-empty finite \(K\subset\mathcal T\). If \(Z\) satisfies (equation 17 of the paper) and
\(\Theta=\Theta^{[\varnothing]}\), then
\begin{equation}
  \Psi_{K,v}(x)
  =
  \E*{
    \Theta_v^\alpha
    \omega_{K,v}(x,\Theta)
  }.
  
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Corollary 66 of arXiv:2608.12947

body:
[Theorem thm:nogradient of arXiv:2510.22778, 'Free denoising diffusion models'] Let $f\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R})$ with $f>0$. Suppose the spectral flow of (equation eq:opsde of the paper) is, for
every initial law, the $m$-mobility Wasserstein gradient flow of an energy
\[
  E[\mu]=\int W\,\mathrm{d}\mu+\tfrac12\iint K(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}\mu(x)\mathrm{d}\mu(y),
  \qquad K\ \text{symmetric and }C^{2}\ \text{off the diagonal},
\]
with a continuous mobility $m>0$, that is
$\partial_{t}\mu+\partial_{x}\big(\mu\,m\,\partial_{x}\tfrac{\delta E}{\delta\mu}\big)^{-}=0$
reproduces (equation eq:opvelocity of the paper). Then $m$ and $f$ are both constant. In particular,
for non-constant $f$ the flow is not a Wasserstein gradient flow of
any such energy, and the convexity method of Section~(sec:inequalities of the paper) does not
apply.

body: [Abstract of arXiv:2609.02711, 'Differentiability of the Leading Lyapunov Exponent \\ of a linear differential equation...'] The study of evolution in temporally fluctuating environments often relies on the analysis of Lyapunov exponents, which quantify the exponential growth of populations. However, when model parameters depend on a stochastic process, calculating the selection gradient—a key tool for predicting the evolution of phenotypic traits—becomes a mathematical challenge. While the periodic case has been resolved, a general approach for random environments remains to be developed. This article proposes a rigorous method to: \begin{enumerate} \item Establish the differentiability of the leading Lyapunov exponent $\Lambda(z)$ with respect to a parameter $z$, providing an explicit integral formula for its derivative $\Lambda'(z)$. \item Develop a numerical algorithm to compute $\Lambda'(z)$ by solving an extended differential equation. \item Apply these results to the analysis of mutant invasion in a resident population at equilibrium, identifying the selection gradient as the derivative $\Lambda'(z)$. \end{enumerate} \footnote{\today}
title: Abstract of arXiv:2609.02711: Differentiability of the Leading Lyapunov Exponent \\ of a linear differential equation...

[Theorem 7 of arXiv:2608.19179, 'A random walk on $p$-groups with a symmetric perfect pairing'] Suppose $M$ is symmetric and non-singular. Then $\Delta_S$ satisfies
   \[
   \Delta_S \Big[ \Ker(M) \Big]=
   \Ker 
   \begin{mat}{ccc|c}
   & & & *\\
   & M& &\vdots\\
   & & & *\\ \hline
   * & \hdots & * & *
   \end{mat} \hspace{1in} \text{ for all } \, M
   \]
   where the entries denoted by $*$ are uniformly random variables, that are independent, subject to the symmetry condition. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Attempt to derive g_alpha from the PWIT recursive distributional equation for the resolvent at z, then differentiate in z. Result: The density is g_alpha(r) = (1/2pi) Delta_z of the log-potential U(z) = -integral log|z-w| dmu_alpha(w), and U is expressed through the limit of the singular-value law of the shifted operator on the PWIT, whose Stieltjes transform satisfies a fixed-point equation in a 2x2 matrix-valued function with alpha-stable-type nonlinearity (as in Bordenave-Caputo-Chafai). The z-dependence enters only through the off-diagonal entries; at z = 0 the equation closes on a single positive stable random variable, which is why g_alpha(0) is explicit. For z not 0 the fixed point involves a two-parameter family of stable laws (radial and angular parts), and I could not reduce it to a scalar equation; the isotropy only removes the angular variable of z, not of the recursion. Tail check: the stated tail r^{2(alpha-1)} e^{-alpha r^alpha/2} is consistent with the expected behaviour that eigenvalues of modulus r come from rows with an exceptionally large entry of size r^alpha, whose density in the stable domain is r^{-alpha-1} ... the exponential factor indicates instead a large-deviation of a sum of alpha-stable variables of the Poisson-Dirichlet type. No closed form. Obstruction: The matrix-valued PWIT fixed point does not reduce to a scalar equation away from z = 0.

[Lemma 21 of arXiv:2609.02065, '\textbf{From Bowditch's question to Goldman's conjecture for type-preserving representatio'] \cite[Lemma 7.4]{ryu} 
        For $n\in \mathbb{Z}$ and an elliptic element $\widetilde{A}\in \mathrm{Ell}_n$ of $\univcover,$ let $A$ be its projection to $\SL$, and for $i,j\in\{1,2\}$ let $a_{ij}$ be the $(i,j)$-entry of $A.$ 
        Then $a_{12}\neq0$ and $a_{21}\neq 0.$  Moreover:
        \begin{enumerate}[(1)]
            \item 
            If $n$ is odd, then $sgn(n)=sgn(a_{12}) = -sgn(a_{21})$.
            
            \item 
            If $n$ is even, then $sgn(n)=-sgn(a_{12}) = sgn(a_{21})$.
        \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 21 of arXiv:2609.02065

body: [Defn 7 of arXiv:2608.12804, 'Scaling Limits for Ising Models on Inhomogeneous Random Graphs and Applications'] Let $\mathcal{S}$ be a Polish space and $\mathcal{P}(\mathcal S)$ denote the set of all probability measures on the Borel $\sigma$-field on $\mathcal S$, equipped with the topology $\Gamma$ of weak convergence. Let $\{\mu_n\}_{n\ge 1}$ be a family of $\mathcal P(\mathcal S)$-valued random probability measures defined on a common probability space $(\Omega,\mathscr{F},\P)$ (i.e. each $\mu_n$: $(\Omega,\mathscr{F}) \to (\mathcal P(\mathcal S), \mathcal{B}\bigl(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal S),\Gamma\bigr))$ is a measurable function, where $\mathcal{B}\bigl(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal S),\Gamma\bigr)$ denotes the Borel $\sigma$-field on $\mathcal P(\mathcal{S})$ generated by $\Gamma$). We say that $\mu_n$ converges weakly in probability to a measure $\mu \in  \mathcal P(\mathcal S)$, if for all $U \in \Gamma$ containing $\mu$, we have $$\P(\mu_n \in U) \rightarrow 1.$$
title: Definition 7 of arXiv:2608.12804

[Proposition prop:match-alloc of arXiv:2510.18392, 'Hyperuniformity of random measures, transport and rigidity'] Let $ \mathsf{P}_{ n},n\geqslant 1$  be  point processes with resp. $ n^{ d}$ points in $  \mathbb  T  _{ n}^{ d}$, and $ p\geqslant 1.$ 
There is a universal constant $ c_{ d,p}>0$ such that 
\begin{align}

   \mathsf W_{ p}^{ p}(\Leb_{ n},\mathsf{P}_{ n})\geqslant c_{ d,p}n^{ d}.
\end{align}
Hence the  {\it linear cost} (proportional to $ n^{ d}$), is the least one can expect.
Then the two following are equivalent:\begin{itemize}
\item [(i)]There is a constant $ c_{ \text{\rm{match}}}$ such that
 $
 \mathbf E \mathsf W _{p}^{ p}(\mathsf{P}_{ n},   \mathsf Z_{ n}) \leqslant c_{ \text{\rm{match}}}n^{ d},$
\item [(ii)] There is a constant $ c_{ \text{\rm{alloc}}}$ such that 
 $
 \mathbf E \mathsf W _{p}^{ p}(\mathsf{P}_{ n},\Leb_{ n})\leqslant c_{ \text{\rm{alloc}}}n^{ d}.
 $
\end{itemize}

body:
Let f(z) = sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n z^n be analytic in a Delta-domain Delta(phi, R) with R > 1 and |arg(z - 1)| > phi > pi/2. If f(z) = (1 - z)^{-alpha} as z -> 1 within the Delta-domain, where alpha not in {0, -1, -2, ...}, then the coefficients satisfy a_n = [z^n] f(z) = \frac{n^{\alpha - 1}}{\Gamma(\alpha)} (1 + O(1/n)) as n -> \infty.
f is analytic in a Delta-domain
alpha is not a non-positive integer

body:
Let f be a C^1 diffeomorphism of a compact Riemannian manifold M and mu an f-invariant Borel probability measure. Since M is compact, log of the norm of Df and of Df^{-1} are bounded, hence integrable, so Oseledets' multiplicative ergodic theorem applies: for mu-a.e. x there are finitely many numbers lambda_1(x) > lambda_2(x) > ... > lambda_{k(x)}(x) (the LYAPUNOV EXPONENTS at x) and a Df-invariant splitting of the tangent space

  T_x M = E_1(x) + ... + E_{k(x)}(x),   Df_x E_i(x) = E_i(f x),

such that for every nonzero v in E_i(x) the limit of (1/n) log |Df^n_x v| as n -> +-infinity exists and equals lambda_i(x). The functions x -> lambda_i(x) and the multiplicities dim E_i(x) are measurable and f-invariant, and if mu is ergodic they are constant almost everywhere; the subspaces E_i(x) are measurable and Df-equivariant, Df_x E_i(x) = E_i(fx). The splitting is in general only MEASURABLE, not continuous, and the convergence is not uniform in x.

Two structural facts that every application uses. (1) TEMPEREDNESS: any measurable positive function that is subexponential along orbits -- such as the angle between the Oseledets subspaces, or the norm of the change to Lyapunov (adapted) coordinates -- can be chosen tempered, meaning (1/n) log of its value at f^n x tends to 0; this is what lets one build Lyapunov charts in which Df is uniformly contracting on the negative-exponent bundle at the cost of a chart size that shrinks subexponentially along the orbit. (2) PESIN BLOCKS: for each l one collects the points where the Oseledets estimates hold with uniform constants depending on l; the resulting sets Lambda_l are COMPACT (after discarding a null set and restricting the subbundles continuously), increase in l, exhaust a full-measure set, and carry uniform hyperbolic-like estimates. They are NOT f-invariant -- an orbit wanders between blocks -- which is exactly why non-uniformly hyperbolic statements are local-and-measurable rather than uniform.

A point x is called (non-uniformly) hyperbolic when no exponent at x is zero; the stable bundle E^s(x) is the sum of the E_i(x) with lambda_i(x) < 0 and the unstable bundle the sum of those with lambda_i(x) > 0. Zero exponents are the obstruction: nothing in this framework says anything about directions with zero exponent.
M is a compact Riemannian manifold and f a C^1 diffeomorphism of M
mu is an f-invariant Borel probability measure (compactness makes the Oseledets integrability condition automatic)
the exponents and multiplicities are measurable and f-invariant, constant a.e. when mu is ergodic; the subspaces are measurable and Df-equivariant
the Oseledets splitting is measurable, generally not continuous, and the Pesin blocks are not invariant

body:
The gcd of two positive integers a >= b is computed by repeated division: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b), terminating when the remainder is 0, at which point the last nonzero remainder is gcd(a, b). Running the steps backward (the extended Euclidean algorithm) produces integers x, y with ax + by = gcd(a, b) (Bezout coefficients). It runs in O(log min(a,b)) division steps.
a, b positive integers

[Proposition of arXiv:2608.29708, 'Intuitionistic and Constructive Modal Logics for Classical Modal Logicians'] (1) $\textbf{KI} \vdash \neg \neg \Diamond \top \to \Diamond \top$.
  (2) $L \nvdash \neg \neg \Diamond \top \to \Diamond \top$ for $L \in \set{ \textbf{FIK}, \textbf{IK} }$.
  \begin{proof}
    (1) Take any $\Box$-p and $\Diamond$-p model $\mathfrak{M} = (W, \leq, \sqsubset, V)$,
    and any $x \in W$ such that $x \Vdash^{\text{h}}_\mathfrak{M} \neg \neg \Diamond \top$.
    By the $\leq$-reflexivity of $x$ and the fact that no world forces $\bot$,
    the assumption implies $x \not \Vdash^{\text{h}}_\mathfrak{M} \neg \Diamond \top$.
    Hence there are $x', y' \in W$ such that $x \leq x'$, $x' \sqsubset y'$, and $y' \Vdash^{\text{h}}_\mathfrak{M} \top$.
    By the $\Box$-p condition, there is $y \in W$ such that $x \sqsubset y$ and $y \leq y'$.
    Since $y \Vdash^{\text{h}}_\mathfrak{M} \top$, we have $x \Vdash^{\text{h}}_\mathfrak{M} \Diamond \top$.
    Therefore, $\textbf{KI} \vdash \neg \neg \Diamond \top \to \Diamond \top$ by completeness.

    (2) Consider the model $\mathfrak{M}_{\textsf{CD}}$ from Proposition (prop:fik-is-weaker-than-eikm of the paper) (2).
    The world $x$ has no $\sqsubset$-successor, so $x \not \Vdash^{\text{h}} \Diamond \top$.
    To see that $x \Vdash^{\text{h}} \neg \neg \Diamond \top$, take any $z \in W$ such that $x \leq z$.
    If $z = x'$, then $z \Vdash^{\text{h}} \Diamond \top$ because $x' \sqsubset y'$.
    If $z = x$, then its $\leq$-successor $x'$ forces $\Diamond \top$.
    Thus, in either case, $z \not \Vdash^{\text{h}} \neg \Diamond \top$.
    By $\mathfrak{M}_{\textsf{CD}}$ satisfying the $\Diamond$-p and FS2 conditions,
    we have $L \nvdash \neg \neg \Diamond \top \to \Diamond \top$ for $L \in \set{ \textbf{FIK}, \textbf{IK} }$ by soundness.
  \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Proposition 2 (Relaxation) of arXiv:2608.06317, 'Sharp Tail Bounds Beyond Twice the Mean'] For $n\in\N_0$ and $t\in\R$,
\[
\begin{split}
\sup_{(X_i)\in D_{\le 1}}\PP{\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\ge t} &= \sup_{w\in [0,n]}\,\,\,\sup_{(Z_i)\in I\cap M(\infty,w)}\PP{\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i \ge t-n+w}\\
&\le \sup_{w\in [0,n]}\,\,\,\sup_{(Z_i)\in M(\infty,w)}\PP{\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i \ge t-n+w}. 
\end{split}
\]

Method: Martingales detectable by computationally practical stopping rules structural calculation Result: Any prescribed polynomial-size family of stopping tests can miss bounded conditional drift on an exponentially large history space. Reveal m fair bits by time m, set X_t=0 through time m and X_(m+1)=f(Y). For predetermined stopping rules T_j, each optional-mean constraint is the linear equation E[f(Y)*1_{T_j=m+1}]=0. If the number of tests plus the mean-zero condition is less than2^m, a nonzero f exists in their common nullspace. Rescale it to supnorm1. Then the process passes every supplied test but E[X_(m+1)|F_m]=f(Y) is nonzero. Check: The witness T*=m+1 on{f(Y)>0} and m otherwise is a stopping time and has E X_T*=E f_+>0. Predetermined test rules are functions of the revealed-bit history; their final-time continuation indicators do not depend on the unknown terminal value. The construction does not claim f or T* is computationally efficient. Obstruction: A polynomial number of linear tests alone cannot reproduce the full martingale property. Selecting a useful computational subclass requires an explicit representation, complexity bound and error tolerance; the nullspace construction does not supply that theory.

[Lemma 14 of arXiv:2605.04168, 'Error analysis for learning fractional stochastic differential equations with applications'] Suppose that the Assumptions of Section \ref{sec:assumptions} are valid and let $\alpha$ be as in Proposition \ref{prop:coefficient-approximation}. Then  
$$
\sup_n \Vert X^n\Vert_{\alpha,\infty}<\infty.
$$
In particular, the $\tilde\delta$-H\"older norm is uniformly bounded for any $\tilde\delta > \alpha$ and consequently, there exists $N$ such that $X^n \in [-N,N]^d$ for all $n\in \mathbb{N}$.

[Lemma 19 (Entropy of bounded-variation calibration classes) of arXiv:2608.24858, 'Bellman Calibration for Marginalized Importance Weighting in Offline Reinforcement Learnin'] Fix \(V<\infty\). There is a constant \(C_V<\infty\) such that, uniformly
over probability measures \(Q\),
\[
  \log N\{\epsilon,\mathcal V_{\widehat w_\pi}(V),L^2(Q)\}
  \le
  \frac{C_V}{\epsilon},
  \qquad 0<\epsilon\le 1 .
\]
The same bound, with a possibly larger \(C_V\), holds for the classes
\[
\begin{gathered}
  \{ab:a,b\in\mathcal V_{\widehat w_\pi}(V)\},\qquad
  \{(x,x^+)\mapsto a(x)b(x^+):
    a,b\in\mathcal V_{\widehat w_\pi}(V)\},\\
  \{(x,x^+)\mapsto b(x^+)^2:
    b\in\mathcal V_{\widehat w_\pi}(V)\}.
\end{gathered}
\]
For all four classes, the entropy constant and the uniform envelope may be
chosen no larger than \(C(1+V)^2\), for a universal \(C\).

[Corollary 9 (Variance decomposition) of arXiv:2607.25949, 'Block-hierarchical covariance decompositions for finite-block additive functionals'] Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{T:downwardDecomp}, let $f$ be the decomposition (\ref{E:decomp}).  Then
\[
\sigma_k^2(f)
=
\langle B_k f,f\rangle
=
\sigma^2_{\mathrm{marg}}(f)
+
\sum_{m=2}^k \sigma^2_{[m]}(f),
\]
where
\[
\sigma^2_{[m]}(f)
=
\langle B_k f^{[m]},f^{[m]}\rangle
=
(k-m+1)\|f^{[m]}\|^2 =(k-m+1)^2\|h_m\|^2 .
\]
In particular,
\[
\sigma^2_{\mathrm{inc}}(f)
=
\sigma^2_{[k]}(f)

Own-work draft, C007 version 2, proof (unaudited); priority not established. For every m>=1 and 0<eta<=1, consider the depth-three mean-field model h_i=sigma(w_i x), z_j=m^(-1)sum_i B_ji h_i, f=m^(-1)sum_j a_j sigma(z_j), with sigma(z)=z/[4(1+z^2)]. Data have x=1 and y Bernoulli(1/2). Every w_i,a_j,B_ji is initially 1/4; these point-mass random variables are independent iid within each array and independent between arrays and runs. Train all layers by one simultaneous half-squared-loss SGD step, with learning-rate multipliers m on a,w and m^2 on B, using independently sampled labels in the two runs. Let L(theta)=E[(f_theta-y)^2/2]. For any compatible permutation P define H_m=sup_{0<=t<=1}[L((1-t)theta^A+tP theta^B)-(1-t)L(theta^A)-tL(theta^B)]_+. Then E inf_P H_m>=eta^2/160000000. All arrays remain constant within a run, so every permutation fixes the endpoints. The width-independent scalar reduction F=a sigma(b sigma(w)) has f0=17/18500 and grad F=(78625,78591,69345)/21390625 at (1/4,1/4,1/4). Along the sampled-update segment, its population risk has second derivative <=-1/10000000; independent labels differ with probability 1/2, giving the bound. The activation and its first two derivatives are globally bounded by 1. This rules out a universal width-only replacement for independent SGD noise in this finite-horizon class. A positive excess above the larger endpoint loss, a prescribed nondegenerate initialization, or low-risk converged endpoints is not established.

[Lem burnIn:XtDtBoundedImpliesYtBounded of arXiv:2607.09841, 'Mixing and cutoff for the systematic scan dynamics of the mean-field ferromagnetic Potts m'] Suppose that for some integer $k\geq0$, a fixed constant $a \in (1/q, 1]$, and a sufficiently small $\varepsilon > 0$ that satisfies $G_{\beta,n}(a) + 2\varepsilon < a$, we have
$\max\limits_{n^{3/4} < i  \leq n} Y_{kn}^{(i)} \leq a,$ and
$\max\limits_{1 \leq i\leq j\leq n} D^{(i)}_{k n + j} < \varepsilon n^{3/4}.$ 
Then, 
\begin{align*}
    \underset{n^{3/4} < i  \leq n}{\max} Y^{(i)}_{(k+1)n} \leq 2\varepsilon + G_{\beta, n}(a).      
\end{align*}
Moreover, $\underset{1 \leq i  \leq n}{\max} Y_{kn+i} \leq a + \frac{1}{n^{1/4}}.$

[Lemma 21 of arXiv:2605.27818, 'Exponential decay of mass for inertial coalescing particles with Hamiltonian noise'] Let $\mathcal C$ be a cell of $\T^2\setminus\mathcal S$ and
$[a_1,b_1]\times[a_2,b_2]\subset\R^2$ its lifted rectangle. Then
$\{a_1,b_1\}$ are two consecutive zeros of $h_1$ in $\T$, and
$\{a_2,b_2\}$ are two consecutive zeros of $h_2$. In particular, we have the following facts.
\begin{itemize}
\item[1.] The function $h_1$ does not vanish on $(a_1,b_1)$, hence has constant sign
there; similarly for $h_2$ on $(a_2,b_2)$.
\item[2.] Every midpoint $q\in\mathcal M\cap\overline{\mathcal C}$ has
the form $q=(q_1,p_2)$ with $q_1\in\{a_1,b_1\}$ and
$p_2\in(a_2,b_2)$ (when $q\in Z_1\times M_2$), or
$q=(p_1,q_2)$ with $p_1\in(a_1,b_1)$ and $q_2\in\{a_2,b_2\}$
(when $q\in M_1\times Z_2$). 
\item[3.] $M_i\cap(a_i,b_i)$ consists of exactly one point, which
is a strict local extremum of $|h_i|$ on $[a_i,b_i]$. In particular,
$\overline{\mathcal C}$ contains exactly four midpoints
of $\mathcal M$: two of type $Z_1\times M_2$ and two of type $M_1\times Z_2$.
\end{itemize}

[Proposition 2 (Ideal-completion extension) of arXiv:2608.25925, '\textbf{Jump Closure and Limit Uniformization\\in the Ideal Completion of the Turing Degre'] Let $P$ be a poset and let $f:P\to P$ be monotone. Define
\[
\widehat f:\Idl(P)\to\Idl(P)
\]
by
\begin{equation}
\widehat f(I)
=\down f[I]
=\{y\in P:\exists x\in I\ (y\leq f(x))\}.

\end{equation}
Then $\widehat f$ is well defined and Scott-continuous. Moreover,
\begin{equation}
\widehat f(\down x)=\down f(x)

\end{equation}
for every $x\in P$.

Let f be in L^1_loc(R^d). Then for Lebesgue-almost every x, (1/|B(x,r)|) integral_{B(x,r)} |f(y) - f(x)| dy -> 0 as r -> 0; such an x is called a Lebesgue point of f. In particular the averages of f over shrinking balls converge to f(x) for a.e. x. The result persists if balls are replaced by any family of sets U_r shrinking NICELY to x, meaning U_r is contained in B(x,r) and |U_r| >= c |B(x,r)| for a fixed c > 0 (cubes centred at x, for instance). It FAILS for families of arbitrary eccentricity: in R^2 there is an integrable f whose averages over rectangles centred at x with sides parallel to the axes and both side lengths tending to 0 fail to converge at almost every x, because the strong maximal function is not of weak type (1,1). The a.e. exceptional set genuinely depends on f and cannot be taken empty. [standard; e.g. Stein and Shakarchi, Real Analysis, Chapter 3, Corollary 1.5 and Section 1.4]

averaging sets shrink nicely to x (bounded eccentricity); unbounded eccentricity breaks the theorem

body: [Theorem 18 (Morse transfer from induced subcomplexes) of arXiv:2609.01882, '\textbf{Coxeter Descents and Parabolic Homotopy Colimits}\\[2mm] \large A Hochster-type de'] For each $D\subseteq S$, the unit matchings in Lemmas~\ref{lem:conereduction} and \ref{lem:descentclosure} give an explicit algebraic Morse reduction of the $D$-relative pair to the suspended augmented chains of $\sd\mathcal K_D$. Consequently any unit acyclic matching on $\sd\mathcal K_D$ may be applied as a second algebraic Morse reduction, shifted one degree upward. If $\mathcal K_D\ne\{\varnothing\}$ and the chosen matching has a critical vertex, the augmentation generator can be cancelled with the suspension of one such vertex; the remaining critical generators represent the shifted reduced Morse complex of $\sd\mathcal K_D$.

[Lemma modifiedEP9.6 of arXiv:2506.10448, 'Hitting probabilities and the Ekstr\"om--Persson conjecture'] Let $\mu$ and $\theta$ be probability measures on a separable metric space $X$, let 
$(V_k)_{k=1}^{\infty}$ be a sequence of Borel subsets of $X$ such that $0<\mu(V_k)<1$ for
every $k\in\mathbb{N}$ and let $\underline r$ be a sequence of positive numbers tending to $0$.
Suppose that there exists a number $s>0$ such that 
\begin{equation}
f_{\theta}(\underline{\rho})=s_2(\underline{\rho})
\end{equation}
for every sequence $\underline{\rho}=(\rho_k)_{k=1}^\infty$ of radii with 
$s_2(\underline{\rho})\leq s$. Assume also that
there exists a constant $C$ such that, for every $k\in\mathbb{N}$ and every $x\in \spt \theta$,
\[
\theta(B(x,2r_k))\leq C\mu_{V_k}(B(x,r_k))
\] 
where $\mu_{V_k}:=\mu(V_k)^{-1}\mu_{|_{V_k}}$.
If there exists $t\in\mathopen]0,s\mathclose[$ such that 
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\mu(V_k)r_k^t=\infty,
\]
then $f_{\mu}(\underline{r})\geq t$.

[Proposition Bounded-regularizer transfer below the
\texorpdfstring{\(\psi_1\)}{psi1} scale of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[proposition]{prop:weibull-exact-transfer}
Fix any \(L>0\).  Assume the hypotheses on the disorder array and \(V\)
from (thm:weibull-bulk of the paper), and assume
that \(\widehat{\mathscr C}_{N,L}^J(V)\) is finite and positive for all
sufficiently large \(N\).  Put
\(\Phi=\Phi_p^{\rm bulk}(V)\) and
\[
 \widehat P^{\,c}_{N,L}(\varepsilon,\eta,R)
 =
 \frac1N\log
 \mathbb E\widehat\mathcal Z_{N,L}^J(V,\varepsilon,f_{\eta,R})
\]
and define
\begin{align*}
 \delta_{L,\mathrm{dr},c}^{J,\mathrm{up}}(V)
 &:=
 \liminf_{R\to\infty}\liminf_{\eta\downarrow0}
 \liminf_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\limsup_N
 [\widehat Q_{N,L}-\widehat P^{\,c}_{N,L}(\varepsilon,\eta,R)]_+,\\
 \delta_{L,\mathrm{dr},c}^{J,\mathrm{low}}(V)
 &:=
 \liminf_{R\to\infty}\liminf_{\eta\downarrow0}
 \liminf_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\limsup_N
 [\widehat P^{\,c}_{N,L}(\varepsilon,\eta,R)-\widehat Q_{N,L}]_+.
\end{align*}
Then every conclusion of (thm:conditional-transfer of the paper) holds with
the two uncut defects replaced by these cutoff defects.  In particular,
if both vanish, the exact max identities
(equation eq:exact-upper-defect-formula of the paper)--(equation eq:exact-lower-defect-formula of the paper)
and the necessary-and-sufficient criterion
(equation eq:exact-universality-iff-localized-defect of the paper) remain valid.
This proposition preserves the Weibull transfer route but makes no
uncut determinant or remote-tail claim.

body: Publication record. Y. Shmalo, Hub paths and the largest component of the barely subcritical configuration model (2026). For the configuration model with a degree sequence whose third moment converges, write eps_n = 1 - nu_n with nu_n = sum d_i(d_i - 1)/sum d_i tending to one from below. In his Saint-Flour notes (Open Problem 4.13) van der Hofstad asked to show that in the barely subcritical regime (eps_n -> 0, n eps_n^3 -> infinity) the largest component has order max{d_max/eps_n, eps_n^(-2) log(n eps_n^3)}, and predicted size (d_max/eps_n)(1 + o_P(1)) when eps_n tends to zero slowly enough. The paper shows neither holds in this generality. The degree sequences have vertices of degree one and three and a polynomial number of hubs of a large common degree d that contribute nothing to the third moment in the limit; paths of K hubs joined by direct edges appear, and the component of such a path is a tree with about K d/eps_n vertices. For K = 2, L_1 >= (2 - eta) d_max/eps_n with high probability; for K growing like sqrt(log n), L_1 >= c sqrt(log n) max{d_max/eps_n, eps_n^(-2) log(n eps_n^3)}. The order of L_1 in these examples is not determined. Paper and code: https://github.com/yspennstate/hub-paths-barely-subcritical (commit 444515b247a0). Not refereed.
title: Hub paths and the largest component of the barely subcritical configuration model: counterexamples to van der Hofstad's Open Problem 4.13 prediction (Shmalo 2026, repository yspennstate/hub-paths-barely-subcritical)

[Proposition thm:RT_specialized of arXiv:2605.17725, 'Limit theorems for random walks with spatio-temporal drift'] Let $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$ be a complete right-continuous filtration, and let
$(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ be a c\`adl\`ag $\mathbb R^d$-valued process of the form
$$
X_t-X_0=\int_0^t F_s\,\mathrm{d} s+M_t+R_t,
$$
where $F$ is progressively measurable, $M$ is a c\`adl\`ag locally square-integrable martingale, and $R$ is a c\`adl\`ag adapted process of finite variation. Let
$\Gamma\in\mathcal F_\infty$, and let $\alpha:[0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ be
nonincreasing càdlàg function with $\lim_{t\to\infty}\alpha(t)=0$.

Assume that there exist a constant $\rho>0$, a finite random time $T_0$, and a nonnegative
càdlàg adapted process $E_t$ such that a.s. on $\Gamma$,

\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)]
$\langle X_{t-},F_t\rangle\ge0\quad\text{for all $t\ge T_0$ such that $\|X_{t-}\|<\rho$ }$;

\item[(ii)]
$
\alpha(t)^2-\alpha(t+1)^2
=
O(\langle M\rangle_{t,t+1})
$ as $t\to\infty$;

\item[(iii)]
$
\langle M\rangle_{t,\infty}=O(\alpha(t)^2)
$ as $t\to\infty$; 

\item[(iv)]
$
V(R,(t,\infty))=o(\alpha(t))$ as $t\to\infty$;

\item[(v)]
for all sufficiently large $t$ and for every stopping time $S> t$,
$$
\mathbb{E}[\|\Delta M_S\|^2\mathbf 1_{\{S<\infty\}}\mid\mathcal F_t]
\le
E_t\,\mathbb P(S<\infty\mid\mathcal F_t)
\quad\text{and}\quad
E_t=O(\alpha(t)^2).
$$
\end{itemize}

Then
$
\mathbb P(\Gamma\cap\{X_t\to0\})=0.
$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition 9 of arXiv:2608.18688, 'Regularity Preservation for Jump-Type Stochastic Transport Equations with Singular Drift'] A local $\mH^{m,\alpha}$-process is called a local $\mH^{m,\alpha}$-martingale if, for any $x\in\mR^d$,  the stopped process $\partial^kX_t^{\tau_n(x)}(x)$, $0\leq |k|\leq m$, $n=1,2,\cdots$ are  martingales. It is called a local $\mH^{m,\alpha}$-processes of bounded variation if, for any $x\in\mR^d$,  $\partial^kX_t^{\tau_n(x)}(x)$, $0\leq |k|\leq m$, $n=1,2,\cdots$ are bounded variation. Furthermore, it is classified as a  local  $\mH^{m,\alpha}$-semimartingale if it can be expressed as the sum of a  local  $\mH^{m,\alpha}$-martingale and a  local  $\mH^{m,\alpha}$-process of bounded variation. 	Additionally, it is designated as a continuous local  $\mH^{m,\alpha}$-semimartingale 
	if both components in the sum are continuous in $(t,x)$.
	
	If $\tau(x)=\infty$ for any $x$ a.s., these are called global $\mH^{m,\alpha}$-martingale etc.

[Proposition 7 (Fixed-time regularity of functionals of the decoupled flow) of arXiv:2605.03057, 'Uniform-in-time quantitative fluctuations of large scale interacting particle systems'] Let Assumption \ref{ass:flow-smothness} hold. Let $ \varphi \in C_b^7\left( \R^d \right) $.
For $ t \ge 0 $, $ x \in \R^d $, and $ \mu \in \Ptwo $, let $ X_t^{x,\mu} $ be the decoupled flow
associated with the McKean--Vlasov equation, and define
\begin{equation*}
u_t\left( x,\mu \right) = \E\left( \varphi\left( X_t^{x,\mu} \right) \right).
\end{equation*}
Then, for every fixed $ t \ge 0 $, all multi-indices $ \gamma $ and $ \beta $, and
  every integer $ n \ge 0 $ with $1 \le \abs{\gamma} + \abs{\beta} + n
  \le 7$, the mixed derivative
\begin{equation*}
\partial_x^\gamma \partial_v^\beta \partial_\mu^n
u_t\left( x,\mu \right)\left( v_1,\dots,v_n \right)
\end{equation*}
exists and is continuous in $\left( x,\mu,v_1,\dots,v_n \right)$. More precisely, every such derivative is a finite sum of terms of the form
\begin{equation}

\E\left(
\nabla^r \varphi\left( X_t^{x,\mu} \right)
\left[
\partial_x^{\gamma_1} \partial_v^{\beta_1}\partial_\mu^{n_1}
X_t^{x,\mu}\left( \mathbf{v}_1 \right),\dots,
\partial_x^{\gamma_r} \partial_v^{\beta_r}\partial_\mu^{n_r}
X_t^{x,\mu}\left( \mathbf{v}_r \right)
\right]
\right),
\end{equation}
where $ 1 \le r \le 7 $, for each $1 \leq j \leq r$, $\mathbf{v}_j$
denotes an $n_j$-tuple of Lions directions, and each
$\partial_x^{\gamma_j} \partial_v^{\beta_j}\partial_\mu^{n_j}
X_t^{x,\mu}\left( \mathbf{v}_j \right)$
is a mixed derivative of the flow of positive total order $1 \le \abs{\gamma_j} + \abs{\beta_j} + n_j
  \le 7$.

body:
[Theorem 1 (\textsf{Dominant chaos with lower-order perturbations}) of arXiv:2608.12451, '2608.12451'] Fix $\mathsf{S}\in\{{ \mathsf{P}},{\mathsf{R}}\}$, $r\in\N$, and
$\lambda\in(0,\infty)$.  For each $n\in\N$, let\footnote{The sum $\sum_{j=1}^0$ is understood to be empty.}

\noi
\begin{align*}
 F_n\in\cC_{r}^{\mathsf{S}}\cap L^4(\PP),
 \quad
 B_n=\sum_{j=1}^{r-1}B_{n,j},
\AND
 B_{n,j}\in\cC_{j}^{\mathsf{S}}\cap L^4(\PP).
\end{align*} 

\noi
Suppose that $F_n+B_n$ satisfies the lattice condition
\eqref{cond_La} with shift $\theta_n>0$, and define
$X_n:=\theta_n+F_n+B_n$.  Put
$\eps_n:=\sum_{j=1}^{r-1}\norm{B_{n,j}}_4$.
For every $n$ such that $\theta_n>0$, with
$c_{\theta_n}:=(1-e^{-\theta_n})/\theta_n$, define

\noi
\begin{align}
 \mathfrak{R}_{\theta_n}(F_n,\eps_n)
 :=
 c_{\theta_n}\bigg[ 2 \|F_n\|_4\eps_n+\eps_n^2+\frac{\eps_n}{2}
 + 14\bigl(1+ \|F_n\|_4+\eps_n\bigr)^3\eps_n  \bigg]
 +\left(1+\frac{c_{\theta_n}}2\right)\eps_n.
 
\end{align}
Then,

\noi
\begin{align} 
\begin{aligned}
 \dTV\bigl( X_n,  P_{\theta_n}\bigr)  
   & \leq
 c_{\theta_n}\bigg[  | m_2(F_n)-\theta_n|  + \frac{2r-1}{2r}\sqrt{\mathfrak{d}_{\mathsf{S}}(F_n)} \\
 &\qquad\qquad\qquad  + \frac23\sqrt{m_2(F_n)\mathfrak d_{\mathsf{S}}(F_n)}
 +b_{\mathsf{S}}\mathfrak d_{\mathsf{S}}(F_n)  \bigg]  
   +\mathfrak R_{\theta_n}(F_n,\eps_n).
\end{aligned}
\end{align}

\noi
In particular, $\mathfrak R_{\theta_n}(F_n,0)=0$.  Hence, when
$\eps_n=0$, one has $B_n=0$ and \eqref{pert_main_bdd} reduces exactly
to Corollary~\ref{cor_P_quant} if $\mathsf{S}={ \mathsf{P}}$ and to
Corollary~\ref{cor_R_quant} if $\mathsf{S}={\mathsf{R}}$.

If, in addition,
$
 \big(\theta_n,  m_2(F_n), \mathfrak{d}_{\mathsf{S}}(F_n)\big)
 \xrightarrow{n\to+\infty}(\lambda, \lambda, 0)$
and
 $\eps_n\to0$,
then
$\dTV(X_n, P_\lambda)\to0$,
the first four moments of $X_n$ converge to those of
$P_\lambda$, and $(X_n^4)_{n\geq1}$ is uniformly integrable.
In the Rademacher case, under $m_2(F_n)\to\lambda$, the condition
$\mathfrak{d}_{\mathsf{R}}(F_n)\to0$ is equivalent to
$\cR(F_n)\to0$ and $\cM(F_n)\to0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: \textsf{Dominant chaos with lower-order perturbations}

[Definition 23 of arXiv:2609.02850, 'Canonical-row Chern flow on Bott--Samelson towers:\\ realizable-volume models for Schubert'] Let $\mathbf i=(i_1,\ldots,i_\ell)$ be a word in
$\{1,\ldots,n-1\}$, let
$\epsilon=(\epsilon_1,\ldots,\epsilon_\ell)\in\{0,1\}^\ell$, and let
$\mathbf d=(d_1,\ldots,d_n)\in\NN^n$.  For $1\le j\le n$, put
\begin{equation}
 T_j=\{0\}\cup\{t\in[\ell]:i_t=j\},
 \qquad
 \tau_j(t)=\max\bigl(T_j\cap\{0,1,\ldots,t\}\bigr),
 \qquad
 \lambda_j=\tau_j(\ell).
\end{equation}
The vertex $v_{j,r}$, for $r\in T_j$, is the rank-$j$ state created at
time $r$; in particular, $v_{j,0}$ is the initial state.  At stage $t$ the
current rank-$j$ state is $v_{j,\tau_j(t)}$.  There is deliberately no
separate vertex for a passive pullback at a time not belonging to $T_j$.

The rooted directed multigraph
$\mathfrak C(\mathbf i,\epsilon,\mathbf d)$ has vertex set
\[
 \{0\}\sqcup\{v_{j,r}:1\le j\le n,\ r\in T_j\}.
\]
For every $t$ with $\epsilon_t=1$, it has one ordinary edge
\begin{equation}
 e_t:v_{i_t,t}\longrightarrow
 v_{i_t+1,\tau_{i_t+1}(t-1)}.
\end{equation}
For every $j$ it has $d_j$ root edges
\begin{equation}
 e_{j,a}:0\longrightarrow v_{j,\lambda_j}
 \qquad(1\le a\le d_j).
\end{equation}
Degrees are counted with edge multiplicity.
title: Definition 23 of arXiv:2609.02850

body:
[Theorem thm:CO of arXiv:2601.09976, 'Stochastic Calculus as Operator Factorization:\\ An Operator--Covariant Derivative and Uni'] Let $X$ be a square-integrable process with natural filtration $(\mathcal{F}_t^X)_{t \in [0,T]}$, energy space~$\mathcal{H}_X$, stochastic integral~$\delta_X$, predictable projection~$\Pi_X$, and operator--covariant derivative $D_X = \delta_X^*$. Assume:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item \textup{Centered integrals:} $\mathbb{E}[\delta_X(u)] = 0$ for all $u \in \mathcal{H}_X$.
\item \textup{Isometry on predictable processes:} $\mathbb{E}[|\delta_X(u)|^2] = \|u\|_{\mathcal{H}_X}^2$ for predictable $u \in \mathcal{H}_X$.
\item \textup{Representation property:} Every $\mathcal{F}_T^X$-measurable $\tilde{F} \in L^2(\Omega)$ with $\mathbb{E}[\tilde{F}] = 0$ can be written as $\tilde{F} = \delta_X(v)$ for some predictable $v \in \mathcal{H}_X$.
\end{enumerate}
Then for all $\mathcal{F}_T^X$-measurable $F \in L^2(\Omega)$:
\begin{equation}
F \;=\; \mathbb{E}[F] + \delta_X(\Pi_X D_X F) \;=\; \mathbb{E}[F] + \int_0^T (\Pi_X D_X F)_t\, dX_t.
\end{equation}
Equivalently, the operator identity $(\mathrm{Id} - \mathbb{E}) = \delta_X \circ \Pi_X \circ D_X$ holds on $L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{F}_T^X, P)$.

[Lem 85 of arXiv:2507.08909, 'Annealed almost periodic entropy'] Assume that~\eqref{eq:traces-fast} holds, and let $\pi$ be a separable unital representation of $\A$.

\[\bbP(\X(\pi_n,O) \ne \emptyset) \to 1.\]
If $\pi \lesssim_{\rm{a}} \l^{\oplus \infty}$, then $\rmh_{\bspi}^0(\pi) = \ul{\rmh}_{\bspi}^0(\pi) = 0$.

Then $\rmh_{\bspi}^0(\pi) = \rmh_{\bspi}^0(\pi^{M^\perp})$ and $\ul{\rmh}_{\bspi}^0(\pi) = \ul{\rmh}_{\bspi}^0(\pi^{M^\perp})$.
\end{enumerate}

[Defn 6 of arXiv:2609.02342, '2609.02342'] Let \(X\) be a topological vector space and
	\((T_t)_{t\geq0}\) a linear semigroup on \(X\). For nonempty open sets
	\(U,V\subset X\), define
	\[
	N(U,V)=\{t\geq0:T_t(U)\cap V\neq\varnothing\}.
	\]
	Given a Furstenberg family \(\mathcal F\) on \(\mathbb R_+\), the semigroup
	\((T_t)_{t\geq0}\) is called \emph{\(\mathcal F\)-transitive} if
	\(
	N(U,V)\in\mathcal F
	\)
	for all nonempty open sets \(U,V\subset X\), and
topologically	\emph{ \(\mathcal F\)-recurrent} if
	\(
	N(U,U)\in\mathcal F
	\)
	for every nonempty open set \(U\subset X\).
title: Definition 6 of arXiv:2609.02342

[Lemma 10 of arXiv:2607.09246, 'Scaling limit of 1+1 dimensional directed polymer with power-law tail and spatial correlat'] Assume that conditions \textbf{(A)} and \textbf{(B)} hold, and let
\(H=\frac32-r\in(\frac12,1)\). For \(k\ge1\), set \(t_0=0\) and
\(s_i=t_i-t_{i-1}\). Then
\[
\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}\limsup_{N\to\infty}
\left\|\psi_N^k
{\mathbbm 1}_{\{\min_{1\le i\le k}s_i\le\delta\}}
\right\|_{\mathcal L_K^k}=0,
\]
and
\[
\lim_{M\to\infty}\limsup_{N\to\infty}
\left\|\psi_N^k
{\mathbbm 1}_{\{\max_{1\le i\le k}|x_i|>M\}}
\right\|_{\mathcal L_K^k}=0.
\]
The same estimates hold with \(\psi_N^k\) replaced by \(\tilde\rho_k\).

body:
For any two probability distributions P and Q on the same discrete finite or countable set X, with pmfs p and q, the Kullback-Leibler divergence satisfies D(P||Q) = sum_{x} p(x) * log(p(x)/q(x)) >= 0, with equality if and only if p(x) = q(x) for every x, i.e. P = Q. This fact is also known as Gibbs' inequality.

        \le Cn^{-c\eps}.
\]

[Theorem 1 (Sufficient Maximum Principle) of arXiv:2604.00937, 'Infinite Horizon Optimal Control of Forward-Backward Stochastic Volterra Equations with De'] Let $\hat{u} \in \mathcal{U}$ with corresponding solutions $\hat{X}(t)$, $(\hat{Y}(t), \hat{Z}(t,\cdot), \hat{K}(t,\cdot,\cdot))$, $(\hat{p}(t), \hat{q}(t,\cdot), \hat{r}(t,\cdot,\cdot))$ and $\hat{\lambda}(t)$ of equations (\ref{b1}), (\ref{b2}), (\ref{eq3.2}) and (\ref{p}) respectively. Suppose that:

\begin{description}
\item[Concavity] The function $x \mapsto h(x)$ and the Hamiltonian
\[
(x,x_1,y,z,k(\cdot),u) \mapsto H(t,x,x_1,y,z,k,u,\hat{\lambda}(t),\hat{p}(t),\hat{q}(t,\cdot),\hat{r}(t,\cdot,\cdot))
\]
are concave for all $t \geq 0$.

\item[Conditional Maximum Principle]
\begin{align*}
& \max_{v \in \mathcal{U}} \mathbb{E}\left[ H(t,\hat{X}(t),\hat{X}_1(t),\hat{Y}(t),\hat{Z}(t,\cdot),\hat{K}(t,\cdot,\cdot),v,\hat{\lambda}(t),\hat{p}(t),\hat{q}(t,\cdot),\hat{r}(t,\cdot,\cdot)) \mid \mathcal{G}_t \right] \\
& = \mathbb{E}\left[ H(t,\hat{X}(t),\hat{X}_1(t),\hat{Y}(t),\hat{Z}(t,\cdot),\hat{K}(t,\cdot,\cdot),\hat{u},\hat{\lambda}(t),\hat{p}(t),\hat{q}(t,\cdot),\hat{r}(t,\cdot,\cdot)) \mid \mathcal{G}_t \right].
\end{align*}

\item[Transversality Conditions]
\[
\varlimsup_{T \to \infty} \mathbb{E}[\hat{\lambda}(T)(\hat{Y}(T) - Y(T))] \geq 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \varlimsup_{T \to \infty} \mathbb{E}[\hat{p}(T)(\hat{X}(T) - X(T))] \leq 0.
\]
\end{description}

Then, $\hat{u}$ is an optimal control for our problem.
title: Sufficient Maximum Principle
