[Thm 51 (Erd\"os-Taylor theorem for SRI chains in $d=2$) of arXiv:2510.22155, 'Random walks in space-time random media in all spatial dimensions: the full subcritical fl'] Let $d=2$ and assume Assumption \ref{ass:SRI}. If $\x_N$ is any sequence in $I^2$ such that $x^1_N-x^2_N$ remains bounded as $N\to\infty$, then $(\log N)^{-1}\sum_{r=0}^N f_N(   R^1_r-   R^2_r) $ converges in law (viewed under $\Ebbnn$) as $N\to \infty$ to an exponential random variable of rate $2/\big(\int f\dr\pi^{\mathrm{inv}}\big)$. 

    Furthermore, for any $t>\varepsilon>0$ the random variable $\sum_{r=N\varepsilon}^{Nt}f_N(   R^1_r-   R^2_r)$ goes to 0 in probability, thus $(\log N)^{-1}\sum_{r=0}^{Nt} f_N(   R^1_r-   R^2_r), $ viewed as a process in the variable $t$, converges in f.d.d.'s to a constant process equal to the same exponential random variable. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Definition 3 (Large deviation principle) of arXiv:2609.03750, '\bf Pullback Measure Attractors, Zero-Noise Limits, and Moderate Deviations for 2D Stochas'] Let \( I \) be a good rate function on \( \mathfrak{U} \). Given a collection \( \{b(\epsilon)\}_{\epsilon > 0} \) of positive reals, a family \( \{\mathcal{Y}^\epsilon\}_{\epsilon > 0} \) of \( \mathfrak{U} \)-valued random elements is said to satisfy an LDP on \( \mathfrak{U} \) with logarithmic scale \( b(\epsilon) \) (equivalently, with conventional speed \(1/b(\epsilon)\)) and rate function \( I \) if the following two bounds hold:
	 
	 $(i)$ \textit{(Upper bound)} For each closed subset \( F \) of \( \mathfrak{U} \),
	 
	 \[
	 \limsup_{\epsilon \to 0} b(\epsilon) \log \mathbb{P}(\mathcal{Y}^\epsilon \in F) \leq - \inf_{x \in F} I(x).
	 \]
	 
	 $(ii)$ \textit{(Lower bound)} For each open subset \( O \) of \( \mathfrak{U} \),
	 
	 \[
	 \liminf_{\epsilon \to 0} b(\epsilon) \log \mathbb{P}(\mathcal{Y}^\epsilon \in O) \geq - \inf_{x \in O} I(x).
	 \]
title: Large deviation principle

[Theorem thm:vc-uniform-convergence of arXiv:2512.04371, 'Constructive Approximation under Carleman's Condition, \\ with Applications to Smoothed An'] Let $\mathcal{H}$ be a class of binary classifiers with VC-dimension $V < \infty$. For i.i.d.\ samples $\{z_i\}_{i \le n}$ drawn from a distribution $\mu$, define the empirical and true error by $\hat{R}_n(h) = n^{-1}\sum_{i \le n} h(z_i)$ and $R(h) = \EE_{z \sim \mu}[h(z)]$ respectively. Then for any $\delta > 0$, with probability at least $1-\delta$ over the sample, uniformly for all $h \in \mathcal{H}$:
\[
|R(h) - \hat{R}_n(h)| \lesssim \sqrt{\frac{V \log(n/V) + \log(1/\delta)}{n}}.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

ds^{(v)}_t=\Big[-\alpha_{d(v)}\,s^{(v)}_t+\sum_{u\sim v}\gamma_{d(u)\to d(v)}\,\sigma\big(s^{(u)}_t-\theta_{uv}\big)\Big]\,dt+b_{d(v)}\,dW^{(v)}_t,
\]
with $\alpha_d\ge\alpha_{\min}>0$, $b_d^2\ge\mu_0>0$, thresholds $\theta_{uv}\ge\theta_{\min}>0$, couplings $\gamma_{d\to d'}\ge0$, $\sigma$ the logistic function, and $\{W^{(v)}\}$ independent Brownian motions. A vertex fails when $s^{(v)}$ crosses a threshold $\theta^{\mathrm{fail}}$ into an absorbing basin $B_{\mathrm{fail}}=[\theta^{\mathrm{fail}},\infty)$ before returning to a safe value $s_{\mathrm{safe}}$.

[Theorem thm:annulusisotopy of arXiv:2608.30973, 'Pseudo-Anosov flow and dynamics on guts'] Assume that \(M\) is atoroidal and admits an almost pseudo-Anosov flow \(\varphi\) without perfect fits.
Let \(S\) be an embedded, compact, oriented, taut surface in \(M\) which is positively transverse to \(\varphi\) minimally.
Suppose that \(A\) is a homotopically non-trivial, oriented annulus with two boundary components lying on opposite sides of \(S\).
In other words, \(A\) is a product annulus in the sutured manifold \((M-S,S_{+},S_{-},\emptyset)\)..

Then, \(A\) is ambiently isotopic to an annulus \(A_{\varphi}\) in \(M-S\), which is either product \(\varphi\)-saturated or transverse to a further blowup of \(\varphi\).
We call that \(A_{\varphi}\) is \emph{in aligned position} with \(\varphi\). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Annulus Isotopy Theorem

body: [Definition def:type graph of arXiv:2607.16911, 'Multipartite random graphs with given degrees: local limit, revisiting the giant, distance'] Consider a digraph $G_S$, with vertex set $V(G_S)$ consisting of all \emph{type triplets}, $V(G_S):=\{(u,v,w):u,v,w \in S\}$ and directed edges go from vertices of the form $(\cdot,v,w)$ to $(v,w,\cdot)$. Denote the edge set of this graph by $E(G_S)$. Thus $E(G_S)$ consists of ordered pairs $(u_0,u_1)$ for $u_0,u_1 \in V(G_S)$. We call $G_S=(V(G_S),E(G_S))$ the \textit{type digraph} corresponding to the type set $S$.

[Lemma outdeg of arXiv:2606.27844, 'Critical percolation on preferential attachment graphs with infinite variance'] \begin{itemize}
    \item[(a)]
    Let $P_1,\dots,P_n$ be independent random variables where $P_j$ is Poisson distributed with parameter $\lambda_j=\sum_{i=j+1}^n \beta(n) j^{-\gamma}i^{\gamma-1}$. Then $\emph{outdeg}(1),$ $\dots,\emph{outdeg}(n) $ can be coupled to $P_1,\dots,P_n$, such that
    $$ \mathbb P\big(\exists j\in\{1,\dots,n\}\,:\,\emph{outdeg}(j)\neq P_j\big)\to0\,.$$
\item[(b)]
    Let $\hat P_1,\dots,\hat P_n$ be independent random variables where $\hat P_j$ is Poisson distributed with parameter $\hat \lambda_j=\sum_{i=1}^{j-1} \beta(n) i^{-\gamma}j^{\gamma-1}$. Then $\emph{indeg}(1),\dots,\emph{indeg}(n) $ can be coupled to $\hat P_1,\dots, \hat P_n$, such that
    $$ \mathbb P\big(\exists j\in\{1,\dots,n\}\,:\,\emph{indeg}(j)\neq \hat P_j\big)\to0\,.$$
\end{itemize}

[Theorem 38 of arXiv:2604.22159, 'Adapted optimal transport between filtered Gaussian processes'] Consider the set-up described above. Let $P_1, P_2, \ldots$ be an arbitrary (deterministic) sequence in $\mathscr{C}(d)$. For each $N$, define
\[
P^{(N)} := \diag(P_1, \ldots, P_N) \in \bR^{Nd \times Nd}
\]
and, using the notation in Lemma \ref{lem:coupling.Gaussian}, define
\[
\pi^{(N)} := \pi^{P^{(N)}},
\]
which is a Gaussian bicausal coupling of $\bX^{(N)}$ and $\bY^{(N)}$. Consider the random variable
\[
\cT(\pi^{(N)}) := \bE_{\pi^{(N)}} [ \|X^{(N)} - Y^{(N)}\|_2^2],
\]
which is the transport cost between $\bX^{(N)}$ and $\bY^{(N)}$ under $\pi^{(N)}$. Then, we have
\begin{equation}  
\lim_{N \rightarrow \infty} \frac{1}{N^2} \cT(\pi^{(N)}) = d^2 \quad \text{almost surely.}
\end{equation}
In particular, we have, almost surely,
\[
\lim_{N \rightarrow \infty} \frac{\cT(\pi^{(N)})}{\AW_2^2(\bX^{(N)}, \bY^{(N)})} = 1.

body:
[Theorem thm:GwithoutSeeds of arXiv:2606.24793, '\LARGE Random sequential nearest-neighbor coloring on trees'] Consider the coloring process on $\mathcal{T}$ without seeds and let $\mathcal G$ denote the associated genealogical graph. Then the following assertions hold almost surely:
\begin{enumerate}
\item The genealogical graph $\mathcal G$ has infinitely many connected components. Furthermore, denoting by $N_n$ the number of connected components of $\mathcal G$ intersecting the sphere $S(o,n)$, there exists a constant $c>0$ (depending only on $K$) such that
    $$\liminf_{n\to \infty} \frac{N_n}{\sharp S(o,n)}\ge c \qquad \mbox{ a.s.}.$$
    \item Every connected component of $\mathcal G$ is an infinite one-ended oriented tree, i.e.\ for every $v \in \mathcal{T}$, its ancestral path $\Gamma(v)$ is infinite while its set of descendants $D(v)$ is finite and satisfies
    \[
    \mathbb{E}[\sharp D(v) \mid \tau_v]<\infty \qquad \mbox{ a.s.}.
    \]

    \item Every connected component $\mathcal C$ of $\mathcal G$ admits a limit direction, i.e.\ there exists an infinite ray $\xi=(w_i)_{i\ge 1}\in \partial \mathcal{T}$ such that, for every vertex $v$ in the component and every $i \ge 1$, the vertices of $\Gamma(v)$ eventually belong to the subtree $\mathcal{T}_{w_i}$. We denote this limit by
    \[
    \mathop{dir} \mathcal C \in \partial \mathcal{T}.
    \]

    \item For every vertex $v \in \mathcal{T}$, there exists, almost surely, a connected component $\mathcal C$ such that $\mathop{dir} \mathcal C \in \partial \mathcal{T}_v$. 

    \item If $\mathcal C,\mathcal C'$ are two distinct connected components of $\mathcal G$, then
    \[
    \mathop{dir} \mathcal C \neq \mathop{dir} \mathcal C' \qquad \text{a.s.}.
    \]
    
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: \textbf{The genealogical graph without seeds}

[Lemma 21 of arXiv:2608.17509, '2608.17509'] The operators \(W_L(r_a)\) and \(\widetilde{W}_{a,L}\) admit a common
Hilbert--Schmidt factorization: there exists
\(V_{a,L}:L^2(0,L)\to L^2(0,\infty)\) such that
\[
        W_L(r_a)=V_{a,L}^{*}V_{a,L},
        \qquad
        \widetilde{W}_{a,L}=V_{a,L}V_{a,L}^{*}.
\]
Consequently, they are positive trace-class operators with the same nonzero
eigenvalues, counted with multiplicity, and for every \(t\in\mathbb C\),
\[
        \det(\operatorname{Id}+t\widetilde{W}_{a,L})
        =
        \det(\operatorname{Id}+tW_L(r_a)).
\]
Moreover, with \(\rho_a:=\sup_{\xi>0}r_a(\xi)\in(0,1)\),
\[
        0\leq W_L(r_a)\leq \rho_a\operatorname{Id},
        \qquad
        0\leq \widetilde{W}_{a,L}\leq \rho_a\operatorname{Id}.
\]

[Lemma 45 of arXiv:2604.25877, 'Asymptotic height of Plancherel random trees'] Fix $t>1$ and $\theta>0$, and let $P\sim \mathrm{Beta}(t,\theta)$ on $(0,1)$. Set
\[
\bar X:=-\log P.
\]
Then the law of $\bar X$ is absolutely continuous on $(0,\infty)$. Moreover, there exists an
integer $k\ge 1$ such that the $k$-fold convolution density of $\bar X$ is bounded on
$(0,\infty)$.

body:
[Theorem 9 of arXiv:2608.29148, '2608.29148'] Let $(M, H, J)$ be a $3$-dimensional strictly pseudoconvex CR manifold and $(\mathcal{C}, [g^{\mathrm{F}}_\th])$ the Fefferman space over $M$. Then, there exists an $S^1$-invariant even Poincar\'e metric $g'$ on $X':=\mathcal{C}\times(0, \e)_r$ with the conformal infinity $(\mathcal{C}, [g^{\mathrm{F}}_\th])$ which satisfies the following conditions:
\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)] The induced ACH metric $\underline{g}$ on $\ol{X}:=M\times[0, \e)_r$ satisfies the self-dual Einstein equation:
\[
\mathrm{Ric}(\underline{g})+\frac{3}{2}\underline{g}=O(r^\infty), \quad W^-(\underline{g})=O(r^\infty).
\] 
\item[(ii)] The $\Theta$-$2$-tensor $F_{ij}$ on $\ol{X}$ is self-dual with respect to $\underline{g}$: 
\[
F^{-}=O(r^\infty).
\]
\end{itemize}
The metric $g'$ is unique modulo $O(r^\infty)$ up to pull-back by $S^1$-equivariant diffeomorphisms fixing points on $\mathcal{C}$. Moreover, the expansion of each component in the normal form of $g'$ with respect to a representative $g^{\mathrm{F}}_\th$ can be expressed by a universal formula in terms of the curvature and torsion of the Tanaka-Webster connection. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Corollary 6 (Gaussian-noise bulk and full-trace LSS) of arXiv:2608.07820, 'Linear Spectral Statistics for Entrywise-Transformed Spiked Wigner Matrices under Shifted '] Let $f$ satisfy \eqref{eq:Gaussian-f-assumptions-main}, let $\lambda\ge0$ be
fixed, and suppose that the deterministic spike obeys
\begin{equation}
 \norm{x}_2=1,
 \qquad
 \norm{x}_\infty=o(N^{-1/4}),
 \qquad
 \sum_{i=1}^N x_i=O(N^{o(1)}).
\end{equation}
Let $\Gamma$ satisfy (G1)--(G4) with $\theta_{f,\nu}$ replaced by $\theta_f$,
and let $\varphi_1,\ldots,\varphi_k$ be analytic on a neighborhood of
$\overline{D_\Gamma}$ and real-valued on its intersection with $\mathbb R$.
Then
\begin{equation}
 \left(
 \mathcal L_{M_{N,\gamma}^f}^{\Gamma}(\varphi_\ell)
 -N\int_{-2}^2\varphi_\ell(t)\rho_{\scal}(t)\,\dd t
 -m_{\varphi_\ell,\Gamma}^{\gamma,f}
 \right)_{\ell=1}^k
 \Longrightarrow
 (G_{\varphi_\ell})_{\ell=1}^k,
\end{equation}
where the limiting vector is centered Gaussian with
\begin{equation}
 \Cov(G_\varphi,G_\psi)
 =\mathcal V_{\kappa_f}^{\Gamma}(\varphi,\psi).
\end{equation}
If $|\theta_f|\le1$, then
$\mathcal L_{M_{N,\gamma}^f}^{\Gamma}(\varphi)
=\Tr\varphi(M_{N,\gamma}^f)$ with probability tending to one, so
\eqref{eq:Gaussian-bulk-CLT-main} is the full-trace CLT.  If
$|\theta_f|>1$ and each $\varphi_\ell$ is also analytic and real-valued on the
real axis near
\begin{equation}
 \rho_f:=\theta_f+\theta_f^{-1},
\end{equation}
then the full-trace CLT is obtained from
\eqref{eq:Gaussian-bulk-CLT-main} by replacing the statistic there with
\begin{equation}
 \left(
 \Tr\varphi_\ell(M_{N,\gamma}^f)
 -N\int_{-2}^2\varphi_\ell(t)\rho_{\scal}(t)\,\dd t
 -m_{\varphi_\ell,\Gamma}^{\gamma,f}
 -\varphi_\ell(\rho_f)
 \right)_{\ell=1}^k
 \Longrightarrow
 (G_{\varphi_\ell})_{\ell=1}^k,
\end{equation}
with the covariance \eqref{eq:Gaussian-covariance-main}.
In particular, all these conclusions hold for every centered and
variance-normalized polynomial-growth transform.

[Dfn 187 (approximate quadratic variation processes) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For $\sigma,\tau\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII\}$, define $\tilde{Q}^{\sigma,\tau}$ to be the piecewise linear process with increments
	\beq
	\Delta\tilde{Q}^{\sigma,\tau}(q_d)
	\equiv
	\Delta\tilde{Q}^{\sigma,\tau}(q_d,B)
	\equiv
	\frac{1}{|B|}
	\sum_{a\in B}
	\Big(\Delta X^{\trunc,\sigma}(q_d,a)\Big)
	\Big(\Delta X^{\trunc,\tau}(q_d,a)\Big)\,.
	\eeq
For the Ising case, we also define
	\beq
	\Delta\tilde{Q}^{\sigma,\Ising}(q_d)
	\equiv \frac{1}{|B||B^{\Ising}|}
	\sum_{a\in B,i\in B^{\Ising}}
	\Big(\Delta X^{\trunc,\sigma}(q_d,a)\Big)
	\Big(\Delta X^{\trunc,\Ising}(q_d,i)\Big)
	=
	\Big( \Delta \bar{D}^\sigma(q_d)\Big)
	\Big( \Delta \bar{D}^{\Ising}(q_d)\Big)
	\eeq
for $\sigma\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII\}$; 
as well as
	\beq
	\Delta\tilde{Q}^{\Ising}(q_d)
	\equiv
	\Delta\tilde{Q}^{\Ising}(q_d,B^\Ising)
	\equiv 
	\frac{1}{|B^{\Ising}|}
	\sum_{i\in B^{\Ising}}
	\Big(\Delta X^{\trunc,\Ising}(q_d,i)\Big)^2\,.
	\eeq
Denote also $E^{\sigma,\tau}\equiv Q^{\sigma,\tau}-\tilde{Q}^{\sigma,\tau}$. We define likewise $\Delta\tilde{Q}^\frozen$ using increments of $X^\frozen$. Then, 
analogously to \eqref{e:barD.vs.plus},
for all $\sigma , \tau \in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII\}$ we have for $B^\frozen \cap [M] = B \neq \emptyset$
	\beq
	\Delta\tilde{Q}^{\frozen,\sigma,\tau}(q_d,B^\frozen)
	=\frac{|B|}{|B^\frozen|}
	\Delta\tilde{Q}^{\sigma,\tau}(q_d,B)
	\,.\eeq
A similar relation holds between $\Delta\tilde{Q}^{\sigma,\Ising}$ and $\Delta\tilde{Q}^{\frozen,\sigma,\Ising}$, and likewise between
$\Delta\tilde{Q}^{\frozen,\Ising}$
and $\Delta\tilde{Q}^{\Ising}$.

[Proposition 4 (Schedule leakage) of arXiv:2608.26585, 'GRAS: Guided Reduced-Variance Proposals\\ and Adaptive Selection for Training-Free\\ Rewar'] Let $\tilde a_t=1-q^\ell(\textsc{mask})$ be the reveal probability actually induced by the guided proposal.
Then
\begin{equation}

\tilde a_t^{\,\mathrm{post}}=\frac{a_t Z^\ell}{1-a_t+a_t Z^\ell},
\qquad
\tilde a_t^{\,\mathrm{ours}}=a_t .
\end{equation}
Consequently: \emph{(a)} $\tilde a_t^{\,\mathrm{post}}$ is strictly increasing in $Z^\ell$, with
$\tilde a_t^{\,\mathrm{post}}\gtrless a_t$ according as $Z^\ell\gtrless1$; \emph{(b)} under the gauge
$\E_{p_\theta^\ell}[g]=0$, Jensen's inequality gives $Z^\ell\ge1$ with equality iff $g$ is
$p_\theta^\ell$-almost surely constant, so guidance strictly accelerates unmasking, by a state- and
step-dependent amount increasing in $\gamma$; and \emph{(c)} $q^\ell$ of \eqref{eq:inside} is exactly
invariant under $\bm g^\ell\mapsto\bm g^\ell+c\bm 1$, whereas
$\tilde a_t^{\,\mathrm{post}}\to1$ as $c\to+\infty$ and $\to0$ as $c\to-\infty$.

[Definition 1 (XY model) of arXiv:2605.28473, 'The BKT transition and surface tension differentiability'] Consider a finite simple graph $G=(V,E)$ with edge weights
    $J=(J_{uv})_{uv\in E}\subset[0,\infty)$.
    Let $\Omega=\S^V$, where $\S\subset\C$ denotes the unit circle, and endow
    $\Omega$ with the product Haar probability measure $\diff\sigma$.
    The \emph{XY model} on $G$ with \emph{coupling constants} $J$ is the Gibbs measure
    $\langle\blank\rangle_{G,J}$ on $\Omega$ defined by the formula
    \begin{equation}
        
        \langle X\rangle_{G,J}:=\frac1{Z_{G,J}}\int_\Omega X(\sigma)
        e^{\frac12\sum_{uv\in\vec E}J_{uv}\sigma_u\bar\sigma_v} \diff\sigma,
    \end{equation}
    where $\vec E$ is the set of directed edges, and $Z_{G,J}\in(0,\infty)$ is the
    \emph{partition function}.
    Often $J$ is taken to be a constant $\beta\in[0,\infty)$, in which case we write
    $\langle\blank\rangle_{G,\beta}$.
    The parameter $\beta$ is called the \emph{inverse temperature}.

    We are interested in the \emph{mass} (the inverse of the \emph{correlation length})
    of the XY model in 2D.
    Write $\Lambda_n$ for the nearest-neighbour graph on $[-n,n]^2\cap\Z^2$.
    Then the \emph{mass} $\frakm_\XY(\beta)$ is defined via
    \begin{equation}
        
        \frakm_\XY(\beta):=\lim_{k\to\infty}-\frac1k\log\lim_{n\to\infty}\langle\sigma_0\bar\sigma_{k
        e_1}\rangle_{\Lambda_n,\beta}\in[0,\infty].
    \end{equation}

    \begin{equation}
d\mathbf{Y}_t=V(Y_t)~d\mathbf{X}_t+V_0(Y_t)~dt,~~Y_0=y_0\in \mathbb{R}^N.
\end{equation}Here $\mathbf{X}$ is a Gaussian rough path including fBM with Hurst parameter $H\in(1/4,1)$, Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, Brownian bridge as examples (the precise conditions on $\mathbf{X}$ are provided in Section \ref{sec:GRP} below). The vector fields $\mathcal{V}=\{V_i\}_{i=1}^d$ are assumed to satisfy Hypotheses $\ref{h1}$ and $\ref{1.2}$. Let $Y$ be the solution to the the RDE. Then for any $m\geqslant 1$ and $0<t_1<\cdots<t_m\leqslant T$, the distribution of $(Y_{t_1},\cdots,Y_{t_m})$ admits a smooth joint density with respect to the Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}^{mN}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Fitting a stack (or any linear predictor) under the per-sample relative L2 loss, mean over rows of ||y_i - yhat_i||^2 / ||y_i||^2, is weighted least squares with case weights s_i = 1 / ||y_i||^2. By the two-regimes corollary those are Aitken's variance-stabilising weights exactly when the error scale is proportional to the target norm (multiplicative error, elasticity of log ||e_i|| on log ||y_i|| equal to one); then the relative-metric fit is the efficient one and its optimism is 2m/n relative to its own noise level, regardless of how concentrated 1/||y_i||^2 is. If the error carries an additive floor, the rows with the smallest targets - exactly the rows the relative weights concentrate on - have the largest floor relative to their target, the concentration re-enters, and Kish's n_eff of the relative weights measures how far the fit is from balanced. The discriminating measurement is the elasticity of the out-of-fold residual norm to the target norm and the nonnegative fit ||e_i||^2 = a + b ||y_i||^2 (the floor share a / (a + b median ||y||^2)) on the calibration rows; on a pool whose targets vary by orders of magnitude (the EMIT radiance outputs) the question is live, on one whose targets are homogeneous (the OCO-2 retrievals, n_eff within a few percent of n) the two metrics coincide and it is moot.
the per-sample relative L2 loss as used by the EMIT/OCO-2 stacking pools; independent errors across rows
the multiplicative-versus-additive question is empirical and is measured by ens_rmt_elast.py (P21 of the RMT program)
title: Relative-L2 Case Weights Are Aitken's Weights When the Error Norm Scales With the Target Norm

body:
For a finite graph G and a positive integer k let P(G, k) be the number of proper colourings of the vertices of G with k colours (adjacent vertices receive different colours). THEOREM (Birkhoff, Whitney): P(G, k) is a polynomial in k of degree |V|, the chromatic polynomial, determined by the deletion-contraction recurrence P(G, k) = P(G - e, k) - P(G / e, k) for any edge e (G - e deletes the edge, G / e contracts it, merging its endpoints and removing loops and parallel copies), with P(empty graph on n vertices, k) = k^n. Facts: P(K_n, k) = k (k - 1) ... (k - n + 1); P(tree on n vertices, k) = k (k - 1)^{n-1}; P(C_n, k) = (k - 1)^n + (-1)^n (k - 1); P is multiplicative over connected components; its coefficients alternate in sign, the leading coefficient is 1, the coefficient of k^{|V| - 1} is -|E|, and the constant term is 0 for a graph with a vertex; the chromatic number is the least positive integer that is not a root; k = 0, 1, ..., chi(G) - 1 are roots; the chromatic polynomial is a specialisation of the Tutte polynomial, P(G, k) = (-1)^{|V| - c(G)} k^{c(G)} T(G; 1 - k, 0). Computing P is #P-hard in general, and evaluating it at k = 3 is #P-complete; the four colour theorem says P(G, 4) > 0 for every planar G.
finite simple graphs (loops make P identically 0; parallel edges do not change P)
k a nonnegative integer in the counting definition; the polynomial identity then holds for all k

[Thm admissibilitycond of arXiv:2605.07920, 'Primitive Sequences for Probability Measures on Compact Intervals'] A sequence $\{\varepsilon_n\}_n$ is admissible for $[a,b]$ if and only if the normalized sequence $\{\gamma_n\}_n$ given by
    \begin{equation*}
        \gamma_n = \frac{n! \varepsilon_n}{(b-a)^n}, \qquad n \geq 0
    \end{equation*}
    has $\gamma_0 = 1$ and is completely monotone --- that is,
    \[
    (-1)^k (\Delta^k \gamma)_n \geq 0, \qquad n,k \geq 0,
    \]
where the forward difference operator $\Delta$ is defined by $(\Delta \gamma)_n = \gamma_{n+1} - \gamma_n$ and $\Delta^k$ denotes its $k$-fold iterate.
title: Thm admissibilitycond of arXiv:2605.07920

[Definition def:e of arXiv:2412.01381, 'Ergodicity and mixing for locally monotone stochastic evolution equations'] We say that the semigroup $(P_t)_{t\ge 0}$ satisfies the \emph{$e$-property} if for every 
$F\in \operatorname{Lip}_b(H)$, for every $x\in H$, and every $\varepsilon>0$, there exists $\delta>0$ such that 
\[
|P_t F(x)-P_t F(y)|<\varepsilon\quad \textrm{ for all }\quad y\in B(x,\delta)\quad \textrm{ and }\quad t\geq 0,
\]
where 
$\operatorname{Lip}_b(H):=\{F:H\to \mathbb{R}:\,F\textrm{ is Lipschitz and bounded}\}$.
title: $e$-property

[Definition 41 (Pathwise uniqueness) of arXiv:2506.09637, 'Nonlinear Stochastic Filtering with Volterra Gaussian Noises'] We say that pathwise uniqueness holds for equation \eqref{sensor_equation} if
the following property is satisfied. Let
\[
    (Z,\mathbf I),\quad
    (\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{t\in[0,T]},\mathbb P)
\]
and
\[
    (\widetilde Z,\mathbf I),\quad
    (\Omega,\mathcal F,(\widetilde{\mathcal F}_t)_{t\in[0,T]},\mathbb P)
\]
be two weak solutions of \eqref{sensor_equation} on the same probability space,
driven by the same enhanced Volterra Gaussian process \(\mathbf I\), and with
the same initial condition \(z_0\). Then
\[
    Z^{(0)}_t=\widetilde Z^{(0)}_t
    \qquad
    \text{for all }t\in[0,T],
    \quad \mathbb P\text{-a.s.}
\]
Equivalently, the solution paths \(Z^{(0)}\) and \(\widetilde Z^{(0)}\) are
indistinguishable.
title: Pathwise uniqueness

[Definition trafod of arXiv:2604.08505, '\LARGE{On $d$-stochastic measures with fractal support and uniform $(d-1)$-marginals, and '] Suppose that $d\geq 2$, that $\mathbf{m} \in \mathbb{N}^d$ fulfills $\min_{j} m_j \geq 2$, and let 
$\mathcal{I}_d^\mathbf{m}$ be defined according to eq. ((ID of the paper)). 
A probability distribution $\tau$ on $(\mathcal{I}_d^\mathbf{m}, 2^{\mathcal{I}_d^\mathbf{m}})$ 
is called 
\emph{generalized transformation matrix} if for every $j \in \{1,\ldots,d\}$ 
and every $k \in \{1,\ldots,m_j\}$
$$
\tau\left(I_1 \times I_2 \times \ldots \times I_{j-1} \times \{k\} \times I_{j+1} \times 
\ldots \times  I_d \right)=\sum_{\mathbf{i}\in \mathcal{I}_d^\mathbf{m}: \,\,i_j=k}\tau(\mathbf{i}) >0
$$
holds. $\mathcal{S}_{\tau} \subseteq \mathcal{I}_d^\mathbf{m}$ will denote the support of $\tau$, i.e., 
$$
\mathcal{S}_{\tau}:=\{\mathbf{i}\in \mathcal{I}_d^\mathbf{m}: \, \tau(\mathbf{i})>0\}.
$$
Moreover, $\mathcal{T}_d^\mathbf{m}$ will denote the family of all $d$-dimensional 
generalized transformation matrices on $\mathcal{I}_d^\mathbf{m}$.
title: Extended version of \cite{TFS}

body: [Abstract of arXiv:2609.02398, '\textbf{Convex Order Comparisons for Sub-Gamma Random Variables}'] Recent work has shown that sub-Gaussian random variables are dominated in convex order by a sharp multiple of a Gaussian. We study the analogous question for the sub-Gamma class underlying Bernstein's inequality, with the Laplace law as the majorant. Here the moment generating function is controlled by a Bernstein-type bound over a finite range of frequencies, rather than by a purely quadratic bound. We derive a variational formula for the optimal multiple, show that it is strictly larger than the natural scale $σ\vee α$, and prove that this value is sharp, being attained by an asymmetric two-point distribution. We then turn to the sub-exponential class, which has a quadratic bound as in the sub-Gaussian case, but only over a bounded range as in the sub-Gamma case. Interestingly, the sub-exponential class displays a different behavior: the optimal multiple is exactly $σ\vee α$, but is attained only when $α\leq σ$; when $α> σ$, the constant remains sharp, but equality cannot hold for any non-affine convex function. Both results rely on a sharp finite-range variant of the Kearns-Saul inequality, which is of independent interest. (abstract text taken from the arXiv listing metadata; the TeX carried no abstract environment)
title: Abstract of arXiv:2609.02398: \textbf{Convex Order Comparisons for Sub-Gamma Random Variables}

	g_n(j, x, t)\lesssim
	\frac{e^{-\frac{3}{8} h^{2}_n(j, x, t)}}{h_n(j, x, t)}+(nk_n)^{-1/2}h_n^{-3}(j, x, t)+n^{-4/5}. 
	\endaligned $$
	\item If $0<t\leq \alpha_n^{-\frac{9}{20}}$ and $1\leq j\leq j_n,$ then 
	\begin{equation}
		\aligned 
	\frac{1+O(h_n^{-2}(j, x,t))}{\sqrt{2\pi}h_n(j, x,t)}e^{-\frac{h^{2}_n(j, x,t)}{2}}\leq	g_n(j,x,t)
		\leq \frac{1+O(h_n^{-2}(j, x,t))}{\sqrt{2\pi}h_n(j, x,t)}e^{-\frac{h^{2}_n(j, x,t)}{2}}+n^{-4/5}. 
		\endaligned 
	\end{equation}
	\item If $0<t\leq \alpha_n^{-\frac{9}{20}}$ and $j_n< j\leq t_n,$ then
	$$g_n(j,x,t)
	\lesssim \frac{1}{h_n(j, x, t)}e^{-\frac{3h^{2}_n(j, x,t)}{8}}+n^{-4/5}.  $$
	\item	In particular, when $j=t_n$, we have $$g_n(j,x,t)\leq 	\exp\big\{-\frac{(j-1)^2}{4\alpha_n}-\frac{(j-1)(\widetilde{a}_n+\widetilde{b}_n x)}{2\sqrt{\alpha_n}} -\frac{(j-1)t}{4}\big\}, \quad \text{for} \quad t\geq 0.$$
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let $Q=[q_{i_1i_2 \ldots i_{m-1}, j_1 j_2 \ldots j_{m-1}}]$ be the transition matrix of its reduced first order chain. Denote
$Q^k=[q^{(k)}_{i_1i_2 \ldots i_{m-1}, j_1 j_2 \ldots j_{m-1}}]$
 Let 
$$

$$  
Then for any eigenvalue of $Q$ other than $\rho(Q)=1$, we have
\be

|\lambda| \le \left ( \frac{\alpha-\beta}{\alpha+\beta} \right )^{\frac{1}{m-1}}.
\ee (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma fixed type deviation bound of arXiv:2411.02898, '\vspace{-1.5cm}The connectivity and phase transition in inhomogeneous random graphs of fin'] Let $Z = X_1 + \dots X_K$, where $X_i$'s are independent random variables with
\[
X_i = \bm{u} \longbm{\Bin{a_1 n (1-\delta)}{p_{k(i)1}}}{\vdots}{\Bin{a_m n (1-\delta )}{p_{k(i)m}}}
\]
where all the binomial random variables appearing above are independent, and $k(i) \in \{ 1, \dots , m\}$ is a fixed number for each $i = 1, \dots , K$. Define \( \gamma (x) = x \log x - x +1 \). We have for $0<x<1$, 
\[
\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(Z \leq x \ensuremath{\mathbb{E}} Z) \leq \exp(-\gamma(x) (1-\delta) \mu u K).
\]
In particular,
\[
\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(Z \leq x(1-\delta)\mu u K) \leq \exp(-\gamma(x) (1-\delta) \mu u K).
\]

body:
Little Picard theorem: if f is entire and nonconstant, then the complement of its image, C minus f(C), contains at most one point; i.e. a nonconstant entire function omits at most one complex value. Great Picard theorem: if f is holomorphic on a punctured disk 0 < |z - a| < r and has an essential singularity at a, then for every ε in (0,r) the image of the punctured disk 0 < |z - a| < ε is all of C with at most one point removed, and every value so attained (again with at most one exception) is attained infinitely often. Both exceptional values are genuinely possible and the count is sharp: exp(z) is entire and omits exactly the value 0, and exp(1/z) has an essential singularity at 0 and omits exactly 0 near 0. Meromorphic versions: a nonconstant meromorphic function on C omits at most two values of the Riemann sphere, and near an essential singularity a meromorphic function takes every spherical value with at most two exceptions.
Little: f entire and nonconstant
Great: f holomorphic on a punctured disk about a with an isolated essential singularity at a

body:
[Prop p:noncolliding of arXiv:2411.10586, 'A convergence framework for Airy$_\beta$ line ensemble\\ via pole evolution'] For any $C>0$ the following is true.
Take any particle-generated $\{Y_t\}_{t\in{\mathbb R}}$ satisfying (a:SDE of the paper), and that its poles are given by a line ensemble $\{x_i(t)\}_{i\in\mathbb{N}, t\in{\mathbb R}}$.
Fix a large $k\in \mathbb{N}$, and denote the stopping time 
\[
    \tau=\inf\{t\geq 0: x_k(t)-x_{k+1}(t)\leq 1/(Ck^{1/3})\}\wedge 1.
\]
We consider the line ensemble $\{x_i(t)\}_{i\in\mathbb{N}, t\in{\mathbb R}}$ conditional on $x_k(0)-x_{k+1}(0)>1/(Ck^{1/3})$ (i.e., $\tau>0$).
For this conditional process,
there exist independent Brownian motions $B_1, \cdots, B_k$ adapted to the filtration ${\mathcal F}_t=\sigma(\{{\bm{x}}(u)\}_{u\leq t})$, satisfying (again in the sense of the differential form of the semimartingale decomposition)
        \begin{equation}
{\rm d} x_i(t)=\sqrt{\frac{2}{\beta}}{\rm d} B_i(t) +\sum_{1\leq j\leq k\atop j\neq i}
\frac{{\rm d} t}{x_i(t)-x_j(t)} + W_t(x_i(t)){\rm d} t,\quad \forall i\in\llbracket 1, k\rrbracket, \; t\in [0, \tau],
\end{equation}
where $W_t$ is a random meromorphic function, defined as
\begin{align}
W_t(w):=-Y_t(w)+\sum_{i=1}^k \frac{1}{x_i(t)-w}.
\end{align}
Moreover, almost surely the following holds: 
\begin{align}
    \int_0^\tau\mathds{1}(\exists 1\leq i<j\leq k: x_i(t)=x_j(t)) {\rm d} t=0.
\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Then, for every \(n\geq1\) and \(\xi\in\Lambda_n(K,\varepsilon)\), one has
\[

&=
\left[
\widehat{\mu_\gamma}(\xi)
-
\sum_{|u|=n+h}
\mu(I_u)\mathrm{e}^{i\phi_\xi(t_u)}

+
\sum_{|u|=n+h}
A_u

\mathrm{e}^{i\phi_\xi(t_u)}

\left[
\sum_{|u|=n+h}
A_u\mathrm{e}^{i\phi_\xi(t_u)}

\mathrm{e}^{i\phi_\xi(t)}
\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{n+h}(t)
\right]
+
E_{\xi,n,h,j}^{\mathrm{safe}}
+
D_{\xi,n,j}^{(0)}
+
S_{\xi,j,n,h}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Moreover, almost surely on

\[
\limsup_{n\to\infty}
\sup_{\xi\in\Lambda_n(K,\varepsilon)}
\left|

\right|
\leq
C_\gamma(K+K_1)2^{-h}
+
C_\gamma
\Delta_{C_\gamma2^{-j}}(\mu).
\]

[Definition def:advancing-state of arXiv:2602.21315, 'The Instability of all Backoff Protocols\thanks{For the purpose of Open Access, the author'] Fix $\lambda \in (0,1)$ and a send sequence $\overline{p}$ with $p_0=1$. Let $j$ be a positive integer.
We say a high-level state $\Psi$ is \emph{$j$-advancing} if 
bin~$j$ is covered and the following properties hold. 
\begin{itemize}
\item $\textup{type}^{\Psi} = \textup{advancing}$. 
\item $j^{\Psi} = j$.
\item $z_{j}^{\Psi} = 0$. 
\item For all $k \in [j-1]$, $z_k^{\Psi} = \mu_k^{\overline{\gamma}}$.
\item If bin~$j$ is many-covered then
$\mathcal{S}^{\Psi}= \{\Upsilon_{j, \geq \widetilde{W}[j]}\}$.
If bin~$j$ is heavy-covered then 
$\mathcal{S}^{\Psi} = \{\Upsilon_{j,\geq j^2}\}$.
\end{itemize}

[Definition 5 of arXiv:2605.05864, 'Classification and Metrization of Classes of Smooth measures'] \begin{enumerate}
\item A smooth measure \(\mu\) is {\it a Kato class measure} if it satisfies \( \lim_{\alpha \to \infty}\|U_\alpha \mu\|_{\infty, q} =0.\) Denote by \(\mathcal{K}\) the set of all Kato class measures.
\item  A smooth measure \(\mu\) is {\it a Dynkin class measure} if it satisfies \(\|U_1 \mu\|_{\infty, q} < \infty \). Denote by \(\mathcal{D}\) the set of all Dynkin class measures.
\item A Kato class measure \(\mu\) is {\it a Green-tight measure} for \(R_1\) if, for any \(\varepsilon >0\), there exists a compact set \(K\) such that \(\|R_1(1_{K^c}\mu)\|_\infty \leq \varepsilon\). Denote by \(\mathcal{K}_\infty= \mathcal{K}_\infty(R_1)\) the set of all Green-tight measures.

\item A Radon measure \(\mu\) has {\it finite energy integrals} if there exists \(C>0\) such that, for any \(f \in \mathcal{F}\cap C_c\), \(\int |f|d\mu \leq C\sqrt{\mathcal{E}_1(f,f)}\). Denote by \(\mathcal{S}_0\) the set of all Radon measures of finite energy integrals.

\item When $(\form,\dom)$ is transient, a Radon measure \(\mu\) has {\it \(0\)-order finite energy integrals} if there exists \(C>0\) such that, for any \(f \in \mathcal{F}\cap C_c\), \(\int |f|d\mu \leq C\sqrt{\mathcal{E}(f,f)}\). Denote by \(\mathcal{S}_0^{(0)}\) the set of all Radon measures of finite \(0\)-order energy integrals.
\end{enumerate}

\end{equation}

[Thm 1.2 of arXiv:2606.16237, 'The Backward Stochastic Partial Differential Integral Equations: Solvability and Compariso'] Assume that Assumption (ass:1.1 of the paper) holds. Then BSEE (equation eq:a2 of the paper) has a unique solution.
Moreover, let $(A, f, g, \varphi)$ and $(A, \bar f, \bar g, \bar{\varphi})$ be two sets of coefficients satisfying Assumption (ass:1.1 of the paper), and $(u, q, r)$ and $(\bar u, \bar q, \bar r)$ be the solutions of BSEE (equation eq:a2 of the paper) with coefficients $(A, f, g, \varphi)$ and $(A, \bar f, \bar g, \bar \varphi)$, respectively, then we have the following estimate
\begin{eqnarray}
&& E \sup_{0 \leq t \leq T} \| u(t) - \bar{u}(t) \|_H^2 + E \int_0^T \| u(t) - \bar{u}(t) \|_V^2 \, dt \nonumber \\
&& + E \int_0^T \| q(t) - \bar{q}(t) \|_H^2 \, dt + E \int_0^T \int_Z \| r(t, e) - \bar{r}(t, e) \|_H^2 \nu(de) \, dt \nonumber \\
&\leq& C \left[ E \| \varphi - \bar{\varphi} \|_H^2 + E \int_0^T \| f(t, \bar{u}(t), \bar{q}(t), \bar{r}(t, \cdot)) - \bar{f}(t, \bar{u}(t), \bar{q}(t), \bar{r}(t, \cdot)) \|_{V^*}^2 \, dt \right. \nonumber \\
&& \left. + E \int_0^T \| g(t, \bar{u}(t), \bar{q}(t), \bar{r}(t, \cdot)) - \bar{g}(t, \bar{u}(t), \bar{q}(t), \bar{r}(t, \cdot)) \|_H^2 \, dt \right].
\end{eqnarray}
Here and in the rest of this paper $C$ is a generic constant depending only on given parameters, and we may indicate the parameters it depends on by a bracket. For example, the above $C= C(l, \lambda, \alpha, \kappa, M, T)$ is a constant depending on the parameters $l, \lambda, \alpha, \kappa, M, T$.

In particular, when $(A, \bar f, \bar g, \bar \varphi) = (A, 0, 0, 0)$, it follows from ((eq:130 of the paper)) that
\begin{eqnarray}
&& E \sup_{0 \leq t \leq T} \| u(t) \|_H^2 + E \int_0^T \| u(t) \|_V^2 \, dt + E \int_0^T \| q(t) \|_H^2 \, dt + E \int_0^T \int_Z \| r(t, e) \|_H^2 \nu(de) \, dt \nonumber \\
&\leq& C\left[ E \| \varphi \|_H^2 + E \int_0^T \| f(t, 0, 0, 0) \|_{V^*}^2 \, dt + E \int_0^T \| g(t, 0, 0, 0) \|_H^2 \, dt \right].
\end{eqnarray} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 1 of arXiv:2608.03338, 'Embedding of sub-stochastic matrices'] Consider\/ $M\in\cM_{d,\leqslant}$ and let\/ $p$ and\/ $q$ be the
  characteristic and the minimal polynomial of\/ $M$,
  respectively. If\/ $p^{}_{\mathsf{c}}$ and\/ $q^{}_{\mathsf{c}}$ are
  the corresponding polynomials of the unique extension of\/ $M$ to\/
  $M_{\mathsf{c}}\in\cM_{d+1}$, one has\/
  $p^{}_{\mathsf{c}} (\lambda) = (1-\lambda) \ts p(\lambda)$ together
  with
\[
  q^{}_{\mathsf{c}} (\lambda) \, = \,
       \lcm ( q(\lambda), 1-\lambda)
       \, = \, \begin{cases}
       q(\lambda) \ts , &  \text{if\/ $1 \in \sigma (M)$}  , \\
       (1-\lambda) \ts q(\lambda) \ts , & \text{otherwise} \ts .
       \end{cases}
\]
Likewise, the corresponding polynomials for\/ $Q$ and\/
$Q_{\mathsf{c}}$ from \eqref{eq:extend} satisfy\/
$p^{}_{\mathsf{c}} (\lambda) = -\lambda \, p(\lambda)$ and\/
$q^{}_{\mathsf{c}} (\lambda) = \lcm ( q(\lambda), -\lambda )$.

[Theorem 4 (Conditional cylindrical universal approximation) of arXiv:2608.08040, 'A cylindrical neural approximation theorem for conditional laws of McKean–Vlasov equations'] Fix $t\in(0,T]$ and let $m\geq2$ be as in Proposition~1. Let $\nu$ be a
probability measure on $\mathcal P_m(\mathbb R^d)$, and let
\[
V:\mathbb R^d\times\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)\longrightarrow\mathbb R^p
\]
be continuous and satisfy the mean square integrability condition of
Section~2.3. For
\[
\mu_t(\mathbf w):=\overline\Phi_t(\mu_0,r_t\mathbf w),
\]
where $\overline\Phi_t$ is the restricted conditional law map of
Proposition~1, the following holds. For every $\varepsilon>0$, there exist
$L,M\in\mathbb N^*$, a conditional network $\widehat N$, a latent dimension
$k$, bounded Lipschitz inner functions $\varphi$, and an outer network $\Psi$
such that
\[
\int_{\mathcal P_m(\mathbb R^d)}
\int_{C_g^{0,\alpha}([0,T];\mathbb R^{q+1})}
\int_{\mathbb{R}^d}
\Bigl|V(x,\mu_t(\mathbf w))
-\Psi\bigl(x,\langle\varphi,
\widehat N(g_M(\mu_0,r_t\mathbf w))\rangle\bigr)\Bigr|^2
\,\mu_t(\mathbf w)(dx)\,\mathbf P^0(d\mathbf w)\,\nu(d\mu_0)
\leq\varepsilon,
\]
where
\[
g_M(\mu_0,r_t\mathbf w)
=\bigl(E_L(\mu_0),S_M(r_t\mathbf w)\bigr)\in\mathbb R^N,
\qquad N=L+d_{\mathrm{sig}}(M,q).
\]

[Lem 29 of arXiv:2608.13727, 'Hitting-time mixing for the star transposition shuffle'] Suppose that
    $
        |c_n^\star(s)|\le \frac12\log\log n-4\log\log\log n.$
    Let \(\mathrm{Fix}_{\star}(\sigma)\) denote the set of fixed points of \(\sigma\) excluding \(1\). For any permutation \(\sigma_n\in\mathfrak S_n\) and any integer \(1\le M_n\le n\) satisfying \(M_n=n^{o(1)}\), \([M_n]_{\star}\subseteq\mathrm{Fix}_{\star}(\sigma_n)\), and
    \[
        |\mathrm{Fix}_{\star}(\sigma_n)\setminus[M_n]_\star|\le K_n,
    \]
    we have
    \[\sum_{[M_n]_\star \subseteq T \subseteq \mathrm{Fix}_{\star}(\sigma_n)} (-1)^{|T|-M_n+1} \, \mathbb{P}(\mathcal{G}(T)) \, \nu^{\star, T}(\sigma_n) 
    = \left(1 + O(n^{-1/2+o(1)})\right) \frac{\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{F}(M_n))}{(n-M_n+1)!}.\]

Asymptotics of Schr\"odinger potentials

[Defi gs12 of arXiv:2507.20324, 'Non-existence of several random fractals in Brownian motion and Brownian loop soup'] Fix $\delta>0$. Let $N(\delta)$ be the smallest integer $n$ such that $2^{-n}<\delta/16$. For $n\geq N(\delta)$, let $\mathfrak{S}_{n}=\mathfrak{S}_{n}(\delta)$ stand for the collection of $\delta$-good boxes, i.e., the set of all $S\in\mathcal{S}_{n}$ with the following properties:
\par
(1) $S$ is visited twice by $W_{t}$ and the trajectories between successive visits reach distance at least $(\delta-2^{-n-1/2})$ to the centre of $S$. More precisely,
\[\mathcal{T}(S):=\tau(S,\partial\mathcal{B}(S,\delta-2^{-n-1/2}),S)<\tau_{\mathbb{D}}.\]
We use $V_{\delta}^{\mathrm{PDCP}}(S)$ to denote this event.
\par
(2) $W[0,\tau(\mathcal{D}_{-n}(S))]$ and $W[\tau(S,\mathcal{C}_{-n}(S)),\mathcal{T}(S)]$ do not intersect.
\par
For $d=2$, we additionally require that:
\par
(3) There exist two different connected components of $\mathcal{B}(S,\delta-2^{-n-1/2})\setminus W[0,\mathcal{T}(S)]$ such that both of them intersect $\mathcal{D}_{-n}(S)$ and are connected to infinity.
title: Defi gs12 of arXiv:2507.20324

body:
[Definition defin:gammadef of arXiv:2604.08462, 'Convergence of $k$-point functions in\\ high dimensional percolation'] We introduce the notation $\Gamma(a_1, \dots, a_k)$ for the event $\{a_1 \leftrightarrow a_2 \leftrightarrow \dots \leftrightarrow a_k\}$ that $a_1, \dots, a_k$ are in the same open cluster. We use the notation $\tau_k(a_1, \dots, a_k)$ for the $k$-point functions:
\[\tau_k(a_1, \dots, a_k) = \mathbb{P}(\Gamma(a_1, \dots, a_k))\ . \]
We occasionally overload notation, writing in case $A = \{x_1, \dots, x_k\}$
\[\Gamma(A) = \Gamma(x_1, \dots, x_k), \]
or
\[\Gamma(z, A) = \Gamma(z, x_1, \dots, x_k)\ ,\]
with similar extensions for e.g.~$\tau_k(A)$.

The open cluster $\mathfrak{C}(x)$ is the connected component of $x$ in the random open subgraph of $\mathbb{Z}^d$. In other words, $\mathfrak{C}(x) = \{y: \, \Gamma(x,y) \text{ occurs}\}$. We also introduce the notion of ``restricted'' connections and clusters. If $A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^d$, we write $\{x \ensuremath{\,{\buildrel A \over \longleftrightarrow}\,} y\}$ for the event that $x$ and $y$ are connected by an open path lying entirely in $A$. We write $\mathfrak{C}_A(x) = \{y: \, x \ensuremath{\,{\buildrel A \over \longleftrightarrow}\,} y\}$ for the connected component of $x$ in the open subgraph of $A$.

We write $x \Longleftrightarrow y$ for the event that there are two edge-disjoint open connections from $x$ to $y$, and we write $x \stackrel{A}{\Longleftrightarrow} y$ for the event that there are two edge-disjoint connections from $x$ to $y$ lying entirely in the set $A$.
title: Definition defin:gammadef of arXiv:2604.08462

[Lemm l:moment-of-chaos-Bc of arXiv:2607.18194, 'Temperature chaos in directed polymers'] As above, let $B_\varepsilon \coloneqq  [s',t']\times [a-\varepsilon,b+\varepsilon]$.
    Fix $t_1<t_2$ such that $[t_1,t_2]\subset [s',t']$.
    Then for all $x_1,x_2, y_1,y_2\in[a,b]$ and all $n\in {\mathbb{Z}_{\geqslant0}}$,
    \begin{multline*}
        \mathbb{E}\left[
            I_n\left(
                (1-\1_{B_\varepsilon}^{\otimes n})
                \, p^{(n)}_{(t_1,x_1),(t_2,x_2)}
            \right)
            I_n\left(
                (1-\1_{B_\varepsilon}^{\otimes n})
                \,p^{(n)}_{(t_1,y_1),(t_2,y_2)}
            \right)
        \right]\\
        \leqslant
        C\exp\left(
            -\frac{c\varepsilon^2}{t_2-t_1}
        \right)
        \mathbb{E}\left[
            I_n\left(
                p^{(n)}_{(t_1,x_1),(t_2,x_2)}
            \right)
            I_n\left(
                p^{(n)}_{(t_1,y_1),(t_2,y_2)}
            \right)
        \right],
    \end{multline*}
    where $C,c>0$ are universal constants. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemm l:moment-of-chaos-Bc of arXiv:2607.18194

[Proposition 46 (One-step tilted spine law and its Beta limit) of arXiv:2604.25877, 'Asymptotic height of Plancherel random trees'] Denote by $\mu_{k,t}$ the conditional law of $P_{\ell+1}$ under the spine measure
$\Q_t$. 
\begin{enumerate}
    \item We have
$$
\mu_{k,t}\!\left(\left\{\frac{j}{m}\right\}\right)
=
\frac{\theta}{\beta_{m,t}(\theta)}\,
\frac{j^{t-1}}{m^t}\,
\frac{\Gamma(m+1)\,\Gamma(m-j+\theta)}
{\Gamma(m-j+1)\,\Gamma(m+\theta)},
$$
\item As $k$ goes to infinity, $\mu_{k,t}$ converges in distribution to a
    $\mathrm{Beta}(t,\theta)$ distribution with density 
    $$f_t(x) =
    \frac{\Gamma(t+\theta)}{\Gamma(t)\,\Gamma(\theta)}\,x^{t-1}\,(1-x)^{\theta-1}\,\mathbf
    1_{(0,1)}(x).$$
\item Consequently, if $ P\sim \mathrm{Beta}(t,\theta)$ and $X_{\ell+1} = -\log
    P_{\ell+1}$, then $X_{\ell+1}$ converges in distribution to $-\log P$.
 \end{enumerate}

[Theorem thm:lower of arXiv:2606.16259, 'Super-Arrhenius relaxation of the triangular plaquette model in any dimension'] Denote the origin of $\mathbb Z^d$ by $O$.
Consider $k\in\mathbb N$, and set $B_k = B(O,3d\,2^{k})$.
Let $(W_0,\dots,W_n)$ be a chain such that $W_0=\{O\}$ and $W_n\cap B_k=\varnothing$.
Then for some index $i$ we have
\[
|W_i\cap B_k| > k.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: {Combinatorial bottleneck}

body: In non-adaptive graph limits, particles are stratified into static fibers indexed by fixed labels $\xi \in \Omega$, with macroscopic state described by $f(t, x, \xi)$. Datong Zhou demonstrates that under adaptive weight evolution, state-dependent plasticity causes particles within the same initial fiber to diverge dynamically. As interaction profiles evolve stochastically, the fiber structure splits, necessitating the structural limit via Aldous-Hoover arrays rather than static fiberwise PDEs.
title: Breakdown of Fiberwise Vlasov Descriptions under Adaptive Plasticity

[Corollary cor:synchronization of arXiv:2608.21931, 'Interacting Urn Schemes on Finite Ancestral Directed Acyclic Graphs'] Consider the sum-reinforcement scheme and suppose that $\overrightarrow{\mathbb{G}}$ has a unique generator
vertex $g$ and no stubborn vertices, that is, $G\cup S=G=\{g\}$. Assume that all
reinforcement matrices are of P\'olya type, that is, $R^{\overrightarrow{e}}=I_k$ for all $\overrightarrow{e}\in\overrightarrow{E}$,
and that the initial configurations are non-random with
$\N{0}{g}=(n_1,n_2,\ldots,n_k)$, where $n_i>0$ for all $i$. Then, for every
$v\in V$,
\[
\U{n}{v}\xrightarrow[]{a.s.}\U{\infty}{g},
\]
where $\U{\infty}{g}$ has a Dirichlet distribution with parameter
$(n_1,n_2,\ldots,n_k)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: \textbf{Synchronization to a random limit}

body: [Theorem 8.1 of arXiv:2503.23159, 'Hall's marriage theorem'] Let (Ti : i ∈I) be a family of finite subsets of an infinite set S. Then the family has a system of distinct representatives if and only if, for every natural number k, any k of the sets contain at least k elements between them.

[Lemma 10 of arXiv:2609.04095, '2609.04095'] Let \(d\ge1\), let \(\omega_0,\ldots,\omega_d>0\), and let
\(\lambda_0,\ldots,\lambda_d\ge0\) be log-concave with interval support
\(\{0,1,\ldots,e\}\), where \(1\le e\le d\).  Put
\[
 \pi_j:=\omega_j\lambda_j,
 \qquad
 M(t):=
 \frac{\sum_{j=0}^d j\omega_jt^j}
      {\sum_{j=0}^d\omega_jt^j}
 \quad(t>0),
\]
\[
 \bar\jmath:=
 \frac{\sum_{j=0}^d j\pi_j}
      {\sum_{j=0}^d\pi_j}.
\]
Then:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
\item \(M\) is strictly increasing on \((0,\infty)\), and there is a
      unique \(t>0\) such that \(M(t)=\bar\jmath\).
\item For this \(t\), choose \(\kappa>0\) such that
      \[
       \widetilde\pi_j:=\kappa\omega_jt^j,
       \qquad
       \sum_j\widetilde\pi_j=\sum_j\pi_j,
      \]
      and put \(\Delta_j:=\pi_j-\widetilde\pi_j\).  Then
      \[
       \sum_j\Delta_j=\sum_jj\Delta_j=0,
      \]
      and \(\{j:\Delta_j>0\}\) is an interval.
\item \(\pi_0\le\widetilde\pi_0\).
\item
      \[
       \sum_jj^2\Delta_j\le0,
       \qquad
       \sum_j\frac{\Delta_j}{j+1}\le0.
      \]
\item If \(\rho>0\) and
      \(\lambda_{j+1}\le\rho\lambda_j\) for \(0\le j<d\), then
      \(t\le\rho\).
\end{enumerate}

[Theorem 134 (Raw covariance-response first-jet selection) of arXiv:2608.04993, '2608.04993'] Assume an admissible testing core in the sense of
\Cref{def:admissible-backward-testing-core}.  Then the backward
value--martingale response program selects the stable first-jet state
$\mathscr W_{Q,\cP}^{1,2}$ with the following properties.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2.5em]
\item Every energy-bounded covariance cross-response generates a unique
fiber-valued local jet $D_Q^{\rm pw}Y_t\in\mathscr E_{\mathfrak a_t}$ by Riesz
representation, with the regularized covariance-pseudoinverse formula
\eqref{eq:backward-pseudoinverse-factorization}.  The common-completion
condition \textup{(A2)} makes its active section a class in
$\mathbb H_{\cP}^2$, and under every law that class is the covariance-energy
class of the classical GKW coefficient.
\item The terminal martingale response calibrates the
$\mathbb H_{\cP}^2$ jet norm isometrically at every stopping horizon, while
the complete path response $(Y,I(Z))$ reconstructs the graph completion up to
stable-causal bi-Lipschitz equivalence.
\item No proper noninjective stable-causal quotient is lossless for
the complete first-jet response.
\item The completed first-jet state is a closed linear relation.  It is the
graph of a single-valued closed response operator exactly when its vertical
space vanishes.  Genuine compression to the inherited value-process topology
then occurs exactly when the value domain is closed; otherwise the recovery
operator is unbounded and the graph topology retains the jet.
\end{enumerate}
The derivative leg uses the covariance channel rather than skew area, while
the zero-order environmental state may still retain area.  Orthogonal
martingale components remain visible in the value trajectory but outside the
covariance jet.  Solver identification is governed separately by
\Cref{def:backward-compatible-interface}.

body: Let f be continuous on the closed interval [a,b]. Part 1: the function F(x) = integral from a to x of f(t) dt is differentiable on [a,b] and F'(x) = f(x) for every x in [a,b]. Part 2 (evaluation): if G is any antiderivative of f on [a,b], meaning G'(x) = f(x) for all x in [a,b], then the integral from a to b of f(x) dx equals G(b) - G(a). Together the two parts show differentiation and (Riemann) integration are inverse processes: every continuous function has an antiderivative, and definite integrals are computed from any one of them.

[Proposition prop:WishartGram of arXiv:2608.04162, 'Correlation Matrices in High Dimensions:\ The Elliptope as a Sample-Correlation Ensemble'] (i) Let $
u>n-1$ be real, let $W$ have the Wishart distribution $W_n(
u,I_n)$, and let $C=D^{-1}WD^{-1}$ where $D=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_n)$ with $\sigma_i^2=W_{ii}$. Then $C$ has density proportional to $\det(C)^{(
u-n-1)/2}$ on $\mathcal{E}_n$; equivalently, $C\sim\operatorname{LKJ}(\eta)$ with $
u=n+2\eta-1$, for every $\eta>0$.
ewline
(ii) For integer $
u=k\geq n$, $C$ is distributed as the Gram matrix $C=V^\prime V$, $V=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)$, of $n$ independent vectors $v_i$ that are uniformly distributed on the unit sphere in $\mathbb{R}^k$. In particular, $C$ is uniformly distributed on $\mathcal{E}_n$ if and only if $k=n+1$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Check whether the ergodic-environment argument for the two-sided statement (Theorem 2.3/3.2) localises to one side. Result: The two-sided 0-1 law (range infinite or not) follows from stationarity of the environment plus a Borel-Cantelli over the sites visited; the one-sided event {sup X_n = infinity} is not invariant under the natural shifts because the walk started at 0 and the environment to the left matter. Under (SE) and (EL) the source notes (3.4) and (3.5) are equivalent, so the question is the 0-1 property itself. A sufficient condition beyond Theorem 3.10: if the environment is i.i.d. and the walk is 'monotone' in the environment (Proposition 4.2 style coupling, which needs (POS1) or its mirror), then P_0(sup X_n = infinity) is a monotone function of a product measure, and the event {sup X_n = infinity} is a tail event with respect to the environment on the right half-line only if the walk's right excursions are determined by the right environment, which fails because the walk can be pushed back by the left environment. I tried the following route: under (SE) and (WEL), the event {sup X_n = infinity} is invariant under the environment shift restricted to trajectories that reach every site to the right, so conditionally on reaching site k the probability of eventually reaching k+1 is the same functional of the shifted environment; if the walk reaches every site to the right a.s. on the event, an ergodicity argument along the sequence of first-hitting times gives 0-1. The gap is exactly that 'reaching k' depends on the environment left of k through the returns. No general 0-1 law obtained; the reduction to a renewal-type ergodicity along right-hitting times is recorded. Obstruction: Left environment influences right excursions; no shift invariance of the one-sided event.

body:
[Lemma 8 (MMSE area upper bound by rate distortion) of arXiv:2605.30321, 'A Bayesian Proof and Interpretation \\ of Talagrand's Majorizing Measure Theorem'] Let \(T\) be finite, let \(X\sim\pi\), and observe
\[
    Y_s=sX+Z,\qquad Z\sim N(0,I_N).
\]
Let
\[
    \mathcal A_\pi
    :=
    \int_0^\infty \mathrm{MMSE}_\pI_{\pi}(s)\,ds
\]
and
\[
    \mathcal R_\pi
    :=
    \int_0^{\operatorname{diam}(T)}
    \sqrt{R_\pi(r)}\,dr,
\]
where
\[
R_\pi(r)
=
\inf\left\{
I(X;X'):\ X\sim\pi,\ X'\sim\pi,\ 
\mathbb E d(X,X')^2\le r^2
\right\}.
\]
Then there is a universal constant \(C<\infty\) such that
\[
    \mathcal A_\pi\le C\mathcal R_\pi.
\]
For instance, one may take \(C=2\sqrt 2\).

body:
[Corollary cor:known-learned-gap of arXiv:2608.20295, 'Physical-Support Confidence Sets for Highly Coherent Dictionaries'] Consider a sequence of problems for which
\[
    I_G^{(r)}\rightarrow\infty,
    \qquad
    I_S\rightarrow\infty,
\]
while $I_D=Ns^6$ remains bounded. If the dictionary were known, the
deployment experiment would eventually separate the competing atom supports.
When the dictionary is learned from finite calibration data, however, every
uniformly valid physical-support confidence correspondence has worst-case
expected diameter at least $cs$. Hence a support decision that is precise
conditional on one fitted dictionary can be strictly more precise than the
physical conclusion justified after dictionary uncertainty is taken into
account. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 56 (Endpoint local dimension on a fixed arc) of arXiv:2606.11758, '2606.11758'] Let \(W\) be in the minimal Kahane--Peyri\`ere regime, and let
\(\widetilde\mu\) be the dyadic scalar cascade on \([0,1]\) generated by \(W\).

\)

\(

\)

\(
    S_\gamma=\{\widetilde\mu([0,1])>0\},
\)
one has
\[
    \alpha_{\min}(\mu_\gamma)
    =
    A_{\mathrm{loc}}(W).
\]

 \]

[Theorem eraGcont of arXiv:2608.09856, '\bf Mass erasure on measured $\bbR$-trees,\\ applications to L\'evy forests'] Let ${\boldsymbol{\mu}}\! \equiv \! (T, d, \rho, \mu)$ and ${\boldsymbol{\mu}}_n \! \equiv \! (T_n, d_n , \rho_n, \mu_n)$, $n\! \in \!  \mathbb{N}$, 
belong to $\mathbb{T}$ (resp.~to $\mathbb{T}^1_{\! c}$). We assume that $\lim_{n\to \infty}{\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{\mathtt{GP}}({\boldsymbol{\mu}}_n, {\boldsymbol{\mu}})\! = \!  0 $ (resp.~that $\lim_{n\to \infty}{\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{\mathtt{GHP}}({\boldsymbol{\mu}}_n, {\boldsymbol{\mu}})\! = \!  0 $). Let $h\! \in \!  \mathbb{R}^*_+$. Then the following holds true. 
\begin{compactenum}

\smallskip

\item[$(i)$] $\sup_{h'\in [h, \infty)} {\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{\mathtt{GP}} ({\cal E}_{h'} {\boldsymbol{\mu}}_n
, {\cal E}_{h'} {\boldsymbol{\mu}}) \to 0$ as $n\! \to \! \infty$. 
 
 \smallskip
 
\item[$(ii)$] Let $(h_n)_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ be $\mathbb{R}^*_+$-valued and converging to $h\! \in \!  \mathbb{R}^*_+$. Let us assume that 
$h^\prime\!  \mapsto \! T_{\! \mu, h^\prime}$ is $d_{\mathtt{Haus}}$-continuous at $h$. Let us set $T^n_{\! \mu_n, h'}\! = \!  (T_n)_{\mu_n, h'}$ for all $h'\! \in \!  \mathbb{R}^*_+$. Then, 
\begin{align}

{\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{\mathtt{GHP}}\big( (T^n_{\! \mu_n, h_n} , d_n, \rho_n , {\cal E}_{h_n} \mu_n)\, &,\,  (T_{\! \mu , h}, d, \rho, {\cal E}_{h} \mu) \big) \longrightarrow 0 \\

 \textrm{and}\quad {\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{\mathtt{GHP}}\big( (T^n_{\! \mu_n, h_n} , d_n, \rho_n ,  \mathtt{P}_{T^n_{\! \mu_n, h_n}} \mu_n)\, &, \, (T_{\! \mu , h}, d, \rho, \mathtt{P}_{T_{\! \mu , h}} \mu) \big)  \longrightarrow 0\, . 
\end{align}
\item[$(iii)$] Let $(h_n)_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ be as in $(ii)$. Let us furthermore assume that $\mathtt{Supp}\,  \mu \! = \! T$ (by 
Proposition (massTprop of the paper) $(v)$, $h^\prime \! \mapsto \! T_{\! \mu, h^\prime}$ is therefore $d_{\mathtt{Haus}}$-continuous). 
Then, 
\begin{align}

\sup_{h^\prime\in [h, \infty) } {\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{\mathtt{GHP}}\big( (T^n_{\! \mu_n, h'} , d_n, \rho_n ,  {\cal E}_{h^\prime}\mu_n)\,&,(T_{\! \mu , h^\prime},  d, \rho, {\cal E}_{h^\prime} \mu) \big) \longrightarrow 0 \nonumber \\
 \textrm{and}  \quad \sup_{h^\prime\in [h, \infty) } {\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{\mathtt{GHP}}\big( (T^n_{\! \mu_n, h'} , d_n, \rho_n , \mathtt{P}_{T^n_{\! \mu_n, h'}} \mu_n)\, &,\,  (T_{\! \mu , h^\prime}, d, \rho, \mathtt{P}_{T_{\! \mu , h^\prime}} \mu) \big)  \longrightarrow 0\, . 
\end{align}
\item[$(iv)$] Let $\mathbf h\! = \!  (h^*_p)_{p\in \mathbb{N}}$ be $\mathbb{R}^*_+$-valued and strictly decreasing to $0$. Let us assume 
that $h\mapsto \! T_{\! \mu, h}$ is $d_{\mathtt{Haus}}$-continuous at each $h^*_p$, $p\! \in \!  \mathbb{N}$. 
Then ${\boldsymbol{\Lambda}}_{\mathbf h, {\boldsymbol{\mu}}_n} \!\!\!   \to \! {\boldsymbol{\Lambda}}_{\mathbf h, {\boldsymbol{\mu}}}$ weakly on $\mathcal{M}_f({\boldsymbol{\ell}}_\bullet^{\uparrow}(\mathbb{N}))$. 

\smallskip

\item[$(v)$] ${\boldsymbol{\lambda}}_{{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_n} \! \!\! \to \! {\boldsymbol{\lambda}}_{{\boldsymbol{\mu}}}$ weakly on $\mathcal{M}_{\! f} (\mathbb{R}_+)$. 
\end{compactenum} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem eraGcont of arXiv:2608.09856

[Defs 19 (Conditional absolute continuity) of arXiv:2509.06869, 'Infinite Interacting Brownian Motions and EVI Gradient Flows'] Let $\QP$ be a Borel probability on~$\U=\U(\R^n)$ and $\mssm_r$ be the Lebesgue measure restricted on $B_r=B_r(0)=\{x \in \R^n: |x|<r\}$.
We say that $\QP$

is \emph{conditionally absolutely continuous}  if 

\begin{equation}\tag*{$(\mathsf{CAC})_{\ref{d:ConditionalAC}}$}

 \QP^{\eta, k}_{r} \ll \mssm_{r}^{\odot k}  \quad r\in \N\comma \ k \in \N_0  \comma \  \QP\text{-a.e.~$\eta$}\comma
\end{equation}
where $\QP^{\eta, k}_{r} := \QP^{\eta}_{r}\mrestr{\U^k(B_r)}$ is the restriction of~$\QP^{\eta}_{r}$ in the $k$-particle configuration space~$\U^k(B_r)$.
title: Conditional absolute continuity

[Prop 16 of arXiv:2604.03206, 'The extreme statistics of some noncolliding Brownian processes'] Let $BLPP(0; (t,m)) = \max_{0\leq t_0 \leq t_1 \leq \cdots \leq t_m = t} \sum_{k=1}^m B^{\mu}_k(t_k) - B^{\mu}_k(t_{k-1})$
    where $B^{\mu}_k$ are independent Brownian motions with drift $\mu_k$. Then, for $m \geq 1$ and $0 < t_1 < \cdots < t_k$,
    $$ \mathbf{Pr}(BLPP(0; (t_i,m)) \leq a_i, 1 \leq i \leq k) = \det(I -\chi_a K \chi_a)_{L^2(\{t_1,\ldots, t_k\}\times \R)}$$
    where
    $$ K(t_i,x;t_j,y) = - e^{(t_j-t_i)\partial^2/2}\ind{t_i < t_j} + K_{flat}(t_i,x;t_j,y)$$
    with $K_{flat}$ given by \eqref{eqn:Kflat} and $\chi_a(t_i,x) = \ind{x \geq a_i}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Prop 16 of arXiv:2604.03206

[Theorem 4 of arXiv:2604.22637, '2604.22637'] For $t\geq 0$, the generating function of
$
  E[e^{-t\sum_{i=1}^n X_i}]
$
is given by
\begin{align}
    \sum_{n=0}^\infty E[e^{-t\sum_{i=1}^n X_i}]z^n 
    = \frac{1}{1 - z(1-p)e^{-t}} \exp\left( \int_0^1 \frac{p z e^{-ts}}{1 - z(1-ps)e^{-ts}} \, ds \right).
\end{align}
title: Theorem 4 of arXiv:2604.22637

[Lemma 6 (Recovery in the limit $\varphi\to1$) of arXiv:2604.20634, 'Distributional Statistical Models:\\ \large Weak Moments, Cumulants, and a Central Limit T'] Let $f\in L^1(\R)$ and let $\psi$ be measurable with $\psi f\in L^1(\R)$.
Fix $\rho\in\mathcal{S}(\R)$ with $0\le\rho\le1$ and $\rho(0)=1$ (for
instance $\rho(x)=e^{-x^2/2}$), and set $\varphi_\varepsilon(x):=\rho(\varepsilon x)$
for $\varepsilon>0$.  Then $\varphi_\varepsilon\in\mathcal{S}(\R)$,
$\varphi_\varepsilon>0$, $\varphi_\varepsilon\to1$ pointwise as
$\varepsilon\downarrow0$, and
\[
\E_{T_f,\varphi_\varepsilon}[\psi]
=\int_\R \psi(x)\varphi_\varepsilon(x)f(x)\,dx
\;\xrightarrow[\varepsilon\downarrow0]{}\;
\int_\R\psi(x)f(x)\,dx .
\]
In particular, $\psi(x)=x^n$ recovers the ordinary $n$-th moment whenever it
exists, and $\psi(x)=e^{itx}$ recovers the classical characteristic function
for every $t\in\R$.

body: In mathematics, Abelian and Tauberian theorems are theorems giving conditions for two methods of summing divergent series to give the same result, named after Niels Henrik Abel and Alfred Tauber. The original examples are Abel's theorem showing that if a series converges to some limit then its Abel sum is the same limit, and Tauber's theorem showing that if the Abel sum of a series exists and the coefficients are sufficiently small then the series converges to the Abel sum. More general Abelian and Tauberian theorems give similar results for more general summation methods.
title: Abelian and Tauberian theorems

Let $\Sigma$ be a symmetric positive semidefinite $M \times M$ matrix (the true, out-of-sample covariance) and $\hat\Sigma$ any symmetric estimate, with entrywise error $\varepsilon := \max_{i,j} |\hat\Sigma_{ij} - \Sigma_{ij}|$. For $c \ge 1$ let $\mathcal{W}_c = \{w : \mathbf{1}^T w = 1,\ \|w\|_1 \le c\}$, let $\hat w \in \arg\min_{w \in \mathcal{W}_c} w^T \hat\Sigma w$ and $w^* \in \arg\min_{w \in \mathcal{W}_c} w^T \Sigma w$. Then (i) $|w^T(\hat\Sigma - \Sigma)w| \le \varepsilon\, c^2$ for every $w \in \mathcal{W}_c$, and (ii) $0 \le \hat w^T \Sigma \hat w - w^{*T}\Sigma w^* \le 2\varepsilon c^2$. The long-only simplex is the case $c = 1$: the out-of-sample risk of the long-only plug-in exceeds the long-only oracle's by at most $2\varepsilon$, whatever the conditioning of $\Sigma$ or $\hat\Sigma$ and whatever the ratio $M/n$. If $\hat\Sigma$ is the sample covariance of $n$ independent cases with sub-Gaussian coordinates, a union bound over the $M(M+1)/2$ entries gives $\varepsilon = O_p(\sqrt{\log M / n})$, so the excess risk is $O_p(\sqrt{\log M/n})$ - against the unconstrained plug-in, whose risk inflation $1/(1 - M/n)$ (Pafka-Kondor, Gaussian, well-conditioned case) grows with $M/n$ and which is unbounded when $\hat\Sigma$ has a near-null direction that $\Sigma$ does not.
Sigma symmetric positive semidefinite; Sigma_hat symmetric (not necessarily PSD)
the tail bound: n independent cases with sub-Gaussian coordinates (bounded errors suffice)
the feasible set W_c is compact and nonempty (it contains every vertex of the simplex)

\begin{equation}
 U_k(z)\in
 \mathfrak m_{d,s}^{\,N_{d,s}(k)},
 \qquad
 N_{d,s}(k)=
 \#\{0\le j<k:j\equiv s\pmod{d^\sharp}\}.
\end{equation}
In particular,
\begin{equation}
 N_{d,s}(k)\ge\left\lfloor\frac{k}{d^\sharp}\right\rfloor,
 \qquad
 \ord_{\mathfrak m_{d,s}}U_k(z)\longrightarrow\infty.
\end{equation}

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Reduce to the multiplicative-coalescent limit of the critical window plus the MST construction from the coalescent. Result: On the complete graph the MST limit is built from the scaling limit of the critical Erdos-Renyi components (as metric spaces) glued along the multiplicative coalescent; the same construction on the torus would follow from (i) C0071 upgraded to metric-space (Gromov-Hausdorff-Prokhorov) convergence of the window clusters, and (ii) the coalescent dynamics of the clusters as p increases through the window, i.e. that clusters merge at rate proportional to the product of their sizes, which is the mean-field merging rule and requires the merged clusters to be 'spread out' (same mechanism as in C0071: clusters wrap around the torus in d > 6 so their mutual boundary is proportional to the product of sizes). So Open Problem 16.4 is the metric upgrade of C0071 plus the wrapping-based merging rule; both are open, and the constant multiple would be determined by the variance v of the local branching structure. Obstruction: Metric-space convergence of window clusters and the product merging rule are unproved on the torus.

\[
\pi_\lambda^{\mathrm{MF2}}(q > 0)
\leq
\pi_\lambda(q > 0)
\leq
\pi_\lambda^{\mathrm{MF1}}(q > 0).
\]
In particular, Mean-Field 1 overestimates the busy probability, whereas Mean-Field 2 underestimates it. (Stated as a conjecture by the paper; open unless the paper says otherwise.)
title: Comparison between the True system and the Mean-Field approximations

[Thm 18 (\Cref{thm: restate of window growing m} in the text) of arXiv:2603.27433, 'The $k$-cycle shuffling with repeated cards'] Let \(n=ml\), such that \(l=\omega(1)\) but \(l=o(\log n)\). Suppose \(2\le k\le n^{c_0+o(1)}\), where \(c_0\in[0,1)\) is an absolute constant, and
$$
t=\frac nk\left(\log n-\frac 12\log l+c\right),
$$
where \(c\in \R\) is an absolute constant. Then, we have
$$
d_{TV}(\sim_l\backslash P_{n,k}^{*t},\sim_l\backslash U_{\S_n})
=
2\Phi(\exp(-c)/2)-1+o(1).
$$
Here, \(\Phi(x):=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^x\exp(-y^2/2)\,dy\) denotes the cumulative distribution function of the normal distribution \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: \Cref{thm: restate of window growing m} in the text

body:
[Lemma lem:uniform-small-kernel-chaos of arXiv:2606.21006, 'Law of the Iterated Logarithm for Weighted Sums of Functionals of Long-Memory Gaussian Seq'] Let \(K_{n,t}\in\mathfrak H_{\mathbb R}^{\odot m}\), \(0\le t\le T\), be deterministic
kernels. Assume that, for some \(C_T<\infty\), \(\beta>0\), and \(\eta>0\),
\[
    \sup_{0\le t\le T}\|K_{n,t}\|_2\le\eta,
    \qquad
    \|K_{n,t}-K_{n,s}\|_2^2\le C_T|t-s|^\beta
    \qquad 0\le s,t\le T .
\]
Let \(L_n:=2\log\log n\), and let \(n_k\) be an increasing sequence such that
\(L_{n_k}\ge c_0\log k\) for all sufficiently large \(k\), with some \(c_0>0\). Then for every
\(\delta>0\) there exists \(\eta_0=\eta_0(\delta,T,m,\beta,C_T,c_0)>0\) such that, if
\(\eta\le\eta_0\), then
\[
    \sum_{k=1}^\infty
    \mathbb P\left(
        \sup_{0\le t\le T}|I_m(K_{n_k,t};W_{n_k})|>
        \delta L_{n_k}^{m/2}
    \right)<\infty .
\]
Consequently,
\[
    \limsup_{k\to\infty}
    \sup_{0\le t\le T}
    \frac{|I_m(K_{n_k,t};W_{n_k})|}{L_{n_k}^{m/2}}
    \le\delta
    \qquad\text{\rm a.s.}
\]

[Prop Harmonicity for the killed semigroup of arXiv:2606.06187, 'How to Study Reflected Brownian Motion in a Quadrant via Kernel Functional Equations?\\ \m'] For all $t\ge0$,
\[
h^\infty = P_t^\dagger h^\infty,
\qquad
h^0 \ge P_t^\dagger h^0,
\]
i.e. $h^\infty$ is harmonic and $h^0$ is superharmonic for the killed
(sub-Markov) semigroup.

$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

\[
    d=d_H^{\mathrm{pr}}(A_0,A_1).
\]
If a random compact correspondence $\widehat C$ has coverage at least
$1-\alpha$ at both parameter values, then
\begin{equation}
    \mathbb E_{\xi_0}
    \operatorname{diam}_{\mathrm{pr}}(\widehat C)
    \ge
    d\left[
        1-2\alpha
        -
        \operatorname{TV}
        \left(
            \mathbb P_{\xi_0}^{N,T},
            \mathbb P_{\xi_1}^{N,T}
        \right)
    \right]_+ .
    
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Defin 1 (Empirical measure) of arXiv:2604.00635, 'Large deviations of the periodic Toda chain'] Given a vector $\bs{x}_N \in \mathbb{R}^N$, the associated empirical measure corresponds to

\begin{align}

\op{L}_N^{(\bs{x}_N)} \overset{\mathrm{def}}{=} \frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^N \delta_{x_i} \, .

\end{align}

Note that the map $\iota : \mathbb{R}^N \to \mathcal{M}_1(\mathbb{R})$, $\iota(\bs{x}_N) := \op{L}_N^{(\bs{x}_N)}$ is continuous.
In particular this means that if $E \subset \mathcal{M}_1(\mathbb{R})$ is a Borel set then
$\iota^{-1}(E) = \big\{ \bs{x}_N \in \mathbb{R}^N \, : \, \op{L}_N^{(\bs{x}_N)} \in E \big\}$ is a Borel set.
title: Empirical measure

Denote $\boldsymbol{\Sigma} \coloneqq \sum^n_{i=1}  \E\left[\mathbf{X}^2_i \middle| \mathscr{F}_{i-1}\right].$ Then for any $t \ge \frac{1}{6}(K + \sqrt{K^2 + 36\sigma^2})$,
    \[
    \mathbb{P}\lr{\norm*{\sum^n_{i=1} \mathbf{X}_i} > t, ~\lambda_{\max}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}) \le \sigma^2}
    \le 50\tr\lr{\min\lrc{1, \frac{t}{K}\frac{\E\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}{\sigma^2}}}\exp\lr{-\frac{t^2/2}{\sigma^2 + \frac{tK}{3}}}.
    \] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

G_N(x_1,\ldots,x_N;\beta)=\prod_{i=1}^{N}\left(1-\frac{2x_{i}}{\beta}\right)^{-L\beta/2}.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Proposition 10 (Symmetry of the burglars laws) of arXiv:2609.03968, 'A one-parameter family of local-time conditioned processes : the generalized Brownian burg'] Let $\lambda$ be an admissible capacity on an interval $I$, and let $\tilde \lambda$ be the symmetric capacity, i.e.\ $\tilde \lambda (x)= \lambda(-x)$ for $x\in-I$. [Theorem thm:density-bound of arXiv:2607.25616, 'Stealthy point processes and lattice induction'] Let $\eta$ be a translation-invariant point process of
intensity $\rho$. Suppose that, for some $r>0$, the process is
supported on $r$-separated configurations. Then
\[
    \sigma_\eta(\Omega)=0
    \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
    \rho\geq\mathcal D(\Omega)
\]
for every open neighborhood $\Omega$ of the origin. In particular,
if $C\subset\Omega$ is a symmetric convex body, then
\[
    \rho\geq2^{-d}\lambda_d(C).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Its sixth Maclaurin coefficient is (61*pi-192)/(240*pi)<0, using pi<22/7. Therefore f cannot have all positive power coefficients in the displayed distance variable u. A different intended expansion variable would require source clarification. This does not refute the separately proved normalized-hole monotonicity or the odd-dimensional polynomial assertion.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:2d14dff23ed67bea8ee6e9a336404434b1f65c6c49ba51c5064e551c4fbdff28","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/2d/2d14dff23ed67bea8ee6e9a336404434b1f65c6c49ba51c5064e551c4fbdff28.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:ac94520dd14667574818c4e5bdd7d6df7d8846c54fdf5cf64184077d7f769f36","bundle_entry_key":"even","bundle_id":"population.probability-hole-coefficient-and-forkjoin-partials-008","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"probability theory","draft":"codex-probability-01a07a40/bundle_008.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.geometry:ideal-voronoi-even-positive-series-sixth-coefficient-obstruction","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Boundary-hole monotonicity and the odd-dimensional polynomial

Status: private author-checked partial candidate. No independent review, no novelty certification, and no claim that the whole source conjecture is solved.

Source: D'Achille, Curien, Enriquez, Lyons and Unel, *Ideal Poisson--Voronoi tessellations on hyperbolic spaces*, archived as `ideal_voronoi_2023`, Proposition 5.1 and equation (5.1), PDF35; Conjecture 7.5, PDF48. The source already computes the dimension-three formula and observes rationality in odd dimensions. Those facts are credited. The claims attempted here are the all-dimensional monotonicity and positive coefficients in every odd dimension. The final addendum gives a candidate counterexample to the even-dimensional positive-power-series clause in its displayed distance variable.

## Exact starting identity

Let $n=d-1\ge1$ and let $H_d(u)$ be the probability that the hyperbolic ball of radius $u\ge0$ about the origin lies inside its ideal Voronoi cell. Write $J_d(u)=1/H_d(u)$. Equation (5.1) and Proposition 5.1 give

$$
J_d(u)=\frac1{c_d}\int_{\mathbb R^n}
\left(\sqrt{\cosh^2u+|x|^2}-\sinh u\right)^{-2n}\,dx,
\qquad
c_d=\frac{\pi^{n/2}\Gamma(n/2)}{\Gamma(n)}.
$$

The normalization follows independently by setting $u=0$ and integrating $(1+|x|^2)^{-n}$ in polar coordinates. In particular $J_d(0)=1$.

## Monotonicity in every dimension

Set $q=e^{2u}$ and substitute $x=e^{-u}z$. Then

$$
e^{-nu}J_d(u)=\frac1{c_d}\int_{\mathbb R^n}D_q(z)^{-2n}\,dz,
\qquad
D_q(z)=\sqrt{(q+1)^2/4+|z|^2}-(q-1)/2.
$$

The denominator is positive. For $z\ne0$,

$$
\frac{\partial D_q(z)}{\partial q}
=\frac{q+1}{4\sqrt{(q+1)^2/4+|z|^2}}-\frac12<0.
$$

Thus the integrand strictly increases with $q$ away from a null set. All integrals are finite by the exact source identity. Pointwise comparison of two values of $q$ proves that $e^{-nu}J_d(u)$ is strictly increasing; no interchange of differentiation and integration is needed. Taking reciprocals proves

$$
u\longmapsto e^{(d-1)u}H_d(u)
\quad\hbox{is strictly decreasing on }[0,\infty).
$$

The strictness follows because the difference of the positive finite integrands is strictly positive on a set of positive Lebesgue measure.

## Positive rational polynomial for odd dimensions

Let $d=2m+1$, so $n=2m$, with integer $m\ge1$. Put $a=e^{-u}$ and $s=\sinh u=(a^{-1}-a)/2$. In the radial integral make the substitution

$$
y=\sqrt{\cosh^2u+r^2}-s.
$$

Its lower endpoint is $a$, and

$$
r^2=(y-a)(y+a^{-1}),\qquad r\,dr=(y+s)\,dy.
$$

After setting $y=az$, the exact integral becomes

$$
J_{2m+1}(u)=C_m a^{-4m}
\int_1^\infty (z-1)^{m-1}(a^2z+1)^{m-1}
\bigl[a^2(2z-1)+1\bigr]z^{-4m}\,dz,
\qquad C_m=\frac{\Gamma(2m)}{\Gamma(m)^2}.
$$

Here the factor $C_m$ is half the ratio of the $(2m-1)$-sphere area to $c_d$. Expand the two bracketed factors as a polynomial in $a^2$. Every coefficient is a strictly positive integrable function of $z>1$: the only apparent subtraction is $2z-1$, which is positive on this domain. The degree is exactly $m$. The resulting integrals are rational because expanding $(z-1)^{m-1}$ reduces them to finite sums of powers of $z$ with integer exponents at most $-2$.

For an explicit formula, let $B$ denote the beta function, and interpret binomial coefficients outside $0,\ldots,m-1$ as zero. Define, for $0\le j\le m$,

$$
b_{m,j}=\binom{m-1}{j}B(3m-j,m)
+\binom{m-1}{j-1}\left[2B(3m-j,m)-B(3m-j+1,m)\right].
$$

This follows from $\int_1^\infty(z-1)^{m-1}z^{j-4m}\,dz=B(3m-j,m)$. All beta arguments are positive integers. Moreover $B(A+1,m)<B(A,m)$, so each displayed coefficient is positive. Hence

$$
p_m(q)=C_m\sum_{j=0}^m b_{m,j}q^{m-j}
$$

is a degree-$m$ polynomial with strictly positive rational coefficients, and

$$
H_{2m+1}(u)=\frac{e^{-2mu}}{p_m(e^{2u})}.
$$

The normalization gives $p_m(1)=1$. The first two cases are

$$
p_1(q)=\frac{q+2}{3},\qquad
p_2(q)=\frac{q^2}{7}+\frac{16q}{35}+\frac25.
$$

The first reproduces the already-known dimension-three formula in Remark 5.2. It is a control, not a newly solved special case.

## An additional odd-dimensional consequence

The polynomial representation makes $J_d(u)$ a positive sum of exponentials with rates in $[n,2n]$. Let $L=\log J_d$. Under the exponential weights, $L'$ is the mean rate and $L''$ its variance. Therefore $L'\ge n$ and $L''\le n^2/4$. The density $f=-H_d'=H_dL'$ satisfies

$$
f'=H_d\bigl(L''-(L')^2\bigr)<0.
$$

This proves the source's proposed decreasing-density property in odd dimensions. It also implies that the median is smaller than the mean. For completeness, if $M>0$ is the median and $v=f(M)>0$, convexity of the survival function gives

$$
H_d(x)\ge\max\{1/2-v(x-M),0\},\qquad x\ge0.
$$

Integrating yields $E X\ge(1/2+vM)^2/(2v)\ge M$, since the difference in the last inequality is $(vM-1/2)^2/(2v)$. Strict convexity makes the first inequality strict on a positive-length interval. The mean is finite by the source exponential tail bound.

## Adversarial checks and remaining gap

The load-bearing points to try to break are the factor from the radial Jacobian, the power $a^{-4m}$, and the distinction between polynomial positivity in $q=e^{2u}$ and power-series positivity in $u$. The check script compares the beta coefficients with an independent expansion and exact integration of the radial polynomial. It also compares the resulting formula with the original angular integral in Proposition 5.1, including even dimensions for the separate monotonicity calculation.

The even-dimensional positive-power-series assertion is not implied by monotonicity. The addendum below supplies a candidate counterexample to that clause in dimension two. No independent referee has checked this packet, and the bounded literature search is not a novelty certificate. Other even-dimensional density and median claims remain unproved here, so this grouped entry retains its partial-candidate classification.

## Addendum: a negative sixth coefficient in dimension two

Author-checked candidate counterexample, 2026-09-07. This uses the source's displayed distance variable $u$ and interprets "power series" as a convergent series in nonnegative integer powers of $u$ about zero. It makes no claim about series in a different variable.

The source's Remark 5.2, equation (5.2), credits its dimension-two formula to earlier work. We do not claim that formula as new:

$$H_2(u)=\frac{\pi}{4\arctan(e^u)\cosh^2u+2\sinh u}.$$

Conjecture 7.5 would require $H_2(u)=e^{-u}/f(u)$ with positive power-series coefficients. Thus $f$ is uniquely determined near zero by

$$f(u)=\frac{(e^u+2e^{-u}+e^{-3u})A(u)+1-e^{-2u}}{\pi},\qquad A(u)=\arctan(e^u).$$

Since $A(0)=\pi/4$ and $A'(u)=1/(2\cosh u)$,

$$A(u)=\frac\pi4+\frac u2-\frac{u^3}{12}+\frac{u^5}{48}+O(u^7).$$

Put $E(u)=e^u+2e^{-u}+e^{-3u}$. The coefficients needed for degree six are $[u^6]E=61/60$, $[u^5]E=-61/30$, $[u^3]E=-14/3$, and $[u]E=-4$. Consequently,

$$[u^6]f(u)=\frac{61}{240}+\frac1\pi\left(-\frac{61}{60}+\frac7{18}-\frac1{12}-\frac4{45}\right)=\frac{61\pi-192}{240\pi}<0.$$

The sign is exact: $\pi<22/7$ gives $61\pi-192<-2/7$. Numerically the coefficient is approximately $-0.000481242280365871$. A function analytic at zero has unique power-series coefficients, so no alternative positive-coefficient series in the same variable can represent this $f$ near zero. This contradicts the stated even-dimensional coefficient clause already at $d=2$.

### Checks and strongest alternative explanation

The coefficient was obtained by exact rational convolution using the recurrence for the reciprocal of $\cosh u$, by high-precision differentiation of the closed formula, and by Cauchy coefficient extraction directly from the original angular integral of Proposition 5.1. The last lane avoids the closed arctangent formula. Reproduction: `check_IPVT_even_coefficients.py`; receipt: `IPVT_even_coefficient_checks.json`.

The strongest interpretation risk is that the authors intended a series in another transformed variable or a different normalization. The archived conjecture writes $f(u)$ in the distance variable and specifies no alternative. The calculation refutes that literal Maclaurin-series clause; it does not refute monotonicity, the odd-dimensional formula, or every possible reformulation. A source clarification or corrected conjecture could change the disposition. The dimension-two hole formula itself is already known; novelty of this coefficient observation has not been established.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:a619d7dacb1a00e81c0fd7880a8238307c0094169dc2d53c70b64cc661abaf09","revision_digest":"sha256:c1961fa2491f341743425430edd8f3e4bccdd8e05c43d796942552a023e45de0","source_id":"owner-probability-exposition-20260907:even","source_revision":"author-checked-private-20260907-v1","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}
title: Dimension two obstruction to the literal positive-series ideal Voronoi hole conjecture
